title: Tri-oxo-triangulene is a polyfunctional catalyst of sequential red-green-blue photoredox systems

text:
Abstract Photocatalysis remains a crucial field to investigate. It is seen as a powerful tool which allows more efficient, relatively greener and economical chemical reactions. Nevertheless, catalysts usually include rare and pricy metals, with supplies being highly dependent on geopolitics. Thus, chemists turned their attention to alternatives such as natural products or organic molecules, conciliating performances, polyvalence and easy access. Among the promising candidates, polyaromatics rise as robust species and precursors of stable radicals which could be used as photocatalysts. Triangulenes are polycyclic hydrocarbons which are expected to shine in multiple fields such as spintronics, energy and data storage or semiconductors. This work reports the studies of photocatalytic reactions including the trioxotriangulene (TOT). Through the studies of three reactions ranging from sulfoxidation to dehalogenation of 4-bromoacetophenone, including the reduction of nitroaromatics, we discuss the performances, the polyvalence and the mechanism of the systems including this triangulene. As a proof of concept, we conclude this work with a description of “a sequential RBG photoredox catalytic system” where the three reactions are successively and selectively performed in a “one-pot” fashion.
A single tri-oxo-triangulene photocatalyst enables wavelength-controlled oxidation and reduction chemistry, allowing sequential red-, green-, and blue-light photoredox reactions in one pot.

title: Tri-oxo-triangulene is a polyfunctional catalyst of sequential red-green-blue photoredox systems

text:
Photochemistry is a valuable tool in organic synthesis 1,2 because it allows desired molecules to be specifically targeted by matching irradiation wavelength to their vertical electronic transitions. Visible-light photochemistry is particularly attractive for sustainable applications; 3 however, most organic molecules have low or even zero absorbance in the 400-700 nm region. Photocatalysis addresses this gap by employing visible light-absorbing catalysts which in their excited states induce the intended transformations. 4 The catalyst transforms absorbed photons via different processes, e.g. (i) photosensitization, leading to direct energy transfer from the catalyst to the substrate, or (ii) single-electron transfer (SET).
Reduction and oxidation are the most employed reactions which can be performed photochemically using photoredox catalysts. Examples of such compounds reported in the literature 5-7 range from metals 8 to porphyrins 9 or ruthenium-based 10 complexes. While these compounds already demonstrated good performance, they include critical raw materials, often toxic or rare and expensive transition metals. Purely organic photoredox catalysts such as flavines 11 can provide a solution to most of these challenges and thus allow efficient and cleaner syntheses. However, they have inherent limitations such as chemical sensitivity due to their functional groups and chemical structure. Furthermore, reported photoredox catalysts are usually specific for a particular transformation, such as photoreduction under a certain redox potential, and cannot be used for a different process without extensive structural modifications. Thus, finding a robust, multipurpose and readily available organic photocatalyst remains an actual challenge in photochemistry.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons 12 (PAHs) are attractive potential photoredox catalysts. Their conjugated structure enhances stability, and their optical properties can be tuned by electron donating/accepting groups. Triangulene 13 and its derivatives are great examples of polybenzenoid molecules belonging to this class of compounds. Triangulene was first theorized by Clar in 1953 and proposed as a diradical non-Kékulé structure. In accordance with Ovchinnikov's rule 33 and Lieb's theorem, 34 this diradical displays a triplet ground state. At a supramolecular level, triangulene derivatives stack into a “pancake”-type π-π stacking 14 and the molecule's flat geometry leads to limited solubility and aggregation behavior. Since triangulenes were already studied for organic batteries, 15,16 they were also hypothesized to find applications 17,18 not only in spintronics, organic semi-conductors, and magnetic materials, but also in photocatalysis. 12-Hydroxydibenzo[cd,mn]pyrene-4,8-dione ( TOTH ) is one of the smallest derivatives of triangulene. 19 This molecule carries one hydroxyl and two carbonyl groups at the three edges. While the diradical is known to be highly reactive, the monoradical tri-oxo-triangulene ( TOT ) 20 is described to be very stable even in the presence of oxygen. These properties, in addition to the TOTH broad absorption profile in the visible region and the recently published 21 gram-scale synthesis, make it a very attractive candidate for photoredox catalysis. Even if TOT has been already used in redox catalysis for the reduction of oxygen, 22 no example of photocatalysis including triangulenes has been reported in the literature to the best of our knowledge and thus, their potential remains unexplored.
In this work, we report the first example of photoredox catalysis with TOTH and its active redox states. Several accessible redox states of TOTH allow it to engage in: 1) photooxidation of tetrahydrofuran (THF), 2) selective sulfoxidation of thioanisole and 3) photoreduction with a single catalyst precursor 23 even up to the challenging reductive dehalogenation of 4-bromoacetophenone. We show that by tuning the conditions, i.e. , irradiation wavelength and the presence of sacrificial electron donors, we can kinetically favor chosen reactions to achieve reaction selectivity. Moreover, these reactions can even be performed sequentially in a “one-pot” fashion only by adjustment of conditions. We discuss the mechanism of TOTH transformations under light irradiation, and we propose mechanisms of photoredox catalytic cycles.

title: Tri-oxo-triangulene is a polyfunctional catalyst of sequential red-green-blue photoredox systems

text:
TOTH was synthesized according to the procedure published in 2019 by Ribar et al. 21 This compound is obtained as a deep blue powder well soluble in concentrated sulfuric acid (96%) or N , N -dimethylformamide (DMF) but poorly soluble in other solvents. TOTH was reported to adopt several redox/acidobasic states. 14 The acidic phenolic OH-group can be deprotonated by amines, e.g. , triethylamine (Et 3 N), which dramatically improves the solubility ( Fig. 1 ). This can be explained by the coulombic repulsion of generated anions disrupting aggregation via the π-π stacking.
The absorption spectra recorded in concentrated sulfuric acid (96%) exhibit a maximum absorption in the UV region (350 nm) as well as a broad band in the range of 500-630 nm, giving the solution a deep purple color. Similarly, in THF, the solution appears purple too, but the solubility is more limited, and the solution is quickly saturated. The absorption in THF is also broader with new absorption bands between 500 and 400 nm. Interestingly, the emission profile varies depending on the excitation wavelength used which indicates that the solution is a mixture of species. When TOTH is deprotonated by the addition of Et 3 N to THF or dissolved in DMF, the solution turns a clear light blue color, and the UV-vis spectra demonstrate an absorption shift towards higher wavelengths both in the UV and visible regions of the spectrum. Neutral solution in THF features red luminescence, similar to H 2 SO 4 solution, but the luminescence is no longer perceptible by the eyes upon deprotonation.
TOTH can be electrochemically converted in up to three redox states. 14 Cyclic voltammetry was performed in dry and degassed DMF with a Pt mesh as the working electrode and Ag/AgCl as the pseudo reference electrode calibrated with Fc/Fc + ( E 1/2 [Fc/Fc + ] = 0.4 V). The voltammogram (Fig. S1) showed reversible oxidation to neutral radical form TOT at 0.44 V. A reduction wave of TOTH is observed at -1.64 V to give the corresponding radical anion TOTH - ˙ . A second reduction wave follows at -2.1 V to give diradical anion TOTH 2 - ˙˙ , in which the two ketyl radicals cannot recombine. All these redox steps are reversible (Fig. S1), although consecutive voltammograms exhibit changes due to electroplating of TOTH on the electrode caused by a local change of pH upon solvent/residual water electrolysis. The third reduction wave overlaps with the solvent background but is clearly visible by square-wave voltammetry (Fig. S1b) at around -3.0 V and is irreversible. It must be noted that all redox states of TOTH are subject to acidobasic equilibria with their (de)protonated forms. In this way, neutral TOTH can deprotonate to TOT - ( Fig. 1 ). These equilibria prohibit the formation of polyanionic species during the catalytic process.
Spectro electrochemical investigation was performed by recording UV-vis absorption spectra during chronoamperometry set at defined potential values (Fig. S2). At a potential of -1.6 V, TOTH absorption features do not change significantly, and only weak bands develop between 390 and 500 nm as well as at around 730 nm. When a potential of -2.1 V is applied, the characteristic absorption peaks of TOT - at 360, 600, and 660 nm decrease and new absorption features develop in the whole visible region and at 310 nm; the spectral changes observed at -1.6 V are also present at the potential of -2.1 V.
The abundance of various TOTH redox states and their absorbance prompted us to perform EPR spectroscopy. A solution of TOTH in DMF did not show any signal; however, when it was irradiated with light, a strong and well-resolved signal was observable ( Fig. 3 ). The signal matches with a triple-folded symmetrical structure as expected for the neutral radical TOT (Fig. S3). This was observed regardless of whether the sample was irradiated with a red LED (620-625 nm) - where TOTH absorbs strongly - or a blue LED (440-450 nm) - where DMF solution shows negligible absorbance. The radical demonstrates remarkable stability as the signal does not show any decay after several minutes of measurement even in the presence of oxygen. Importantly, when the experiment was repeated in the presence of Et 3 N, no signal was observed under irradiation (440-450 or 620-625 nm).
Upon irradiation, neutral TOTH undergoes disproportionation to give TOT and TOTH - ˙ . The radical anion then dimerizes to TOT 2 H 2 by a ketyl mechanism, similar to the well-known benzophenone photochemical dimerization. 24,25 Traces of this dimer are detected by mass spectrometry (see Fig. S4). This reaction also explains gradual decolorization or color change observed in photocatalytic runs by disruption of conjugation of two TOTH units. In the presence of Et 3 N, the redox potential of the radical matches that of the amine, enabling single electron transfer (SET) between them. This process regenerates TOTH , while Et 3 N serves as a sacrificial electron donor and is oxidized to a radical cation. This then undergoes H abstraction to ultimately give iminium, which is hydrolyzed to diethylamine and acetaldehyde, both detected by GC-MS (Fig. S5) and NMR (Fig. S12) experiments. The TOT 2 H 2 dimer reacts further, either by second ketyl dimerization or supramolecular stacking, to give large aggregates evidenced by the appearance of the Tyndall effect (Fig. S6a). These aggregates were further confirmed by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Fig. S6b) and dynamic light scattering (DLS, Fig. S7, right). On the other hand, gel permeation chromatography (GPC) did not identify any species of molecular weight <700 g mol -1 (Fig. S7, left). This suggests that the dimer further aggregates non-covalently, e.g. by π-π stacking, and these aggregates disintegrate during the GPC separation on the column. Altogether, TOTH features several accessible photoactive redox states, which confirms its high potential for photoredox catalysis ( Fig. 2 ).
TOTH disproportionation upon irradiation opens the way to use it in photoredox catalysis. Three benchmark reactions were considered in this regard: photosulfoxidation of thioanisole to sulfoxide, nitro-group reduction, and reductive dehalogenation of 4-bromoacetophenone. Preliminary studies showed that, from the selected benchmark reactions, the deep-potential reductive dehalogenation of 4-bromoacetophenone is the most sensitive to reaction conditions ( e.g. oxygen). We have thus investigated the influence of varying reaction conditions on the yield ( Table 1 ).
Solvent choice influences the TOTH solubility and hence the course of all catalytic reactions. Altogether, seven common organic solvents were tested (entries 1-5, 7 and 12 in Table 1 ). While no conversion was observed in aromatic solvents (toluene and pyridine), a gradually increasing yield was observed in the series of acetonitrile (ACN), dichloromethane, ethanol, THF, and DMF, well corresponding with TOTH solubility in these solvents. The solvent choice influences the color and therefore the absorption spectrum. Moreover, some solvents were found non-innocent during the photocatalytic runs, e.g. , formation of γ-butyrolactone in THF mixtures after irradiation was confirmed by NMR and GC-MS (Fig. S9 & S10), which demonstrates that the TOTH acts as an oxidant. In fact, when pyridine or ACN was employed as a solvent, a very complex pattern of solvent-associated signals was recorded by 1 H NMR after photocatalytic runs (Fig. S8, S11 and S12).
The presence of atmospheric oxygen is detrimental to the reductive dehalogenation and no conversion under an ambient atmosphere was detected ( Table 1 , entry 6). On the other hand, simple argon purging of the solution for 5 minutes is sufficient to reach 28% yield in 12 hours in THF, which only negligibly increases to 30% if a thorough freeze-pump-thaw degassing procedure is employed ( Table 1 , entries 7 & 8).
Irradiation wavelength strongly affects the obtained conversion. More energetic light provided higher yields consistently in all tested solvents and 450 nm irradiation was the energetic threshold at which the reaction proceeded at convenient rates. An increase of the photon energy by 0.27 eV ( i.e. , 410 nm) provided doubled yields at the same reaction times ( Table 1 , entries 8 and 10); however, this is due to the contribution of a non-catalyzed photochemical reaction (see also below). No conversion was detected when the reaction was irradiated with a 625 nm LED or when the reaction was performed without irradiation at all ( Table 1 , entries 11 and 13). An almost quantitative yield of acetophenone is obtained after two days of irradiation at 440-450 nm. Therefore, the solvent plays a significant role as the obtained yields significantly vary from one to another ( Table 1 , entries 7 and 12).
During bromoacetophenone reduction, electrons are provided by a sacrificial electron donor. Although solvents such as THF can be oxidized by TOT to regenerate initial TOTH , this process is more efficient when amines such as Et 3 N are added. The amount of added Et 3 N plays a role and highest yields are achieved when 4-8 equivalents vs. bromoacetophenone are added. Further increase of sacrificial electron donor concentration leads to a drop of catalytic activity, presumably due to the shift of acidobasic equilibria of different TOTH oxidation states ( Fig. 2 ).
The TOT catalyst loading was investigated ( Fig. 5 ). Interestingly, a sharp maximum of catalytic activity was observed with a concentration of 0.1 g L -1 (1-2% mol with respect to the substrate). Such an efficiency peak suggests that supramolecular aggregation of the catalyst in its redox states occurs, as also evidenced by AFM, DLS, etc. (see above). At 2.5 × 10 -4 mol L -1 level, the concentration of catalytically active species is the highest, while at higher catalyst loadings, large-scale aggregation prevails leading to a decrease of catalytic activity.
The well-known thioanisole photosulfoxidation to methyl(phenyl)sulfoxide was chosen as a benchmark reaction to test the oxidation capabilities of TOTH under red-light irradiation. TOTH (0.3 mg, 0.9 μmol, 1.1% mol vs. substrate) was solubilized in DMF (3 mL) in a 4 mL vial. Thioanisole (10 μL, 0.085 mmol) was added to the solution. The mixture was sonicated for 5 minutes and then purged with oxygen. The flask was closed and equipped with an oxygen filled balloon. The vial was stirred under irradiation for 1 day (under 440-450 nm) or 96 hours with 620-625 nm LEDs (3 W nominal power, photon flux 5.70 × 10 -8 E s -1 cm -3 ; emission profiles of LEDs used are displayed in the SI). Aliquots were taken during the reaction and analyzed by HPLC ( Fig. 6 ) and the structure of the product was confirmed by GCMS (Fig. S13). The reaction kinetics follow first-order kinetics with a rate constant of 4.4 × 10 -6 (±3 × 10 -7 ) mol L -1 s -1 and reach >90% yield in 96 hours. The quantum yield calculated for this reaction is Φ Ox = 0.001. The calculated turn-over number (TON, based on a yield of 90% in 96 h) is 10 839, leading to a turn-over frequency (TOF) equal to 112 h -1 , which is high, 26 demonstrating the efficiency and the robustness of TOTH in sulfoxidation. Interestingly, when the reaction is performed with atmospheric oxygen, only 51% yield is obtained (compared to over 90% in pure oxygen). Furthermore, if a higher photon energy irradiation is used (440-450 nm LEDs, 3 W nominal power, photon flux 6.50 × 10 -8 E s -1 cm -3 ), the photoredox catalysis is enhanced and reaches a quantitative yield within 12 hours.
Thioanisole can be oxidized following two different mechanisms: 23,27 (i) energy transfer via photosensitization of triplet oxygen and (ii) single electron transfer (SET) directly from thioanisole and subsequent formation of hydroperoxides. To identify the mechanism, the photosulfoxidation was repeated in the presence of a singlet oxygen quencher Co(acac) 3 . 28 The rate of the oxidation was not significantly influenced despite the large excess of the quencher (see Fig. S14 & S15), which confirms that the mechanism does not involve singlet oxygen and is proceeding solely through SET and the formation of the hydroperoxide anion. 29 LCMS analysis of the reaction mixture performed after the photosulfoxidation run showed the presence of a species with a mass corresponding to the adduct of TOT 2 H 2 with molecular oxygen O 2 (Fig. S16 & S17). However, the exact structure remains unelucidated. Using anthracene as the starting material, anthraquinone is obtained after 16 hours of irradiation at 620-625 nm (Fig. S18). Together with the solvent oxidation described above, these reactions show a broad scope of substrates that can be photocatalytically oxidized by TOTH .
TOTH disproportionation under irradiation shows that TOTH can both donate and accept an electron rather efficiently. While the oxidized species is active in photooxidation, e.g. photosulfoxidation, the reduced species can be involved in photoreduction. To test this hypothesis, reduction of a nitroaromatic compound was selected as the second benchmark reaction. The photoreduction of methyl 4-nitrobenzoate using green irradiation (520-525 nm, 3 W nominal power, photon flux 2.19 × 10 -8 E s -1 cm -3 ) was monitored. Reactants were dissolved in DMF ( TOTH : 0.3 mg, 0.9 μmol, 2% mol, methyl 4-nitrobenzoate: 10 mg, 0.055 mmol) in a 4 mL vial, which was then purged with argon, and then 8 eq. of triethylamine (Et 3 N) with respect to the nitro-substrate was added. Et 3 N fulfils the role of a sacrificial electron donor, 30 allowing TOTH to regenerate in the photocatalytic cycle. Also, the basicity of Et 3 N deprotonates TOTH ( Fig. 1 ) and further improves its solubility in DMF.
The photoreduction was monitored in real time by HPLC analysis of aliquots taken during the reaction ( Fig. 7 ). After seven days of irradiation, 32% yield of methyl 4-aminobenzoate was determined with the overall conversion of 48%, leading to a quantum yield of Φ Red = 0.008. The TON and TOF found for this reaction are respectively 2839 and 17 h -1 . Interestingly, several products of nitro group partial reduction were detected as well (Fig. S19), including the hydroxylamine, azo-, and azoxy-derivatives. Such species are known to form under nitro-group reduction by zinc and thus indicate that the reduction also proceeds via a sequence of SET. The 1 H NMR analysis performed on the mixture showed a new set of aliphatic signals assigned to the Et 2 NH developing, thus confirming the oxidative decomposition of the Et 3 N (Fig. S20). Both decomposition products, acetaldehyde and Et 2 NH, have been identified by GC-MS (Fig. S5).
Remarkably, when the mixture of TOTH and an aromatic nitro compound is irradiated, the characteristic blue color of the mixture disappears. However, the mixture evolves differently depending on the wavelength used: when 525-530 nm LEDs are used, the solution slowly turns green overtime. When the vial is irradiated with 620-625 nm LEDs, the solution switches to colorless within a few seconds. This is not observed with aliphatic nitro derivatives. Unlike the irreversible color change under green light, when the red irradiation is interrupted, the blue color partially and progressively recovers. UV-vis investigations showed that the kinetics of this phenomenon is dependent on the concentration and the electron-deficiency of the nitro derivatives (Fig. S21). Higher concentration and the presence of other electron-withdrawing groups consistently lead to faster and deeper decolorization, however, always followed by partial slow recovery of the blue color. This suggests rapid formation of a charge-transfer complex between the electron-poor nitroaromatics and the electron-rich TOTH - ˙ scaffold, which in turn favors relatively low yields and slow kinetics of the reduction due to the low concentration of free TOTH - ˙ and energetically disfavored electron transfer to such a charge-transfer complex.
The rich landscape of reduced TOTH species ( Fig. 4 ) offers possibilities to engage in even challenging reduction reactions. The 4-bromoacetophenone photocatalytic reductive dehalogenation S RN 1 to acetophenone is a deep-potential reaction (around -1.81 V vs. SCE), 31,32 which has been selected as the third benchmark reaction. Given the challenging potential, the reaction is very sensitive to reaction conditions (see above); these were optimized to TOTH (0.3 mg, 0.9 μmol, 2% mol vs. substrate), 4-bromoacetophenone (10 mg, 0.050 mmol) and Et 3 N (56 μL, 0.40 mmol, 8 eq. vs. substrate) dissolved in 3 mL DMF by sonication. The deep blue solution was deoxygenated via argon purging. Initial experiments with 410 nm LED light in THF showed significant contribution of the non-catalyzed 4-bromoacetophenone photoreduction (28% vs. 16% yield for catalyzed and non-catalyzed reactions, respectively). With 440-450 nm irradiation, the non-catalytic photoreduction of the substrate was not observed and hence this wavelength range was used for the kinetic studies (see the control experiment in Fig. S23). Under these conditions, HPLC analysis gave a yield of 91% of acetophenone after 96 hours of irradiation ( Fig. 8 ) and the structure of the product was also confirmed by NMR and MS (Fig. S5 and S8). The TON and TOF calculated for this reaction are respectively 5871 and 61 h -1 .
Monitoring the kinetics of the reduction showed intriguing behavior. While one would expect a (pseudo)first order-type of kinetics, the plot suggested a more complex pathway. After the initial fast yield growth, a minor (but fully reproducible) deceleration of the reaction rate is observed followed by another enhancement of the photoreduction kinetics. Such a kinetic curve suggests contribution of two different catalytically active species, which is consistent with the observed conversion of TOTH to TOT 2 H 2 and TOTH - ˙˙ . These species feature higher absorbance at 440-450 nm (Fig. S2), which makes either of them catalyze the reaction further at an increased rate. The apparent quantum yield calculated in this reaction is Φ = 0.005, but due to the complex evolution of absorbance during the course of the reaction, this value is associated with large uncertainty.
The catalytic activity of TOTH in both oxidative and reductive photoreactions can be summarized in the following scheme. Upon irradiation, TOTH disproportionation occurs. Under an air or oxygen rich atmosphere, TOT acts as an oxidation catalyst: a clear example is the photosulfoxidation of thioanisole by single electron transfer from the sulfur atom, while O 2 reoxidizes TOTH - ˙ regenerating the initial TOTH state. When the solution is deoxygenated and in the presence of a sacrificial electron donor (Et 3 N), TOT is rapidly converted to initial TOTH by the reaction with Et 3 N. Meanwhile, the TOTH - ˙ acts as a single-electron donor: either forming charge-transfer complexes with electron-deficient species ( e.g. , under 620-625 nm irradiation in the presence of nitroaromatics) or eventually engaging in photoreduction. Prolonged irradiation leads to formation of TOTH 2 - ˙˙ and TOTH - ˙ dimerization to TOT 2 H 2 . These species also exhibit catalytic activity; however, they only absorb light with wavelength <600 nm (Fig. S2) and act as efficient deep potential photoreductants ( Fig. 9 ). This is supported by the determined redox potentials: TOT (0.44 V) is close to Et 3 N (0.83 V) and O 2 (0.60 V), TOTH - ˙ (-1.64 V) overlaps with those of nitrobenzoate (-1.01 V and -1.83 V), and TOTH 2 - ˙˙ (-2.10 V) with bromoacetophenone (-1.92 V).
The photocatalytic experiments with individual substrates (thioanisole, nitrobenzoate, and bromoacetophenone) proceed at convenient rates when irradiated at different wavelengths and/or performed under different conditions. This inspired us to employ TOTH in a sequence of photoredox reactions performed in a “one-pot fashion” controlled by conditions changed during the photocatalytic run ( Fig. 10 ). In this respect, TOTH , thioanisole and 4-bromoacetophenone were loaded in a 4 mL vial (under optimized conditions described above), the vial was purged with oxygen, and 620-625 nm irradiation was applied. Over the period of 4 days, gradual formation of the corresponding sulfoxide was observed by HPLC up to ca. 80% yield, while bromoacetophenone remains intact in the solution. Then, the irradiation was stopped, Et 3 N was added, the vial was purged with argon and 440-450 nm irradiation was initiated. Due to the lack of oxygen as a reagent for the oxidation and the presence of a sacrificial electron donor, photocatalytic oxidation of the substrate by TOT is disabled. Instead, enhanced formation of TOTH - ˙ , TOT 2 H 2 and TOTH 2 - ˙˙ leads to reductive behavior of the TOTH photocatalyst. Therefore, over the period of two days, gradual and quantitative formation of acetophenone was achieved, while the sulfoxide yield remained intact ( Fig. 10 ). This concept can even be extended to a full “red-green-blue” sequence when nitrobenzoate is added to the mixture as well; however, the mixture of products in this case becomes difficult to separate and quantify by HPLC (Fig. S22, left), preventing us to provide clear kinetic curves.
It must be noted that the observed sequence of photoredox reactions performed under irradiation at different wavelengths does not violate Kasha's rule, as this rule only applies to the relaxation of higher excited states of single species. However, in our case, there are different redox states (and potentially also (de)protonation states) which are responsible for the observed photoredox processes. In fact, if 4-bromoacetophenone reduction is performed in high excess of Et 3 N while irradiated by 620-625 nm light, the product of reductive dehalogenation is observed in about seven days, which, however, is less convenient than shorter reaction times obtained with more energetic light. In conclusion, the selectivity consists in kinetic control, where the reaction processing is dependent on the conditions.

text: We report the first application of a triangulene derivative as a versatile photoredox catalyst. We demonstrate that not only TOTH can efficiently reduce substrates like 4-bromoacetophenone and methyl 4-nitrobenzoate, but it can also efficiently oxidize thioanisole by easily tuning the experimental conditions and switching the light to a different wavelength. The pluripotent photocatalysis is enabled by light-induced disproportionation of TOTH followed by a sequence of single-electron transfer steps, either with a sacrificial oxidant or electron donor. The relatively complex pathway yields active redox states of TOTH , such as diradical anions and even dimers, which also contribute to the observed photoredox processes. These findings are supported and consistent with the proposed mechanism. By matching the conditions to the optimum of a selected photoredox reaction, even sequences of photocatalytic reactions can be performed in a “one-pot” fashion up to a full “red-green-blue” complex system. Concerning the recyclability of the photocatalysts, the polyaromatic character of TOTH made the migration on a silica chromatography column impossible. If the catalyst cannot be recovered, it also makes it easier to be purified. This work opens new perspectives for triangulene derivatives and pushes forward the investigation of fully organic materials in intertwined reaction networks to photocatalytically construct complex organic molecules.

title: Recent advancements in visible light-induced, vitamin-catalysed chemical transformations

text:
Abstract Vitamins play a vital role in organic transformations, particularly in the field of organocatalysis. Vitamins have been found to function as photoredox catalysts in an array of synthetic processes, supporting advancements in the realm of photocatalysis over the past few decades. Several applications of vitamins as photoredox catalysts are covered in this article. Furthermore, the mechanistic aspects that provide insights into the functions of vitamins in significant chemical transformations are thoroughly discussed, offering an understanding of reaction pathways and strengthening the applications of vitamins in organocatalysis methods.

text:
Vitamins play an essential role in biological processes, ensuring the proper function of metabolic pathways. Beyond this well-established function, a fascinating avenue of exploration is the potential of vitamins to act as catalysts in organic synthesis. 1 In the past, vitamins have been reported to function as coenzymes, which are organic compounds that aid in enzyme-catalysed chemical reactions. 2 Vitamins are small, photoactive, and sustainable organic compounds with a number of functional groups, such as the hydroxyl, amino, and carboxyl groups. They are highly advantageous due to their availability, nontoxicity, stability, and cost. There are many catalytic uses of vitamins in organic as well as photochemical reactions. Because of their rich coordination chemistry, facilitating coordination via the side chains and the amino, carboxylate, and hydroxyl groups, they are appealing bioligands for the development of novel hybrid inorganic-organic compounds. Since vitamins have many different ways to bind to metals, they are excellent candidates for the formation of metal complexes. 3 Vitamins are vital to both human and animal life since the body cannot synthesize them or cannot produce sufficient amounts of them. 4 Vitamins are categorized according to their biological action. Vitamin B 1 (VB 1 ), also known as thiamine hydrochloride, is a water-soluble vitamin involved in the transmission of neuronal impulses, the synthesis of nucleic acids (DNA) and the production of energy from food. 5 In recent years, vitamin B 2 , i.e. riboflavin (RF), 6 and its derivatives have garnered significant attention as special redox organocatalysts that facilitate a wide range of catalytic oxidations. 7,8 As the fundamental building blocks of redox-active coenzymes, flavin derivatives (FLs) can withstand changes in redox potentials and can serve as the reaction sites of many heat- and photo-induced activities. 9-12 (-)-Riboflavin (vitamin B 2 ) has intrinsic energy transfer (ET) as well as single electron transfer (SET) patterns, which can be stimulated upon irradiation, 14 making it an extremely flexible organocatalyst for a number of transformations. 13 Vitamin B 12 is extremely soluble in water. Advanced organic synthesis requires the development of environmentally sustainable synthetic methods. In this manner, “green” and sustainable approaches seek to reduce waste production and steer clear of the usage of dangerous or poisonous materials. 15-18 In the chemical industry, a lot of organic conversions are still carried out by employing almost stoichiometric amounts of catalysts, producing huge amounts of chemical waste. Most catalytic processes depend on expensive, toxic heavy metals such as Pd, Pt, Ru, and Ir. 19 More strict environmental regulations and growing environmental concerns require the development of chemical processes that are both economically and ecologically beneficial. According to this viewpoint, the search for more effective and environmentally friendly catalysts has been at the center of organic chemistry research. Over the past two decades, there has been renewed interest in the application of visible-light photochemistry in organic synthesis; organic photochemistry dates back more than a century to Giacomo Ciamician's laboratory. A major step toward Ciamician's goals has been the ongoing advancement of photoredox catalysis methods, which use photosensitizers that absorb visible light to produce high-energy excited states that can produce reactive radicals using low-energy reactants through energy transfer processes and single-electron transfer (SET). 20-23 Many persistent problems in medicinal chemistry, 25-27 natural product synthesis, 28-30 cross-coupling reactions, 31,32 materials chemistry, 33,34 and other fields have been resolved using this simple and effective method for radical generation. 24 In addition to its influence on the field of organic chemistry, photoredox catalysis is commonly regarded as a more environmentally friendly, or “greener,” option for chemical synthesis, satisfying a number of the green chemistry principles. 37 Due to their water and air compatibility and ease of use, vitamin B 1 , vitamin B 2 , vitamin B 12 , vitamin B 7 , and vitamin C have become popular naturally derived photoredox catalysts in combination with a number of organocatalysts ( Fig. 1 ). 35,36
The photocatalyst (PC) moves from the ground state (S 0 ) to a singlet excited state (S 1 ) by absorbing visible light. Moreover, the intersystem crossover (T 1 ) increases the probability that the strongest PCs create a persistent triplet excited state. The T 1 excited state typically mediates intermolecular interactions, resulting in further chemical transformations that are typically dependent on single electron transfer (SET). When exposed to light, a photoexcited PC may donate or receive electrons and become a more potent oxidant and reducer. An oxidative or reductive quenching cycle is commonly used to describe mechanistic activities ( Scheme 1 ). In a reductive quenching cycle, the photoexcited PC* initially acts as an oxidant by absorbing an electron from an electron donor (D), also known as a reductive quencher. This leads to the formation of a PC˙ - radical anion with substantial reducing potential. Tertiary amines are the most often used reductive quenchers. However, in an oxidative quenching cycle, the photoexcited PC* transfers an electron to an electron acceptor (A, oxidative quencher) by acting first as a reductant. As a result, a PC˙ + radical cation is generated, which has a higher oxidative potential than PC*. Common oxidative quenchers include dicyanobenzenes, polyhalomethanes, and aryldiazonium salts. Energy transfer through the excited PC to the substrate is also known to result in chemical modifications. 41 A lot of studies have been conducted recently to develop catalytic systems that utilize natural building blocks. In continuation of our study, 42,43 this review is intended to provide a brief overview of some important aspects of photoredox catalysts, particularly vitamin-derived photocatalytic systems for organic synthesis, and comprises vitamin-catalysed photochemical transformations from 2015 to 2026.

text:
Green chemistry is a scientific methodology that revolutionizes the synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) by focusing on the development of sustainable, non-toxic chemical methods that reduce or eliminate hazardous compounds. Metal catalysts offer unparalleled reactivity and remarkable control over the complex molecular architecture for medicinal alterations compared to catalytic frameworks. However, they are costly, scarce, and highly regulated in terms of metal residue contamination of pharmaceuticals. Such problems can be completely eliminated using synthetic organophotocatalysts, which entirely prevent metal toxicity by relying on tiny organic molecules to boost light-induced single-electron conversions to circumvent these problems. They often involve multi-step, petroleum-derived syntheses, but they offer an extremely large and extremely adaptable redox scope for difficult, novel reactions. Vitamin-based catalysts are a natural subset of organophotocatalysts, providing the benefits of metal-based catalysts and organic dye-based catalysts together. Although with a smaller range of redox values and lower photostability than synthetic dyes, they exhibit a superior green footprint, inexpensiveness and excellent biocompatibility in the final step of drug functionalization.
Chao et al. 44 described a catalytic system for arene migration via ether to carboxylic acid conversion using water as an environmentally conscious solvent and riboflavin tetraacetate (RFT), a widely available ester of natural vitamin B 2 , as the corresponding photocatalyst; this system does not require any external oxidants, bases, metals, inert gas protection, or extended reaction times ( Scheme 2 ). In addition to the substrates of recognized substituted 2-phenyloxybenzoic acids, a series of equivalents derived from naphthalene and heterocycles were also transformed for the first time into the corresponding aryl salicylates. Mechanistic investigations, particularly a few kinetic isotope effect (KIE) experiments, indicated that the bifunctional flavin photocatalyst facilitated a series of electron transfer-proton transfer events. A proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 3 . Using an external base, carboxylic acid 1 was first dissolved in water or an organic solvent. Simultaneously, RFT was protonated and converted into RFTH + due to its mild basicity. When exposed to blue light irradiation in an aqueous solution, excited RFTH + acts as a strong oxidant (1.8-2.0 V), promoting the one-electron oxidation of carboxylate A (1.77 V) and converting to RFTH˙. Carboxylate radical B undergoes intramolecular addition to the neighbouring arene ring, resulting in the formation of intermediate C. The C-O bond was then homolysed and rearomatized to form phenoxy radical D. The transfer of electrons between radical D (1.21 V) and semiquinone RFTH˙ (∼-0.8 V) may produce related phenoxide D and protonated RFTH + . In the end, the proton of RFTH + goes to intermediate E to produce product 2, as RFT recovers in the ground state.
A green catalytic technique for oxidizing alkynes to yield 1,2-diketones using a photocatalytic system based on vitamin B 2 was published by D. Shen et al. 45 in 2023 ( Scheme 4 ). In this reaction, Sc(OTf) 3 , NaCl, vitamin B 2 derivative and riboflavin tetraacetate (RFT) were employed as cocatalysts under blue light exposure. With both H 2 O and O 2 acting as oxygen sources during product formation, the system is devoid of sacrificial reagents. A proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 5 and is based on existing data and associated reports. However, the excited [RFT-2Sc 3+ ]* complex might oxidize Cl - to Cl˙ by one electron. The radical anion [RFT˙ - -2Sc 3+ ] was eventually reoxidized by O 2 to afford O 2 ˙ - . In potential pathway I, the alkyne was more probable to be attacked by O 2 ˙ - before Cl˙ to generate radical intermediate A, which then combined again with Cl˙ to produce intermediate B. The C-C bond of B most likely went through the second one-electron oxidation via the [RFT-2Sc 3+ ]* complex to produce radical cation C. The nucleophilic addition of intermediate C and H 2 O may then produce radical D. However, in potential pathway II, the [RFT-2Sc 3+ ]* complex may potentially oxidize the diaryl acetylene to produce radical cation E. After that, H 2 O was added to E as the nucleophile to produce radical F, which subsequently underwent keto-enol tautomerization to form radical G. After that, G and O 2 ˙ - underwent radical recombination to produce intermediate H. It should be mentioned that peroxo compounds have the ability to undergo oxygen atom transfer reactions with organic substrates and function as oxidants. Therefore, the hydroperoxo species H was transformed into the desired diketone 4a, where the oxygen atoms originated from both H 2 O and O 2 , by losing H 2 O or oxidizing other species.
According to Gryko et al. , 46 the dicarbofunctionalization of bromoalkenes using electrophilic olefins is accelerated by vitamin B 12 and produces substituted pyrrolidines and piperidines in respectable yields after 15 minutes of exposure to light ( Scheme 6 ). They assumed that the “supernucleophilic” Co( i ) version of vitamin B 12 might react with specially created bromoalkenes in the mechanistic path. When heated or exposed to light, 5 becomes alkylcobalamin A, which then produces radical B and intermediate C. Radical B may undergo reduction to produce 3-methylpyrrolidine D, which combines with the Co( ii ) species to produce F and then 3-methylenepyrrolidine 6a shortly after dehydrocobaltation, or combines with a specific electron-deficient olefin, if one is present, to produce substituted pyrrolidine 8a ( Scheme 7 ).
Hisaeda et al. 47 used the B 12 complex as the catalyst and [Ir(dtbbpy)(ppy) 2 ]PF 6 as the photosensitizer and presented the progress of a visible light-activated catalytic pathway that offers a practical and effective method for amide synthesis ( Scheme 8 ). In a one pot synthesis procedure, trichlorinated organic compounds were transformed into amides in the presence of an amine under aerobic conditions. Based on the above results, a proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 9 . When exposed to visible light, [Ir(dtbbpy)(ppy) 2 ]PF 6 is induced to excited state A, which is subsequently reductively quenched to the one-electron reduced species B via the sacrificial reductant i-Pr 2 NEt. The B 12 complex can be reduced to a supernucleophilic Co (I) species by the redox potential of B, which is -1.42 V vs. Ag/AgCl ( E 1/2 Co (II/I) = -0.61 V vs. Ag/AgCl). Carbon-centered radical C was created by the nucleophilic attack carried out by the Co (I) species of the B 12 complex on benzotrichloride through an alkylated complex acting as an intermediary. Under anaerobic conditions, radical couples form 12, which is then further dechlorinated to produce 13. According to our earlier findings, under aerobic conditions, radical C quickly interacts with oxygen to form benzoyl chloride through a number of radical reaction steps. A radical trapping test verified that radical species were produced throughout the process. The yield of 12 dropped to 20% when the radical trapping reagent, 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N -oxide (DMPO), was introduced at the start of the process, suggesting that a radical was involved. Ultimately, diethylamine and benzoyl chloride were mixed to produce amide 11.
An easy approach for the direct photocatalytic formation of benzo-3,4-coumarins via biaryl carboxylic acids utilizing (-)-riboflavin as a photocatalyst in the presence of visible light was described by Gilmour et al. 48 ( Scheme 10 ). This synthetic method is simple to employ, uses a cheap catalyst, and does not require any metal additions. A proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 11 based on previous studies. When visible light is present, the catalytic process starts by protonating (-)-riboflavin (RF), and at λ max = 402 nm, the protonated flavin is strongly absorbed. The protonated flavin radical (RFH˙) and carboxy radical B are then produced by a single electron transfer via carboxylate anion A to RFH + . These radicals can then cyclize to produce intermediate C. Ultimately, intermediate C is oxidized and rearomatized with the flavin radical RFH˙ in a SET/deprotonation or hydrogen atom transfer reaction to produce the final product. Reduced (-)-riboflavin (RFH 2 ) underwent molecular oxygen reoxidation.
The photocatalytic efficacy of the Cu( ii )-vitamin C complex immobilized on titanium dioxide nanoparticles was investigated by Rezaeifard et al. 49 and utilized in the photo-derived homocoupling process of aryl boronic acids under heterogeneous conditions. Despite the utilization of any supplementary substances, like a base or oxidant, the homocoupling process produces the appropriate symmetrical biaryls in 50-97% yields at room temperature in the air under the age of visible light irradiation. Several substituents on aryl boronic acids, including halogen, carbonyl, and nitro groups, have been supported by this technique. The highest possible perceived quantum efficiency (AQY) at 410 nm was found in the light-induced photocatalytic activity of the aforementioned catalyst assessed by action spectra, indicating a visible-light-mediated photocatalytic reaction ( Scheme 12 ).
Jamshidinajafabadi and collaborators 50 in 2025 presented an effective photocatalytic system using a natural-based nanostructured catalyst consisting of a copper complex using a g-C 3 N 4 -vitamin B 5 hybrid supported on magnetic nanoparticles. Its band gap shifted from 2.8 eV (g-C 3 N 4 -B 5 ) to 2.45 eV (g-C 3 N 4 -B 5 -Cu@γ-Fe 2 O 3 ). Numerous significant reactions, such as the aerobic photooxidation of benzylic alcohols 18 to aldehydes 19 and the simultaneous formation of imines 21 and benzimidazoles via the dehydrogenative coupling of primary benzylic alcohols along with aromatic amines and diamines under visible-light irradiation, were effectively catalysed by the aforementioned magnetic nanohybrid of the g-C 3 N 4 -B 5 -Cu@γ-Fe 2 O 3 photocatalyst ( Scheme 13 ).
A visible light-induced coupling process between alkyl halides and phenylacetylene derivatives for the production of C(sp 3 )-C(sp) bonds has been developed by Shimakoshi et al. 51 ( Scheme 14 ). Under mild conditions, an effective dual-catalyst reaction system was developed. When exposed to light, the B 12 complex functioned as an effective catalyst and exhibited maximum turnover. A proposed reaction mechanism shown in Scheme 15 is used for the B 12 -catalyzed coupling reaction. The excited state of PS ( E (L*/L - ) = 0.70 V vs. SCE in CH 3 CN for P1) oxidizes radical D to generate carbocation E, followed by the energetically favored deprotonation of E to produce end product 24. They used the B3LYP functional in conjunction with the 6-31G** basis to conduct standard DFT computations in order to better comprehend the deprotonation of carbocation by i-Pr 2 NEt. The DFT calculations verify the suggested mechanism involving an energetically preferable deprotonation step.
Ouyang et al. 52 recently proposed the oxidative coupling of benzylamines and oxidation of thioanisoles utilizing a heterogeneous photocatalytic system that utilizes chromophores (TAPP-biotin PS). Chromophore components (porphyrin, coumarin, anthraquinone, or pyrene) are biotinylated to produce a catalytic system, which is then grafted onto magnetic beads coated with streptavidin. The anticipated imines and sulfoxides were produced by the photocatalyst employing 5,10,15,20-tetrakis(4-aminophenyl)porphyrin (TAPP) in extremely high yields, with turnover numbers (TON) close to 10 000 ( Scheme 16 ). Photocatalytic processes (˙O 2 - and 1 O 2 ) are driven by photogenerated reactive oxygen species. After light absorption, the TAPP-biotin PS changed to a stimulated singlet state (1PS*), as shown in the proposed reaction mechanism in Scheme 17 . It subsequently underwent intersystem crossover (ISC) to arrive at a more stable triplet state (3PS*). ˙O 2 - and PS + are obtained through electron transfer. A ground-state PS molecule and a PhCH 2 NH 2 + radical are produced when the generated PS + absorbs an electron via benzylamine 25. Phenylmethanimine is formed when the PhCH 2 NH 2 + radical combines with ˙O 2 - . This compound then combines with another benzylamine molecule to produce imine product 26. Benzylamine and 1 O 2 can also be combined to form a phenylmethanimine intermediate.
For the first time, Osaka et al. 53 showed the Giese reaction utilising easily accessible alkyl tosylates as alkyl radical sources. The reaction continued effectively using vitamin B 12 or Co(TTMP) catalysts, Mn reductant and a proton donor in the presence of visible light irradiation ( Scheme 18 ). The creation of alkyl-cobalt( iii ) intermediates through the SN 2 -type oxidative addition of alkyl tosylates into nucleophilic cobalt( i ) is an essential step in this process. Therefore, the reaction efficacy was impacted by the bulk surrounding the TsO group with alkyl tosylates. However, the regioselective functionalization of polyol molecules was made possible by classical tosylation and the Giese reaction that followed. Based on these findings, a proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 19 . Alkyl tosylates 29 were added to nucleophilic cobalt( i ) A via the SN 2 -type oxidative process, resulting in alkylcobalt( iii ) B. Co-C bond breakage then occurs when exposed to visible light, producing alkyl radical 30 and planar-cobalt( ii ) C. After the addition of an active olefin to β-position 31, the produced alkyl radical is reduced with Mn and protonated to form adduct 32. Mn reduction of planar-cobalt( ii ) C terminates the catalytic cycle and produces nucleophilic cobalt( i ) A.
Pitre et al. 54 published a protocol employing vitamin B 12 photocatalysis and dichloromethane (CH 2 Cl 2 ) as the methylene supplier to facilitate the cyclopropanation of electron-deficient alkenes ( Scheme 20 ). CH 2 Cl 2 goes through a nucleophilic substitution of the SN 2 type, resulting in Co III -CH 2 Cl intermediate A by utilizing vitamin B 12 's extremely nucleophilic Co I oxidation state. This intermediate can be photolyzed via green (525 nm) LED radiation to produce ˙CH 2 Cl radical C. In electron-deficient alkenes, this radical takes part in a polarity-matched Giese addition. Co II then traps the carbon-centered radical to produce intermediate D. Ultimately, the required cyclopropane product 35 is obtained by the reduction of D accompanied by 3- exo-tet cyclization. The generation of ˙CH 2 Cl radicals was demonstrated by radical trapping experiments, whereas UV-vis measurements supported the suggested SN 2 process. Significantly, the system demonstrated good chemoselectivity and functional group tolerance while exhibiting a wide substrate scope, comprising acrylates, acrylamides, acrylonitrile, and derivatives of dehydroamino acids. Substrates with protic or amine functionalities, which are usually troublesome in traditional photoredox techniques, were effectively cyclopropanated. In addition to CH 2 Cl 2 , the procedure was expanded to include isotopically labeled CD 2 Cl 2 , which provided direct access to deuterated cyclopropanes with therapeutic value, and 1,1-dichloroethane, which provided methyl-substituted cyclopropyl adducts ( Scheme 21 ).
Chao et al. 55 reported the catalytic epoxidation of α,β-enone using a minor energy transfer route and a majority single electron transfer, producing peroxide in situ . At room temperature and under visible light irradiation, they employed low-cost natural vitamin B 2 (riboflavin, RF) or the simplest ester (riboflavin tetraacetate, RFT) as the photocatalysts, 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]-7-undecene (DBU) as the organic base and electron source, and ambient air as the terminal oxidant ( Scheme 22 ). A proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 23 , which is deduced from previous reports and the present data. When exposed to visible light, the excited RFT transforms into a potent oxidant (RFT*), abstracting one electron of the reductant DBU. Following the creation of the superoxide radical anion (O 2 ˙ - ), molecular oxygen oxidized the resultant RFT˙ - for regeneration. The O 2 ˙ - was then transformed into HOO - using the additional one electron provided by DBU or simply by disproportionation, which targeted the Michael acceptor (α,β-enone) to produce the epoxy ketone. However, with this epoxidation reaction, the stimulated riboflavin may transfer energy to O 2 to make 1 O 2 , which oxidized DBU and produced the equivalent DBU-peroxide (DBU + -OO - ), serving as a nucleophilic oxidant. Furthermore, the reaction between DBU and O 2 ˙ - may have produced DBU + -OO - .
Hisaeda et al. 56 disclosed that the solvothermal synthesis method was utilized to produce new bimetal complex {Zn 4 Ru 2 (bpdc) 4.4 C 2 NH 8 ·9DMF} n (H 2 bpdc = 4,40-biphenyldicarboxylic acid). Ru@MOF was formed via cation exchange after the photosensitizer [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2 + was adsorbed within the bimetal complex ( Scheme 24 ). Another cobalamin derivative (B 12 ) effectively immobilized on Ru@MOF was heptamethyl cobyrinate. When exposed to visible light in the solid state, the resulting hybrid complex, B 12 eRu@MOF, demonstrated notable reactivity in the dechlorination reaction involving 1,1-bis(4-chlorophenyl)-2,2,2-trichloroethane (DDT) in a N 2 standard atmosphere. After three recycling cycles, the catalytic process of B 12 eRu@MOF can still achieve over 80% conversion. Additionally, a heterogeneous catalyst like B 12 eRu@MOF was favorable for cobalamin-mediated reactions, like the 1,2-migration of an acetyl group. These results prompted them to propose a reaction mechanism, as shown in Scheme 25 . The supernucleophilic Co (I) entity mixes with the substrate to form an alkylated cobalt complex when electron transfer via the [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ photosensitizer converts the Co (II) complex to Co (I) . When visible light irradiation breaks the carbon-cobalt bond in the alkylated cobalt complex, alkyl radical intermediate A and a Co( ii ) species are supposed to be generated. The solvent's hydrogen radical abstraction results in the simple reduced product. Radical intermediate A has an adequate time to transform into acetyl migrating radical B, even if the MOF channel can extend its lifetime. A hydrogen radical may be abstracted by radical B to create acetyl-migrated products 39 and 40.
Gryko and coworkers 57 contend that vitamin B 12 acts as a catalyst to interact with DACs to produce alkyl cobalamins, and homolytic cleavage of the aforementioned Co-C bond produces C-centered radicals that react with SOMOphiles. The result of the reaction is derived via the delicate balance among three concurrent alterations of the produced radical. Conventional regioselectivity is modified by this radical-driven process, which advances conventional approaches ( Scheme 26 ). Based on prior knowledge, it is reasonable to suppose that under the applied conditions, the Co (III) form of the catalyst is reduced to the “supernucleophilic” Co (I) species, which generates alkyl radical 42 by attacking the donor carbon atom of DAC. In the intended case, it combines with the activated olefin to produce intermediate D, which then reduces to the required alkylated product 43 ( Scheme 27 ).
Sun and colleagues 58 developed a biological cascading reaction for the formation of chalcones facilitated by visible light and catalysed by enzymes . This method relies on the persistent decarboxylative coupling reaction between cinnamic acids and aroylcarboxylic acids in the presence of 30 °C water. Chalcone variations were produced by employing this strategy, five of which were natural products. The catalytic cycle of the whole procedure was realized for the very first time when a visible light-mediated system was added to the biological chain reaction. This approach successfully encouraged the on-site replenishment of coenzyme components. Vitamin B 12 (VB 12 ) showed a superior photocatalytic effect. This procedure broadens the biological cascade's application and offers a fresh approach to the generation of chalcone derivatives ( Scheme 28 ). On the basis of the aforementioned experimental findings and earlier research, decarboxylative coupling was described, for which a proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 29 . In the reaction system's buffer environment (K 3 PO 4 , pH = 7.0), 44 (p K a ≈ 3.5) first experiences spontaneous deprotonation to create 44 - . There is no need for laccase catalysis because this activity is thermodynamically spontaneous. Next, type I Cu 2+ is reduced to Cu + , while type I Cu 2+ takes one electron from the α-C in 44 - and transforms it to the benzoyl formic acid radical intermediate A˙.
Finally, benzoyl radical B is produced when the unstable A˙ quickly decarboxylates (releasing CO 2 ). Instead of directly catalyzing deprotonation, laccase's primary role in this phase is to oxidize 44 - . In the buffer solution, 44 spontaneously completes a pretreatment called deprotonation, which produces an anion form that is easier to oxidize for the later transfer of electrons. Subsequently, the type I Cu + in the laccase active center completes self-oxidation (Cu + -Cu 2+ ) by transferring electrons to the O 2 bound to the type II/III Cu clusters via the internal electron transport chain (type I-type II-type III Cu clusters). O 2 is simultaneously oxidized to a superoxide anion (O 2 ˙ - ). This results in the reduction of NADP + to NADP(H). This suggests that in addition to being the last electron acceptor, O 2 is also a crucial intermediary that links 44 - oxidation and NADP + reduction. The VB 12 photocatalytic system is capable of recovering the reduction product NADP(H) to NADP + in a closed loop cycle, greatly increasing the reaction effectiveness and accomplishing the coenzyme's reuse and renewal. Following a coupling reaction with the cinnamic acid anion under set A's catalysis, free radical B decarboxylates to generate end product 46 following a single electron transfer. To finish the photocatalytic step, the activated VB 12 * is reduced to ground state VB 12 . Benzil 46′ is also produced during this procedure via a free radical self-coupling phenomenon.
Reaction proticity was shown by Julian G. West et al. 59 to have a significant and consistent impact on VB 12 HAT reactivity with significant synthetic consequences. They were able to create a hydrogenative oxetane ring-opening reaction using this hypothesis-driven reaction design, enabling a novel route for the production of saturated alcohols by oxetanes with protic conditions of reaction. Ring-opening isomerization was made easier by switching to an aprotic solvent containing sub-stoichiometric acid, which produced allylic alcohols from a variety of oxetane substrates ( Scheme 30 ). Combining these concepts, a proposed reaction mechanism for VB 12 -catalyzed opening of a hydrogenative oxetane ring is shown in Scheme 31(a) . To overcome the ring-opening activation obstacle and produce greater electrophilic species A, the oxetane substrate is first protonated. According to earlier findings, the stretched ring can then be cleaved by supernucleophilic reduction of VB 12 to yield Co( iii ) alkyl intermediate B. When exposed to visible light, this species emits carbon-centered radical C via the LiH of the Co-C bond. Donating HAT to the appropriate radical site yields hydrogenated alcohol product 48. According to the advantageous, though not necessarily essential, impact of thiols, the HAT donation step can take place via VB 12 or thiol catalysis. Under these conditions, TRIP disulfide and VB 12 might be reduced to produce a thiolate anion and Co( i ), respectively. The active HAT donors Co( iii )-H and thiol S-H are produced when these species are protonated. Co( ii ) and a thiyl radical should then be expelled by subsequent HAT donation toward the ring-opened radical. Lastly, reduction might complete the suggested reductive HAT cycle by reforming Co( i ) along with thiolate. They concentrated their investigation on the ring-opening isomerization system to take into account the impact of TFA loading on both the reaction efficiency and selectivity for isomerization, proposing that an effective isomerization system with ring opening required a compromise between Co( iii )-H, a probable acidic activator, a possible HAT donor, and Co( ii ), a crucial radical trap, and Scheme 31(b) describes the proposed methodology. Similar to the mechanism proposed for hydrogenative ring opening, Zn/TFA reduces VB 12 to its supernucleophilic Co( i ) state, and protonation activates the oxetane. Sub-stoichiometric TFA activates it in the beginning, but acidic Co( iii )-H might protonate it in later cycles. Co( ii ) and intermediate carbon-centered radical C′ might be released by cleaving and irradiating the oxetane ring again. Here, Co( ii ) HAA forms allylic alcohol product 49 at the neighboring carbon in the absence of excessive proton supplies or a thiol HAT addition, which is comparable to the olefination procedure suggested in their earlier technique and CarH enzymatic photodetection. The resultant Co( iii )-hydride could undergo proton transfer through a deactivated oxetane to activate the ensuing ring opening and rebuild the Co( i ) nucleophile in order to complete the cycle.
Schmidt and colleagues 60 ( Scheme 32 ) employed potassium peroxydisulfate to serve as a sacrificial oxidizing agent and riboflavin to act as a photocatalyst; they synthesized benzothiazoles from thiobenzanilides under visible light irradiation in a yield of up to 97%. A proposed reaction mechanism is shown in Scheme 33 . When the singlet and triplet excited states of RFTA are photogenerated, thiobenzanilides may function as quenchers through an electron-transfer process, resulting in the radical anion RFTA˙ - and the associated thiobenzanilide radical cation (50˙ + ). Interestingly, the riboflavin moiety is also capable of serving as a base (p K a of [RFTA-H]˙ = 8.3), helping to deprotonate 50˙ + . Thiobenzanilide radical cation 50˙ + is deprotonated to produce the sulfur radical, which is then cyclized and subsequently rearomatized via whatever oxidant species to produce 2-substituted benzothiazoles 51. To complete the catalytic cycle and bring RFTA to the ground state, peroxide disulfate is required.
Gryko and colleagues 61 used the special nucleophilic and photochemical characteristics of vitamin B 12 and related complexes to produce carbon radicals using a number of precursors, such as diazo compounds, strained electrophiles, and alkyl halides. They investigated the use of this catalytic framework, enabling regioselective epoxide ring-openings in a recent noteworthy example. Epoxides are useful building components for the formation of nonsymmetrical alcohols; however, there are still issues with regioselectivity (branched vs. linear), particularly with aryl epoxides, that react mostly at the benzylic position. In this study, scientists created a tandem catalytic system using vitamin B 12 and nickel catalysis to selectively couple epoxides with aryl halides by exposure to visible light, producing linear alcohols ( Scheme 34 ). According to them, the process starts when Co I attacks the less hindered carbon of epoxide 52 nucleophilically, producing alkylcobalamin intermediate A. Following reductive elimination, the primary alkyl radical B produced by subsequent Co III -C bond photolysis joins the nickel cycle via aryl halide 53 to form the C-C bond. The natural thermodynamic propensity for the formation of benzylic radicals is overridden by this sterically regulated pathway, which also overrides the inclination of aryl epoxides to generate branched alcohol product 54. The process worked well with both aliphatic and aryl epoxides, and it could handle either electron-rich or electron-poor aryl halides, particularly difficult heteroaryl substrates. Crucially, vitamin B 12 photocatalysis and nickel catalysis worked together to create reactivity that nickel could not achieve. In a later paper, the scientists also demonstrated the ability to expand this approach for radical creation by opening an oxetane ring ( Scheme 35 ).
This reactivity was further developed in aqueous micellar medium by Gryko et al. 62 In this study, radical Giese-type additions to electron-deficient olefins are followed by the opening of the ring of the aforementioned epoxides and aziridines, which is facilitated via vitamin B 12 catalysis. Additionally, each product was made as a single linear regioisomer. This study marks a significant advancement in reaction sustainability by substituting more sustainable aqueous conditions, including alcohol cosolvents, for organic solvents ( Scheme 36 ).
West and co-workers 63 established an alternative method that directly transforms epoxides into Markovnikov alcohols, working in sequence regarding thiol-derived hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) catalysis ( Scheme 37 ). They demonstrated the regioselective opening of epoxide rings utilizing vitamin B 12 . The reaction starts with Co I 's initial nucleophilic attack on the epoxide's slightly hindered carbon, producing alkylcobalamin intermediate A, which photolyzes to produce primary alkyl radical B. West's methodology uses a TRIP thiol cocatalyst to transmit a hydrogen atom, efficiently resembling hydride nucleophiles and producing associated alcohol product 59 at elevated regioselectivity, while this method supervised this radical to a nickel-driven cross-electrophile coupling cycle and aryl halides. The reaction demonstrated a variety of functional group tolerance parameters, comprising electrophilic and reductively labile components that would ordinarily be susceptible to reduction or cleavage via hydride nucleophiles. The aforementioned ease of application highlights its potential for synthesis. According to the author, turning over the thiol catalyst in the midst of a protic solvent depends on Co II intermediate C produced following the radical production stage. The functional ease of the reaction highlights the synthetic potential of this technique. This work offers a novel method for the development of synergistic vitamin B 12 photocatalysis with thiol HAT catalysis ( Scheme 38 ).

title: Recent advancements in visible light-induced, vitamin-catalysed chemical transformations

text: Visible light-induced, vitamin-catalyzed chemical transformations have recently emerged as a viable and sustainable approach in modern organic synthesis. Vitamins such as riboflavin (vitamin B 2 ), cobalamin (vitamin B 12 ), and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) have been demonstrated to be viable options as photocatalysts or photoredox mediators since they are naturally abundant, low in toxicity, biocompatible and environmentally friendly. Upon exposure to visible light, these vitamins can generate reactive intermediates using radical and electron-transfer pathways, thus enabling a variety of useful chemical reactions to take place under mild conditions. This review encourages standard and synthetic organic chemists to establish more sustainable procedures utilizing vitamins in multicomponent reactions and oxidation, reduction, rearrangement, cyclization, cross-coupling and photooxidation reactions by illustrating the chemical properties, catalytic efficiency, recycling, and thermal durability of vitamins.

title: Molecular oxygen-enabled photocatalyzed oxygenative coupling via C-H functionalization: advances and mechanistic insights
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/ This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported Licence . You can use material from this article in other publications without requesting further permissions from the RSC, provided that the correct acknowledgement is given.
text:
Visible-light photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful platform for the activation and functionalization of inherently inert C-H bonds, enabling synthetically valuable transformations under mild, sustainable, and operationally simple conditions. Among the oxidants employed in these processes, molecular oxygen holds particular significance owing to its abundance, low cost, and dual function as both a terminal oxidant and an oxygen atom source. This perspective provides a concise yet comprehensive overview of recent advancements in oxygen-enabled photocatalytic C-H functionalization, with a focus on oxygenative C-C, C-N, C-S and C-O coupling reactions. Developments in transition metal-catalyzed and metal-free photoredox systems are critically discussed. Mechanistic insights into reactive oxygen species generation, and radical intermediacy are highlighted to elucidate the underlying principles governing these transformations. Collectively, the advances summarized herein underscore the growing impact of O 2 driven photoredox catalysis in delivering efficient, atom-economic, and environmentally benign routes for the construction of diverse molecular architectures, thereby reinforcing its importance in contemporary organic synthesis.
This perspective highlights visible-light photoredox-enabled oxygenative C-H functionalization using molecular oxygen as a sustainable oxidant, covering metal-free and transition-metal catalyzed strategies for C-C and C-heteroatom bond formation.
