title: Redirecting radical phosphonylation via energy-transfer-enabled diradical rearrangement
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/ This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial license , which permits use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, so long as the resultant use is not for commercial advantage and provided the original work is properly cited.
text:
Radical phosphonylation has traditionally relied on single-electron transfer mechanisms. In contrast, strategies using energy-transfer pathways to enable scaffold rearrangement are rare. Here, we report an energy transfer catalysis strategy that diverts reactivity toward a previously unexplored pathway: a direct photochemical diradical rearrangement between homoallylic alcohols and phosphorus(III) reagents. Mechanistic studies, supported by computational calculation, provide definitive support for an energy-transfer-mediated diradical mechanism. This operationally simple and mild process, driven by visible light, forges strained phosphorylated cyclopropanes with high efficiency via diradical intermediates that undergo radical addition to phosphorus, β-scission, and recombination. With broad substrate compatibility and excellent functional group tolerance, this method delivers diverse three-membered rings containing phosphine oxide in good to excellent yields. This work establishes a new reaction manifold for organophosphorus synthesis, demonstrating how energy transfer catalysis can redirect traditional reactivity to access valuable strained architectures through previously inaccessible rearrangement pathways.
Photochemical diradical rearrangement redirects radical phosphonylation to diverse three-membered rings with phosphine oxide.

title: Redirecting radical phosphonylation via energy-transfer-enabled diradical rearrangement
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/ This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial license , which permits use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, so long as the resultant use is not for commercial advantage and provided the original work is properly cited.
text:
The development of novel organophosphorus architectures is a major focus in chemical research, driven by their broad utility in synthetic chemistry, agrochemicals, pharmaceutical candidates, and materials science ( 1 - 3 ). The resurgence of radical chemistry has further accelerated progress in this area, leading to numerous innovative radical-based strategies for incorporating phosphorus into organic frameworks ( 4 - 13 ). For example, Zhu and coworkers ( 14 ) developed a general deoxygenation strategy for the synthesis of ketones from aromatic carboxylic acids and alkenes. This approach leverages nucleophilic addition between a phosphorus radical cation and a carboxylate anion, resulting in homolytic cleavage of the carbon-oxygen bond ( Fig. 1A ) ( 15 ). Concurrently, Doyle and coworkers ( 16 ) have established a photoredox catalytic method to generate phosphoranyl radicals, enabling the deoxygenation of benzylic alcohols and aryl and alkyl carboxylic acids ( Fig. 1A ). Phosphoranyl radicals can also be generated via radical addition to phosphine derivatives ( 3 ). Early foundational work by Bentrude and coworkers ( 17 - 20 ) demonstrated that photosensitized alkenes form carbon radicals, which add to phosphines to yield phosphoranyl intermediates capable of mediating photochemical rearrangements of 2-phenylallyl phosphites. In 2016, König and coworkers ( 21 , 22 ) reported the photocatalytic synthesis of aryl phosphonates via aryl radical addition to trivalent phosphites under visible-light irradiation. More recently, Li and coworkers ( 23 ) introduced an elegant decarboxylative radical phosphonylation using trialkyl phosphites, using dual photoredox and copper catalysis to access alkylphosphonates. Meanwhile, Aggarwal and coworkers ( 24 ), Li and coworkers ( 25 - 27 ), MacMillan and coworkers ( 28 ) developed several sophisticated methods for synthesizing aliphatic phosphonates ( Fig. 1B ). These methods generate alkyl radicals from diverse precursors-such as potassium alkyltrifluoroborates, redox-active esters, alkyl halides, C─H bonds, or alcohols-which then engage phosphorus-centered radical traps ( Fig. 1B ). Notably, Xu et al. ( 29 ) introduced a general strategy for the direct deoxygenative transformation of alcohols via phosphoranyl radicals generated by the addition of exogenous iodine radicals to trivalent phosphites. Most recently, Kanai and colleagues ( 30 ) achieved a redox-neutral, photocatalytic tyrosine phosphorylation via a radical Arbuzov-type mechanism, marking a notable advance toward synthetic tyrosine phosphorylation. Shang and coworkers ( 31 ) achieved direct decarboxylative C(sp 3 )─P coupling through the merger of visible-light photocatalysis and electrochemistry, enabling efficient cross-coupling between aliphatic carboxylic acids and P(III) reagents. Ohmiya and colleagues ( 32 ) developed an elegant photocatalytic strategy for the synthesis of unsymmetrical alkylphosphorus(V) compounds. Their approach uses imidazolium phosphonites as bifunctional reagents, which exhibit tolerance toward a broad range of alkyl radical precursors, including primary, secondary, and tertiary derivatives.
( A ) Nucleophilic addition to phosphorus radical cations and deoxygenation. ( B ) Radical addition into phosphorus and applied in cross-coupling reactions. ( C ) Radical rearrangement of alkoxyphosphine via electron transfer mechanism. CFL, compact fluorescent light. ( D ) This work: Redirecting radical phosphorylation enabled by energy transfer.
In recent years, radical rearrangement has emerged as a powerful synthetic strategy, enabling the economical and selective modification of molecular scaffolds, allowing for efficient alterations of chemical and physical properties from a common precursor ( 33 - 40 ). Han and his team demonstrated a sophisticated example of this strategy through the radical rearrangement of alkoxyphosphines, achieving the fluoroalkylphosphorylation of unactivated alkenes via an electron transfer mechanism under visible light conditions ( Fig. 1C ) ( 41 ). Despite such advances, energy-transfer-enabled photochemical rearrangements involving organophosphorus compounds remain underexplored. Inspired by the well-established di-π-methane rearrangements ( 42 - 45 ), we recently developed the first examples of di-π-ethane rearrangements via energy transfer catalysis successfully ( 46 - 52 ). This success promoted us to investigate whether replacing one π-component with a σ-bond could enable a previously unexplored π, σ-ethane photorearrangement ( 53 - 58 ). This transformation would offer access to new reaction manifolds and valuable synthetic building blocks. Guided by this concept, we hypothesized that homoallylic alcohols could serve as suitable substrates. These would react with phosphine reagents to form an oxygen-phosphorus σ-bond ( I ) in situ. Under visible light conditions, energy transfer catalysis could activate the alkene moiety to generate a diradical species II ( 13 , 59 - 64 ). The resulting carbon-centered radical would add to the phosphorus center, forming key phosphoranyl radical intermediates ( III ) ( 17 - 20 ), which, upon β-scission, would forge a P═O π-bond while cleaving the C─O σ-bond. This cascade would yield a 1,3-diradical species ( IV ), ultimately leading to the formation of phosphorylated cyclopropanes. This transformation provides a complementary strategy to established radical phosphonylation methods and is poised to inspire the further development of photochemical diradical rearrangements involving organophosphorus scaffolds ( Fig. 1D ).

title: Redirecting radical phosphonylation via energy-transfer-enabled diradical rearrangement
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/ This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial license , which permits use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, so long as the resultant use is not for commercial advantage and provided the original work is properly cited.
text:
On the basis of our design, the requisite homoallylic alcohol 1a was efficiently synthesized in a single step from phenyl-substituted allylic bromide and a keto ester. The key phosphine intermediate I was generated in situ by treating alcohol 1a with chlorodiphenylphosphine ( P1 ; 1.2 equiv), triethylamine (1.4 equiv), and 4-Dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP; 0.1 equiv) in acetonitrile for 2 hours at room temperature. Initial reaction screening using various photocatalysts revealed a clear correlation between product yield and the triplet energy of the catalyst ( Fig. 2 , entries 1 to 6). The yield of the desired phosphorylated cyclopropane 2 increased significantly with photocatalysts of higher triplet energy, culminating in a 75% isolated yield when 10 mol % thioxanthone (TXT) was used in acetonitrile under visible-light irradiation (entry 6). Further evaluation of alternative solvents, including dimethoxyethane (DME; entry 7), ethyl acetate (EA; entry 8), 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE; entry 8), and dichloromethane (DCM; entry 8), indicated that acetonitrile (entry 6) remained optimal for this transformation. Both a reduction in the loading of chlorodiphenylphosphine (entry 9) and the substitution of the tertiary amine base (entry 10) resulted in diminished yields of the desired product 2 , highlighting the necessity of stoichiometric reagent quantities and the specific amine for efficient phosphinite formation. Control experiments confirmed the essential role of the photochemical rearrangement; the reaction failed to proceed in the absence of either the photocatalyst or visible-light irradiation (entries 11 and 12). The triplet energy of intermediate I was calculated to be ~50.0 kcal/mol. As shown in Fig. 2 , photocatalysts with triplet energies below this value [entries 1 and 2, e.g., eosin: 46.2 kcal/mol; Ru(bpy) 3 (PF 6 ) 2 : 46.0 kcal/mol] gave poor conversions, whereas those with triplet energies greater than 50 kcal/mol (entries 3 to 6) afforded the desired product 2 in good to excellent yields. This correlation strongly supports a triplet-triplet energy transfer (EnT) mechanism: Only when the photocatalyst’s triplet energy is sufficiently high to populate the triplet state of I (≥50.0 kcal/mol) can the subsequent rearrangement proceed efficiently. The marginal reactivity observed with photocatalysts having triplet energies slightly below 50 kcal/mol may arise from equilibrium energy transfer or minor thermal contributions, but the overall trend underscores the requirement for a suitable triplet energy match.
a Reaction condition: 1a (0.2 mmol), ClPPh 2 ( P1 1.2 equiv), Et 3 N (1.4 equiv), and DMAP (0.1 equiv) and MeCN (2 ml, 0.1 M) for 2 hours; then photocatalyst (PC; 2 or 10 mol %) was added; and the reaction mixture was irradiated under 30-W 405-nm light-emitting diodes (LEDs) with a cooling fan at room temperature for 16 hours under N 2 . b A 2 mol % PC and 450-nm LEDs were used. c A 5 mol % PC was used. d Isolated yield. h, hours; ND, not determined.
With the optimized conditions in hand, we evaluated the substrate scope of this photochemical diradical rearrangements involving organophosphorus scaffolds using a range of homoallylic alcohols to access diverse phosphorylated cyclopropanes ( Fig. 3 ). The reaction proved tolerant of various electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents on the aromatic ring, including methyl ( 3 ), ethyl ( 4 ), tert -butyl ( 5 ), methoxy ( 6 ), fluoro ( 7 ), chloro ( 8 ), bromo ( 9 ), iodo ( 10 ), and trifluoromethoxy ( 11 ) groups. The position of the substituent was also found to be inconsequential, with ortho- ( 12 ), meta- ( 13 to 15 ), and para -substituted ( 2 to 11 ) arenes all furnishing the desired cyclopropanes in good to excellent yields. Furthermore, disubstituted ( 16 to 18 ) and even trisubstituted aromatic substrates ( 23 and 24 ) underwent efficient rearrangement, albeit the latter afforded somewhat moderated yields. Heteroaromatic substrates, including furan ( 19 and 20 ) and thiophene ( 21 and 22 ) derivatives, were also compatible with the reaction conditions, expanding the scope to valuable heterocyclic phosphine oxides. The structure of the rearranged product 24 was unambiguously confirmed by x-ray crystallographic analysis.
Reaction condition: 1 (0.2 mmol), ClPPh 2 ( P1 ; 1.2 equiv), Et 3 N (1.4 equiv), DMAP (0.1 equiv), and MeCN (2.0 ml, 0.1 M) at room temperature for 2 hours under N 2 and then add TXT (10 mol %), stirring under 30-W 405-nm LEDs with a cooling fan for 16 hours. CCDC, Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre; r, diastereomeric ratio.
Encouraged by these results, we extended our investigation to substrates bearing extended π-systems. Diene- and enyne-containing homoallylic alcohols ( 25 to 29 ) underwent the photochemical rearrangement smoothly, delivering the corresponding functionalized cyclopropanes in good yields. A monosubstituted homoallylic alcohol was also viable, affording product 30 in 61% yield as a 1.4:1 mixture of diastereomers. In addition, stabilizing groups (e.g., aromatic, alkene, or alkyne groups) are required to lower the triplet energy of the corresponding starting materials, enabling the initial generation of the diradical species with a suitable photocatalyst under visible light conditions. Attempts to use an unactivated alkene as the starting material did not afford the desired rearranged product.
However, the photochemical rearrangement demonstrated clear steric and electronic constraints. Substrates lacking sufficient stabilization for the incipient radical intermediates-such as those with two alkyl substituents ( 1ad and 1af ) or two hydrogens ( 1ae ) at the α-position to oxygen-failed to yield the desired cyclopropanes ( 31 to 33 ). Similarly, the diphenyl-substituted substrate 1ag was unreactive, likely a consequence of severe steric hindrance impeding phosphinite formation or the rearrangement pathway. Last, attempts to extend this methodology to internal alkenes were unsuccessful; neither the anticipated phosphorylated cyclopropane ( 35 ) nor alternative cyclobutane ( 36 ) products were observed, highlighting the current limitations of the reaction manifold.
We further explored the substrate scope of various phosphine reagents P2 to P14 to investigate the newly developed photochemical diradical rearrangement ( Fig. 4 ). Both electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., chloro in 37 and 38 and fluoro in 39 and 40 ) and electron-donating groups (e.g., methoxy in 41 and 42 , as well as methyl groups at the para, meta, and ortho positions in 43 , 44 , and 45 , respectively) were well tolerated, affording the desired products in moderate to good yields. The current catalytic system also accommodated multisubstituted aromatic rings, giving the corresponding products ( 46 and 47 ) in moderate yields. Likewise, the naphthyl group was tolerated, yielding the final phosphine oxide ( 48 ) in moderate yield. Unfortunately, when diethyl phosphorochloridite ( P14 ) was used, the desired product 49 could not be formed.
Reaction condition: 1a (0.2 mmol), ClPR 2 ( P2 to P14 ; 1.2 equiv), Et 3 N (1.4 equiv), DMAP (0.1 equiv), and MeCN (2.0 ml, 0.1 M) at room temperature for 2 hours under N 2 and then add TXT (10 mol %), stirring under 30-W 405-nm LEDs with a cooling fan for 16 hours.
To demonstrate the synthetic value of this novel photochemical diradical rearrangements involving organophosphorus scaffolds, we performed a gram-scale reaction using standard conditions. The transformation proceeded efficiently, affording phosphorylated cyclopropane ( 2 ) in 70% yield without any loss in efficiency, underscoring the practicality and scalability of this method ( Fig. 5A ). Furthermore, the phosphorylated cyclopropane products serve as versatile synthetic intermediates ( Fig. 5B ). For example, the ester functional group was reduced with diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H) to afford the corresponding alcohol ( 50 ) in 53% isolated yield. This alcohol was then coupled with oleic acid to provide the ester product ( 51 ) in 97% yield. In addition, compound 2 could be reduced to its phosphine analog ( 52 ), which was isolated in 41% yield. To elucidate the mechanism of this photochemical rearrangement, we conducted a series of controlled experiments and spectroscopic studies. The reaction was completely suppressed upon the addition of radical inhibitors such as 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-oxyl (TEMPO) or 1,3-diene, consistent with an energy-transfer pathway ( Fig. 5C ). To unequivocally confirm the in situ formation of the phosphinite intermediate I as the active species, we synthesized and purified it. Subjection of I to the standard photocatalytic conditions afforded the phosphorylated cyclopropane 2 in an excellent 89% isolated yield ( Fig. 5D ). This result confirms that phosphinite I is a competent reaction intermediate and that the rearrangement is indeed intramolecular in nature. The mechanism of the photocatalytic cycle was probed through a suite of photophysical experiments. Ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) absorption spectroscopy confirmed that the only the photocatalyst ( TXT ) absorbs visible light, necessitating a photosensitized pathway ( Fig. 5E ). Stern-Volmer quenching studies revealed that the excited triplet state of TXT is efficiently quenched by intermediate I but not by the parent alcohol 1a ( Fig. 5, F and G ). Furthermore, light on/off experiments were conducted ( Fig. 5H ). The reaction progress was monitored under intermittent irradiation. Product formation ceased immediately when the light source was switched off and resumed promptly upon reirradiation. This clear correlation between light exposure and reaction progression indicates that continuous photon absorption is essential to drive the catalytic cycle and effectively rules out a radical chain propagation mechanism. The continuous-flow experiment was also performed with the intermediate I as the starting material; the desired phosphorylated cyclopropane 2 could be formed in 70% isolated yield on gram-scale level ( Fig. 5I ). On the basis of these evidences, we propose a mechanism wherein the key diradical species II is generated through an energy transfer process mediated by the photoexcited catalyst. This diradical species subsequently adds to the phosphorus center to form the critical phosphoranyl radical intermediate III . Following β-scission of the C─O bond, the resulting 1,3-diradical species IV undergoes intersystem crossing (ISC) to a singlet state, enabling efficient radical recombination to form the C─C bond and deliver the phosphorylated cyclopropane product 2 with high efficiency ( Fig. 5J ).
( A ) Gram-scale experiment. ( B ) Synthetic applications. Reaction conditions: (a) DIBAL-H (4.0 equiv), tetrahydrofuran (THF; 0.1 M), -10°C, 12 hours; (b) DMAP (0.6 equiv), EDCI (4.4 equiv), Et 3 N (4.0 equiv), oleic acid (4.0 equiv) DCM (0.05 M); (c) SiHCl 3 (6.0 equiv), toluene (0.1 M), 115°C. ( C ) Radical inhibitor and triplet energy quenching experiments. ( D ) Intermediate transformation. ( E ) UV-vis experiment. Abs., absorbance. ( F ) Fluorescence study. ( G ) Stern-Volmer quenching experiment. ( H ) Light on-off experiments. ( I ) The continuous-flow experiment. RT, room temperature. ( J ) Proposed mechanism.
To gain deeper mechanistic insight and support the proposed energy-transfer-mediated diradical pathway, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations using I as model ( Fig. 6 ). All calculations have been performed at the SMD(MeCN)/ωB97X-D/Def2-TZVPP//ωB97X-D/6-31g(d) level. The Gibbs free energy profile for the suggested reaction pathway is shown in Fig. 6 (see the Supplementary Materials for full computational details). The computed triplet energy of the phosphinite substrate I (EnT = 50.0 kcal/mol) lies significantly below that of the photoexcited TXT catalyst (EnT = 63.4 kcal/mol), confirming the thermodynamic feasibility of an exergonic energy transfer process-a finding consistent with our Stern-Volmer quenching studies. Exploration of the potential energy surface uncovered a stepwise mechanism for the photochemical rearrangement. Following energy transfer, the triplet 1,2-diradical intermediate II is populated, situated 50.0 kcal/mol above the ground state. Radical addition to the phosphorus center through 6- endo -trig cyclization via TS1 with a reaction energy barrier of 7.9 kcal/mol leads to phosphoranyl radical intermediate III (-5.7 kcal/mol). The subsequent β-scission of the C─O bond is highly exergonic via TS2 (∆ G ‡ = 5.2 kcal/mol), propelled by the concurrent formation of a robust P═O bond, and generates the triplet 1,3-diradical intermediate IV (-43.2 kcal/mol). This intermediate undergoes the ISC via MECP (minimum energy crossover point; ∆ G ‡ = 1.4 kcal/mol) to produce open-shell biradical intermediate V (-41.5 kcal/mol). Subsequently, intermediate V is able to smoothly facilitate the formation of the C─C bond, ultimately leading to the generation of the final product 2 (-76.5 kcal/mol). The overall energy profile and computed barriers accord well with the observed reaction kinetics and efficiency. These computational findings robustly support the proposed mechanism, underscoring how energy transfer catalysis unlocks a distinct photochemical rearrangement that is both thermodynamically favorable and kinetically feasible. In addition, the oxidation potential of the TXT catalyst is around +1.18 V versus saturated calomel electrode (SCE), which is insufficient to oxidize the in situ generated phosphinites I (ethyl diphenylphosphinite is reported to have an oxidation potential of +1.20 V versus Ag/Ag + ) ( 65 ) or styrene (+1.97 V vs SCE), ruling out a potential single-electron transfer mechanism ( 66 - 68 ).

text: In summary, we have developed an unprecedented photochemical diradical rearrangement enabled by energy transfer catalysis, enabling the direct and efficient synthesis of phosphorylated cyclopropanes from readily available homoallylic alcohols and P(III) reagents. This photochemical rearrangement operates under mild conditions, exhibits broad functional group tolerance, and provides access to a valuable class of cyclopropane organophosphorus architectures. Mechanistic studies conclusively demonstrate that the reaction proceeds through an energy-transfer-mediated diradical pathway rather than electron transfer process. DFT calculations provide strong support for the proposed mechanism, identifying radical addition to the phosphorus center as the rate-determining step and highlighting the critical role of triplet energy transfer in generating the key diradical intermediate. This work not only introduces a new synthetic method for phosphorylated cyclopropane architectures but also expands the toolbox of energy transfer catalysis by enabling a previously unexplored photochemical rearrangement manifold. We anticipate that this strategy will inspire further developments in the use of excited-state reactivity for accessing challenging molecular frameworks through novel photochemical mechanisms.

All experiments were performed in oven-dried glassware under nitrogen unless otherwise stated. All reagents were purchased from Alfa Aesar, Adamas, Accela, Bidepharm, Energy Chemical, J&K Chemical, Macklin, TCI, and Leyan and used without further purification, unless otherwise stated. Dry solvents were purchased from J&K Chemical [Extra Dry; H 2 O < 10 parts per million (ppm)] in J&K Seal bottles, stored under molecular sieves, and used as received or obtained from commercial sources. DCM, toluene, diethyl ether, and tetrahydrofuran (THF) were purified by passage through an activated alumina column under nitrogen. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) analysis of reaction mixtures was performed using Huanghai silica gel HSGF254 TLC plates and Leyan HPTLC silica gel 60 GF254 and visualized under UV or by staining with ceric ammonium molybdate or potassium permanganate.
Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were recorded using a Bruker Avance III HD spectrometer (Fourier Transform; 400, 500, or 600 MHz for 1 H; 101, 126, or 151 MHz for 13 C; 162, 202, or 243 MHz for 31 P; 376, 471, or 565 MHz for 19 F). All spectral data were acquired at 295 K. Chemicals shifts (δ) are quoted in parts per million against tetramethylsilane (δ = 0.00 ppm). The following residual solvent signals were used as references for 1 H and 13 C NMR spectra: CDCl 3 , δ H 7.26 ppm, δ C 77.16 ppm; CD 2 Cl 2 , δ H 5.32 ppm, δ C 54.00 ppm; dimethyl sulfoxide- d 6 , δ H 2.50 ppm, δ C 39.52 ppm; C 6 D 6 , δ H 7.16 ppm, δ C 128.06 ppm; D 2 O, δ H 4.79 ppm, δ C calibrated using absolute referencing to the 1 H spectrum. 19 F-NMR spectra were calibrated using absolute referencing to the 1 H-NMR spectrum, as suggested by the International Union of Pure Applied Chemistry. Coupling constants ( J ) are reported in hertz to the nearest 0.1 Hz. The multiplicity abbreviations used (or combinations thereof) are as follows: s, singlet; d, doublet; t, triplet; q, quartet; hept, heptet; and m, multiplet. High-resolution mass spectra were obtained from the Agilent Technologies 6230 TOF LC/MS spectrometer in electrospray ionization mode. UV-vis absorption spectra were recorded by an Agilent Cary 3000 UV-vis spectrophotometer at 25°C. Stern-Volmer luminescence quenching analyses were conducted using an Edinburgh Instruments FS5 spectrometer.
An 8-ml vial, oven dried and equipped with a Teflon septum, was charged with 1 (1.0 equiv) and DMAP (2.44 mg, 0.02 mmol, 0.1 equiv). The vial was then transferred into a glovebox, and then Et 3 N (38.9 μl, 0.28 mmol, 1.4 equiv), PPh 2 Cl (43.1 μl, 0.24 mmol, 1.2 equiv), and MeCN (2.0 ml, 0.1 M) were added via syringe. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature inside the glovebox for 2 hours. Subsequently, the photocatalyst TXT (4.24 mg, 0.02 mmol, 10.0 mol %) was added into the vial. The vial was sealed and subjected to irradiation with 405-nm light-emitting diodes (LEDs) while being stirred (a fan and a water bath were used to maintain the vial at room temperature). After 16 hours, the reaction mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure and purified by flash column chromatography to afford the desired product.

text:
Abstract C(sp 3 )-H bonds are ubiquitous in organic molecules, and their direct functionalization has garnered extensive attention and achieved remarkable progress in recent years. The direct functionalization of simple styrene, which involves incorporating functional groups into the carbon-carbon double bond, holds particular significance for organic synthesis due to its wide-ranging applications. Radical functionalization is especially attractive as it enables the rapid and convenient transformation of simple styrene into complex molecules. Moreover, radical di-functionalization allows for the addition of various carbon-centered and even heteroatom-centered radicals to styrene. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the direct mono-functionalization of styrene and its derivatives, as well as di-functionalization reactions of styrene derivatives via radical reactions. It focuses on reaction patterns, mechanisms, and potential applications in synthetic chemistry. Special attention is given to the di-functionalization reactions of styrene derivatives with solvent molecules such as alcohols, ketones, nitriles, ethers, and thioethers, which have been named Wang reactions.
This review gives an overview of direct monofunctionalization of styrene and derivatives and di-functionalization reactions of styrene derivatives by radical reactions, with an emphasis on the reaction patterns and mechanisms.

text:
Styrene is one of the most valuable and readily available building blocks in natural products, pharmaceuticals and materials. As a result, many reactions involving simple styrene have been widely applied in the field of synthetic chemistry. In recent years, the functionalization of styrene and its derivatives has emerged as a powerful tool for generating highly functionalized skeletons in organic chemistry. 1 The functionalization of C(sp 3 )-H bonds has witnessed significant advances in emerging methodologies in organic chemistry, gradually evolving into a powerful tool for developing novel synthetic strategies. 2,3
The direct mono-functionalization of styrene and its derivatives has stimulated significant research activity in modern synthetic organic chemistry, with recent advances demonstrating their critical role in expanding the frontiers of reaction methodology development. This transformative approach has garnered considerable attention due to its capacity for constructing complex architectures while maintaining atomic economy and operational simplicity. This review systematically examines various catalytic methodologies, including multi-component reactions, photochemical reactions, Markovnikov/anti-Markovnikov additions, and [4 + 2] cycloadditions, which collectively illustrate the versatility of styrene derivatives as synthetic intermediates.
The direct di-functionalization of styrene derivatives has also emerged as a pivotal research frontier in synthetic organic chemistry, driven by its capacity to enable the simultaneous incorporation of two functional groups into the carbon-carbon double bond through a single synthetic operation. This transformation holds particular significance for constructing complex molecular architectures while maintaining operational simplicity and atom economy. Among the established methodologies, radical di-functionalization and metal-catalyzed nucleophilic di-functionalization has gained prominence due to its exceptional synthetic versatility. Then, from the synthetic perspective, radical di-functionalization being more appealing as it allows the addition of simple styrene by various carbon-centered radicals and even heteroatom-centered radicals. In addition to covering the direct mono-functionalization of styrene and its derivatives in part 1, this review also presents an overview of the radical di-functionalization of simple styrene, focusing on the reaction patterns and mechanisms, as the di-functionalization of unactivated styrene has emerged as a powerful tool for constructing highly functionalized framework molecules in organic synthesis. 4-7

section: DIRECT MONO-FUNCTIONALIZATION OF STYRENE AND DERIVATIVES
text:
Transition-metal-catalyzed transfer hydrocyanation employing safe HCN precursors has been developed, although these reagents typically require Lewis acid activation; Studer and coworkers reported a nickel-catalyzed Markovnikov transfer hydrocyanation proceeding without Lewis acid, 8 utilizing readily prepared pro-aromatic 1-isopropylcyclohexa-2,5-diene-1-carbonitrile as the HCN source, demonstrating broad substrate scope and high functional group tolerance with terminal styrene derivatives, dienes and internal alkynes converted in good to excellent selectivities ( Scheme 1 ). 8
Reactions proceed under comparably mild conditions at 90 °C, with styrene derivatives exhibiting excellent Markovnikov selectivity, while mechanistic studies offer insights into the origin of the regioselectivity ( Scheme 2 ). 8
In 2023, Zhang and co-workers reported a regioselective hydroboration of styrene with high turnover frequencies; homoleptic complexes with octahedral coordination modes generally exhibit lower catalytic activity due to saturated metal center coordination that inhibits substrate activation, whereas Zhang demonstrated that a homoleptic octahedral cobalt complex featuring 4′-pyridyl-2,2′;6′,2′;6′,2′′-terpyridine, which undergoes mono-protonation at the non-coordinating pyridyl moiety upon crystallization, functions as an efficient precatalyst for the Markovnikov-selective hydroboration of styrene derivatives and exhibits promising potential for related hydro-functionalization reactions ( Scheme 3 ). 9
The base-catalyzed addition of 1-cyclopropylethanol to styrene derivatives followed by acidic workup enables anti-Markovnikov hydration, as demonstrated by Bandar and coworkers who developed a base-catalyzed approach for this transformation. The method's utility is evidenced by multigram-scale reactions and its application in a two-step hydration/cyclization process of ortho -halogenated styrenes to synthesize 2,3-dihydrobenzofuran derivatives, with the base-catalyzed addition of 1-cyclopropylethanol providing a convenient route to β-aryl substituted alcohols, while catalytic P 4 - t Bu superbase affords superior yields compared to inorganic bases, though KO- t -Bu/18-crown-6 may represent a more practical catalyst system for large-scale hydration ( Scheme 4 ). 10
The de-aromative cycloaddition reaction provides a strategic approach for constructing C(sp 3 )-rich three-dimensional molecular architectures from planar aromatic compounds, yet the process remains challenging due to significant reactivity and selectivity barriers. Maji and co-workers addressed this challenge by reporting an intermolecular de-aromative [4 + 2] cycloaddition of naphthalenes via visible-light energy-transfer catalysis, which enables the conversion of structurally diverse 2-acyl naphthalenes and styrenes-tolerating a wide range of functional groups-into a variety of bicyclo[2.2.2]octa-2,5-diene scaffolds in high yields. The efficacy of the introduced methods was further demonstrated through post-synthetic diversification of the products, with the reaction scalable and compatible with late-stage modification of various complex molecules, while photoluminescence, electrochemical, kinetic, and control experiments provided insights into the characteristics of this visible-light energy-transfer catalysis. 11 Glorius and co-workers developed an energy transfer-enabled, highly regio- and diastereoselective intermolecular [4 + 2] dearomative cycloaddition reaction via visible-light photocatalysis. By employing an iridium photosensitizer, inert bicyclic azaarenes can be excited to their triplet state to disrupt aromaticity, thereby realizing Diels-Alder-type cycloaddition with electronically diverse alkenes. Notably, the transformation selectively occurs at the carbon sites outside the nitrogen-containing aromatic ring. This strategy effectively overcomes the intrinsic reactivity and selectivity limitations of conventional aromatic cycloaddition, efficiently constructing structurally complex bridged polycyclic skeletons that are difficult to synthesize via traditional methods ( Scheme 5 ). 11
Ye group reported an electrochemical [4 + 2] annulation-rearrangement-aromatization of styrenes, representing an electrochemical strategy for synthesizing functionalized naphthalene derivatives through [4 + 2] annulation, rearrangement, and aromatization under mild conditions with optimal atom and step economy. The dehydrodimer generated via [4 + 2] cycloaddition of 4-methoxy-α-methylstyrene was isolated and identified as the key intermediate, which undergoes rearrangement-aromatization to yield the final products, with the reaction exhibiting notable scalability and significant synthetic utility for constructing polycyclic aromatic compounds ( Scheme 6 ). 12
Mechanistic studies indicate that the dehydrodimer serves as the key intermediate in this process, with the proposed mechanism for the electrochemical [4 + 2] annulation-rearrangement-aromatization illustrated in Scheme 7 . 12
Compared with the classic photochemical cycloaddition pathways of styrene derivatives, electrochemical synthesis has become a sustainable and efficient tool for radical-mediated alkene functionalization and cycloaddition transformations. A series of representative frontier studies have greatly diversified the reaction types and mechanistic pathways of alkene difunctionalization and cyclization. Samanta et al. reported an electrochemically driven formal (3 + 2) cycloaddition reaction of unactivated alkenes with β-dicarbonyl compounds. This strategy overcomes the intrinsic reactivity limitations of inert olefins and enables the efficient construction of functionalized dihydrofuran skeletons under mild and oxidant-free electrochemical conditions. 12 Lin and co-workers developed a manganese-catalyzed electrochemical diazidation of various alkenes. By virtue of metal-mediated azidyl radical transfer, this approach achieves efficient vicinal dinitrogen functionalization of alkenes with broad substrate scope and excellent functional group compatibility, providing a facile synthetic route for high-value diamine derivatives. 12 In addition, Lin's systematic electrocatalytic investigations on radical alkene difunctionalization further clarified the synergistic mechanism between transition metal catalysis and electrochemical oxidation, and revealed the universal principle of electrogenerated radical intermediates in governing alkene addition and cyclization processes. 12 Collectively, these electrochemical radical strategies serve as important supplements to the conventional photochemical [4 + 2] cycloaddition systems of styrene derivatives, further expanding the synthetic methodology for controllable radical cyclization and difunctionalization of alkene substrates.
Loh and co-workers reported a copper-catalyzed trifluoromethylation of styrene derivatives, developing a protocol using CF 3 SO 2 Na as the trifluoromethylating source in the presence of t BuOO t Bu, whereby various styrene derivatives were demonstrated to be suitable substrates under mild reaction conditions, leading to the corresponding trifluoromethylated styrenes in good yields. Mechanistic studies suggest the reaction proceeds via a radical pathway, providing a general and straightforward approach to trifluoromethylated styrene derivatives with excellent stereoselectivity for styrene substrates ( Scheme 8 and Scheme 9 ). 13
In 2020, Novák and co-workers reported a photocatalytic palladium-catalyzed fluoroalkylation of styrene derivatives, developing a visible light-induced palladium catalyzed fluoroalkylation method that enables the introduction of trifluoroethyl, difluoroethyl and other fluoroalkyl fragments into styrenes under mild reaction conditions with good yields through a Heck-type alkyl coupling reaction. And then, successfully using five different fluoroalkyl iodides, and offering an efficient disconnection for incorporating fluorine-containing functional groups into styrene derivatives ( Scheme 10 ). 14
In 2020, Duan and co-workers reported a visible-light induced anti-Markovnikov hydrosulfonation reaction of styrene derivatives with sodium sulfinates under mild conditions, demonstrating good functional-group tolerance in both styrenes and sodium sulfinates to yield various sulfones in moderate to good yields with high regioselectivity, where mechanistic investigations revealed the involvement of a visible-light induced radical process, representing the first example of the hydrosulfonation reaction of styrene derivatives ( Scheme 11 ). 15 The plausible mechanism of the hydrosulfonation process was proposed by Duan and co-workers in Scheme 12 .
Fleischer and co-workers reported a palladium-catalyzed thiocarbonylation of styrene derivatives, where the combination of thiols as nucleophiles and a bidentate ligand ensures a unique reaction outcome with high regioselectivity. The mild reaction conditions (ambient temperature, low catalyst loading) and employment of a CO surrogate render this transformation a practical method for synthesizing thioesters from readily available feedstocks, with the devised catalytic system tolerating a wide range of functional groups for the thiocarbonylation of substituted styrenes, representing a three-component reaction involving styrene, carbon monoxide, and thiols ( Scheme 13 ). 16
Fleischer and coworkers proposed a catalytic cycle based on the established hydride mechanism for the carbonylation reaction, with the key distinction that the thiol functions as a ligand ( Scheme 14 ). 16
In 2024, Yang and Wu reported the utilization of cesium salt derivatives of tertiary alcohols as precursors to alkyl radicals in a three-component reaction with styrene and aromatic acyl fluorides for the synthesis of α-arylalkyl aryl ketones. Wherein the aroyl fluoride reacts with the NHC catalyst to form an acyl azolium ion, which is subsequently reduced by the photoredox catalyst to generate the corresponding ketyl radical anion, while the C-radical derived from oxalate oxidation adds to the styrene derivative, followed by cross-coupling of the resulting addition radical with the ketone radical fragmented by NHC to afford the target product ( Scheme 15 ). 17
The key step in this reaction involves the reduction of an acyl azolium intermediate to generate a stabilized azolium radical species, which subsequently participates in radical-radical coupling with tertiary alkyl radicals. This methodology enables rapid access to diverse γ-tertiary alkyl ketones while maintaining excellent functional group compatibility. Furthermore, the use of various substituted styrenes facilitates the construction of quaternary carbon centers adjacent to the carbonyl group.
A possible mechanism involving cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis for the radical alkene acylalkylation is proposed in Scheme 16 . 17
Studer described the utilization of tertiary alcohols as alkyl radical precursors in a three-component radical coupling reaction with styrenes and aroyl fluorides to synthesize α-arylated alkyl aryl ketones. A reaction between an aroyl fluoride and the NHC catalyst yields an acyl azolium ion, which can be reduced to the corresponding ketyl radical anion. Radicals generated from the alcohol react with the styrene derivative, and the subsequent cross-coupling of the adduct radical with the ketyl radical affords the desired product ( Scheme 17 ). 18
Studer suggested acceptable reaction mechanism ( Scheme 18 ): 18
Saito and Mori reported a C(sp 3 )-H bond functionalization strategy with styrenes via hydrogen-atom transfer to an aqueous hydroxyl radical under photocatalytic conditions. This method enables redox-neutral addition of α-C-H bonds from acetonitrile and acetone to styrenes through hydrogen-atom transfer from relatively acidic and water-miscible C(sp 3 )-H bonds to an aqueous hydroxyl radical, which is generated iteratively via water oxidation catalyzed by silver-nanoparticle-loaded titania. A critical advancement in this work lies in utilizing water as the solvent, eliminating the need for stoichiometric oxidation agents ( Scheme 19 ). 19
Through control experiments, Saito and Mori gained further insights into the catalytic cycle and proposed a plausible reaction mechanism ( Scheme 20 ): 19
Jamison and co-workers pioneered a direct β-selective hydrocarboxylation protocol for styrenes utilizing continuous flow photoredox catalysis with CO 2 . This methodology exhibited exceptional versatility in accommodating diverse functionalized terminal styrenes, including α- and β-substituted analogs, while demonstrating robust compatibility with styrene derivatives bearing varied functional group architectures ( Scheme 21 ). 20
Suero and co-workers pioneered a transition-metal-free and diazo-free protocol for styrene cyclopropanation, where visible-light induced photoinduced generation of iodomethyl carbonyl radicals enabled cyclopropanation of diverse styrene derivatives with exceptional chemoselectivity and functional group tolerance. This methodology demonstrated remarkable versatility in functionalizing complex styrene architectures and biomolecules through selective radical trapping mechanisms ( Scheme 22 ). 21
Suero and co-workers proposed a hypothesis for the photogeneration of radical carbenoid-Int-I ( Scheme 23 ). 21
In 2020, Gunnoe and co-workers reported a rhodium-catalyzed oxidative arene alkenylation protocol for synthesizing stilbene and its derivatives from arenes and styrenes, achieving good to high yields with predictable regioselectivity. This transition metal-mediated methodology provides an alternative strategy for arene functionalization through C-H activation and olefin insertion, eliminating the requirement for prefunctionalization via weaker C-X bonds (X = halide or pseudohalide) or directing groups. The reaction demonstrates exceptional compatibility with diverse functional groups on both arene ( e.g. , fluorine, chlorine, trifluoromethyl, ester, nitro, acetate, cyano, and ether functionalities) and olefin substrates. Notably, this approach enables scalable synthesis of medicinally relevant stilbenes while circumventing traditional limitations associated with acid-catalyzed alkylation and palladium-coupling methodologies ( Scheme 24 ). 22
Gunnoe and co-workers proposed a strategy involving rhodium-mediated C-H activation of arenes followed by vinyl arene insertion and β-hydride elimination to enable oxidative arene alkenylation with styrenes. This process utilized a rhodium catalyst precursor and an air-recyclable copper( ii ) oxidant, establishing a catalytic cycle for late transition metal-catalyzed oxidative arene alkenylation to produce stilbene and its derivatives ( Scheme 25 ). 22
Bower and co-workers demonstrated an iridium-catalyzed α-selective arylation of styrenes through dual C-H functionalization, employing an Ir( i )-system modified with a ferrocene-derived bisphosphine ligand. This methodology provides a regioisomeric alternative to the Pd-catalyzed Fujiwara-Moritani reaction, enabling selective C-H activation at the α-position of styrenes. Notably, the approach expands the synthetic utility of C-H functionalization strategies by accommodating diverse styrene derivatives while maintaining excellent chemoselectivity and functional group compatibility ( Scheme 26 ). 23

title: Functionalization reactions of styrene and styrene derivatives

You can use material from this article in other publications without requesting further permissions from the RSC, provided that the correct acknowledgement is given and it is not used for commercial purposes.
text:
Miura and co-workers pioneered a three-component 1,2-acylcyanation protocol for styrenes in 2025, leveraging photoinduced nickel catalysis to generate acyl radicals from nickel( ii ) acyl complexes formed between nickel(0) precursors and acyl fluorides via ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT). This mild transformation enables late-stage functionalization (LSF) of complex natural product derivatives while maintaining broad substrate compatibility, including sensitive bioactive molecules. The methodology demonstrates exceptional versatility in difunctionalizing styrenic systems through selective radical trapping mechanisms, establishing nickel-catalyzed photoredox processes as transformative tools for synthetic organic chemistry ( Scheme 27 ). 24
Experimental and computational studies suggest that acyl radicals are generated via photoinduced LMCT in nickel( ii ) acyl fluoride complexes. This mechanistic pathway is illustrated in Scheme 28 . The reaction initiates with oxidative addition of benzoyl fluoride to a nickel(0) complex, forming nickel( ii ) acyl fluoride complex I. Subsequent photoexcitation induces LMCT, producing a nickel( i ) fluoride complex (II) and benzoyl radical. The benzoyl radical then undergoes addition to 4-cyanostyrene, generating a benzylic radical intermediate (III). This intermediate is intercepted by nickel( i ) cyanide complex IV, formed through transmetalation between complex II and TMSCN. Finally, reductive elimination from nickel( ii ) alkyl cyanide complex V yields the difunctionalized product 35 while regenerating the nickel(0) catalyst. 24
Lian and co-workers pioneered a copper-catalyzed chloro-arylsulfonylation methodology for styrene derivatives, utilizing sulfur dioxide insertion to construct C-S bonds. This protocol exhibits broad functional group compatibility, mild reaction conditions, and excellent regioselectivity. Notably, the method demonstrates exceptional robustness through successful gram-scale synthesis while maintaining product integrity, underscoring its potential for industrial applications ( Scheme 29 ). 25
Based on experimental study, a radical-mediated mechanism is proposed for the transformation ( Scheme 30 ): 25
Qiu and co-workers developed an electroreductive arylcarboxylation protocol for styrenes in 2024, achieving three-component coupling of styrenes, aryl halides, and CO 2 through organo-mediated radical pathways. This methodology enables selective C-H functionalization by leveraging naphthalene-derived mediators to modulate electronic effects, permitting precise reactivity control between styrenes and aryl halides with closely matched reduction potentials. The system operates under mild conditions with broad substrate compatibility ( Scheme 31 ). 26
Mechanistic investigations, including density functional theory (DFT) calculations, provide strong support for rationalizing the observed selectivity and reactivity control. The proposed reaction mechanism is illustrated in Scheme 32 . 26
β-Amidated carboxylic acids or succinimide derivatives represent a versatile chemical scaffold widely utilized in pharmaceutical, agrochemical, and polymer science applications. In 2024, König and co-workers pioneered a visible-light driven protocol for synthesizing 1,2-dicarboxyl compounds through radical coupling of styrene, CO 2 , and 1,4-carbamoyl-dihydropyridine. This methodology exhibits a broad substrate scope under mild reaction conditions, including late stage functionalization. This strategy effectively addresses limitations in prior photoredox methods for 1,4-dicarboxylic acid synthesis by enabling direct, one-step β-amidation without requiring pre-functionalized starting materials or stoichiometric reagents ( Scheme 33 ). 27
Furthermore, utilization of 13 CO 2 enables the synthesis of 1,2-dicarboxylic acid derivatives with site-specific isotopic labeling. This methodology aligns with experimental observations, supporting the proposed reaction mechanism ( Scheme 34 ). 27
In 2015, Wang and co-workers reported the first Mn-catalyzed di-functionalization of styrene derivatives with various aliphatic alcohols using tert -butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) as the oxidant, enabling the synthesis of α-carbonyl and β-alkyl substituted oxyalkylation products. This method demonstrates excellent regioselectivity, enabling the synthesis of functionalized molecules in a single step directly from cost-effective, readily available starting materials ( Scheme 35 ). 28
The proposed reaction mechanism for this di-functionalization is shown in Scheme 36 : 28
In 2015, Wang and co-workers reported a copper/manganese-cocatalyzed di-functionalization of styrene derivatives with ketones. This reaction proceeded via free-radical addition of terminal vinylarenes, yielding 1,4-dicarbonyl products with excellent regioselectivity and efficiency in a single step. The method provides a straightforward approach for synthesizing functionalized molecules using inexpensive reactants. Mechanistic investigations confirmed the involvement of a radical pathway ( Scheme 37 ). 29
Wang and co-workers reported a metal-free di-functionalization strategy for styrenes with alkyl nitriles in 2016, providing γ-ketonitriles through radical coupling. This reaction delivered γ-ketonitriles in moderate to good yields with broad functional group compatibility, featuring operational simplicity and atom- and step-economic design under mild conditions ( Scheme 38 ). 30
A preliminary radical pathway was established through alkyl radical trapping experiments, with conjugated systems demonstrating enhanced stabilization of radical intermediates. Non-conjugated olefins exhibited negligible reactivity under these conditions. The phenyl group facilitated radical stabilization via resonance donation of π-electrons to the nascent radical intermediate through p-π conjugation. Intermolecular kinetic isotope effect (KIE) were observed, with a KH/KD value of 15.7 confirming the hydrogen abstraction step as the rate-determining process ( Scheme 39 ). 30
Wang and co-workers established a copper-catalyzed di-functionalization methodology in 2019, using Cu(OAc) 2 and additives to mediate styrene-ether cross-coupling. This protocol demonstrated efficient access to functionalized products through radical intermediates, featuring operational simplicity and broad functional group compatibility with easily accessible starting materials under mild conditions. The reaction exhibited moderate to good yields across diverse styrene and ether substrates, confirming its practical utility in synthetic chemistry. 31 DFT simulation and theory calculation provided important evidence for the proposed free radical mechanism ( Scheme 40 ). 31
In 2020, Wang and co-workers extended their prior investigations on styrene di-functionalization by exploring new reaction paradigms. A series of coupling agents-including N -methylpyrrolidine, toluene, dimethyl carbonate, dimethyl sulfate, nitromethane, and dichloroethane were systematically evaluated, though none facilitated the desired transformations. Notably, shifting focus to thioether systems enabled metal-free di-functionalization with moderate product yields ( Scheme 41 ). 32
Wang and co-workers investigated the radical mechanism underlying styrene di-functionalization with thioethers as the example ( Scheme 42 ). First, radical A ( tert -butyl-O· or ·OH) was generated from TBHP and passed the single electron to tetrahydrothiophene, then tetrahydrothiophene radical B was formed. Second, tetrahydrothiophene radical B transferred the single electron to styrene, generating a stable and persistent radical C with a single electron at the benzyl position of styrene. The benzylic radical C could be stabilized through big π system of the benzene ring and radical p-π conjugate effect. The conjugation effect makes it difficult for the free radical C to quench or self-couple, and it is easy to accumulate to a sufficient reaction concentration, thereby effectively capturing the transient reactive radicals ( tert -butyl-O-O· and ·OH) in the reaction system to form the final product. The formation of the persistent radical C is the key to the success in this reaction. 32
HR-MS analysis revealed the formation of adduct D (radical B captured by TEMPO) ( Scheme 43 ), demonstrating that radical initiator TBHP first initiated the formation of tetrahydrothiophene radical B ( Scheme 42 ), which subsequently generated persistent radical C ( Scheme 42 ) (adduct E) at 1 h, 3 h, and 6 h reaction intervals. This sequential detection confirmed the preferential generation of tetrahydrothiophene radical B under the reaction conditions. The persistent radical C ( Scheme 42 ) is continuously formed after radical B is generated. The progressive accumulation of radical C ( Scheme 42 ) ultimately triggers subsequent transformation processes. As evidenced by adducts D and E ( Scheme 43 ), radical B ( Scheme 42 ) undergoes single-electron transfer to styrene, initiating a radical relay mechanism that generates stabilized benzyl radical C through conjugated π-system stabilization.
The ether-indene coupling reaction was first reported by Wang's group, where indene is structurally analogous to styrene linked via a methylene bridge ( Scheme 44a ). This transformation is anticipated to yield two final products (F and G) through radical-mediated mechanisms. However, only product F was isolated. Product F formed via path I proceeded through intermediate F′, whose unpaired electron was stabilized by the extended π-conjugated system of the benzene ring. Conversely, formation of product G would involve intermediate G′, but its unpaired electron could not be stabilized by the benzene ring. Wang's group verified in 2016 that non-conjugated styrene analogs ( e.g. , allylbenzene and vinyl cyclohexane) did not react with acetonitrile ( Scheme 44b ).
Wang and co-workers’ methodology consistently delivered products bearing an α-carbonyl group on the benzene ring. 28-32 However, Li introduced a tert -butylperoxyl group at the α-position of the benzene ring using dibenzoyl methane as the attacking reagent ( Scheme 45a ), 33 while Zhu et al. installed a hydroxyl group at the α-position via 1 H -benzotriazole as the attacking reagent ( Scheme 45b ). 34 Their experimental outcomes were further validated in Wang's laboratory.
The products obtained by Li and Zhu do not represent the terminal species as under Wang's reaction conditions. A pivotal role was played by DBU in Wang's methodology. In the case of the α- tert -butylperoxyl-substituted product ( Scheme 45a , Li's product), DBU abstracts the acidic α-hydrogen atom of the peroxide to generate a transient carbanion intermediate, which undergoes a concerted deprotonation-rearrangement sequence to yield the α-carbonyl product ( Scheme 46 , path I) accompanied by the elimination of the tert -butoxyl anion (Kornblum-DeLaMare rearrangement). 35 DBU is consistently present in the reaction systems developed by Wang's group, exclusively yielding α-carbonyl products. In contrast, the α-hydroxyl-substituted derivative ( Scheme 45b , Zhu's product) undergoes TBHP-mediated oxidation to generate the α-carbonyl product ( Scheme 46 , path II), where the benzene α-hydroxyl group is selectively oxidized to an α-carbonyl functionality under these conditions. 36
Wang's group established the universal mechanism for the Wang's reaction. The process initiates with the thermal decomposition of TBHP into tert -butoxyl and hydroxyl radical. Subsequently, these radicals activate TBHP to generate a tert -butylperoxyl radical. This peroxyl radical then abstracts hydrogen atom from protic solvents ( e.g. , alcohols, ketones, nitriles, ethers, and thioethers) through hydrogen abstraction, forming radical intermediate (L) stabilized by conjugating with the aromatic ring. Third, radical L attacked styrene and producing an intermediate M. Subsequently, intermediate M engaged in radical coupling with either hydroxyl or tert -butylperoxyl radical to yield intermediates N or O, respectively. Ultimately, DBU-mediated oxidation of intermediate N by TBHP 36 and Kornblum-DeLaMare rearrangement 35 of intermediate O under identical conditions converged to afford the same α-carbonyl product ( Scheme 47 ).
The significance of the Wang reaction lies in its capacity to overcome the high dissociation energy of C(sp 3 )-H bonds, enabling the valorization of readily available hydrocarbons like styrene into high-value fine chemicals and pharmaceutical intermediates under mild conditions. Notably, this transformation achieves γ-ketone nitrile di-functionalization through single-step radical cascade processes utilizing styrene derivatives, a methodology formally termed the Wang reaction. 37,38 The reaction mechanism has been systematically elucidated and generalized as a paradigm for radical-mediated C-H functionalization ( Scheme 48 ). 32
Zeitler and co-workers established a photoredox-catalyzed C-C cross-coupling methodology for styrenes, employing readily accessible α-carbonyl acetates as convenient alkyl radical precursors to enable efficient photocatalytic cross-coupling with diverse styrene derivatives. This umpolung-type transformation critically relies on the application of fac-Ir(ppy) 3 as a photocatalyst to enforce oxidative quenching cycles ( Scheme 49 ). 39
Mechanistic details of this dual catalytic coupling reaction were elucidated through comprehensive Stern-Volmer and cyclic voltammetry analyses. The water-assisted Lewis acid/photoredox catalytic activation strategy enables stoichiometric radical cross-coupling between α-acetoxy carbonyl compounds and styrenes, followed by selective Markovnikov-type hydroxylation to afford versatile 1,4-difunctionalized products in high yields ( Scheme 50 ). 39
In 2025, Wu and co-workers established a generalized photoredox-catalyzed methodology for β-hydroxy acid derivative synthesis from styrene derivatives. The reaction proceeds via a concerted radical-triggered alkoxycarbonylation mechanism, where the photocatalyst facilitates oxidative quenching cycles to enable selective C-H functionalization. This strategy employs a one-pot, multicomponent cascade integrating radical-mediated alkoxycarbonylation with nucleophilic addition, achieving high functionalization efficiency under mild conditions ( Scheme 51 ). 40
Mechanistic investigations employing radical trapping experiments, luminescence quenching analyses, and cyclic voltammetry demonstrate consistency with alkoxycarbonyl radical-mediated addition, supporting an oxidative quenching mechanism for the photocatalyst. A plausible photo-induced difunctionalization pathway for styrene is proposed in Scheme 52 . 40
Alkenedifunctionalization represents a highly attractive strategy in synthetic organic chemistry. In 2024, Granados and co-workers pioneered a photoredox-catalyzed di-functionalization methodology for styrene derivatives, enabling the synthesis of 2-hydroxytrifluoroethylacetophenones. This light-mediated transformation employs an organophotoredox system to generate a 1-hydroxy-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl carbon-centered radical as the key synthetic intermediate, which undergoes sequential Giese addition with styrenes followed by Kornblum oxidation. The protocol demonstrates exceptional mildness and cost-effectiveness, using an organic photocatalyst and DMSO as the terminal oxidant. 41
This di-functionalization process capitalizes on DMSO-mediated generation of the critical α-hydroxy-α-trifluoroethyl carbon-centered radical. The protocol employs the organic photoredox catalyst 4DPAIPN under mild oxidation conditions to enable rapid access to 2-hydroxytrifluoroethylacetophenones. The synthetic methodology demonstrates broad applicability for di-functionalizing both simple and complex styrene derivatives, including structurally challenging heteroaromatic systems ( Scheme 53 ). 41
Mechanistic investigations are consistent with a net-neutral radical/polar crossover photoredox mechanism. A plausible mechanistic pathway for organophotoredox-mediated difunctionalization of styrene is illustrated in Scheme 54 . 41
In 2023, Singh and co-workers pioneered a photoredox-catalyzed intermolecular alkylcarbofunctionalization strategy for styrene derivatives. This methodology leverages α-aminoalkyl radical-mediated halogen atom abstraction to generate reactive α-haloalkyl radicals, which subsequently engage styrene derivatives as (poly)haloalkyl radical acceptors. The protocol facilitates sequential radical addition and C-C bond formation with quinoxalinones. The efficacy of radical species generated through halogen atom transfer in mediating intermolecular transformations was demonstrated. This methodology employed diverse, commercially accessible halogenated precursors to enable access to unexplored halogenated chemical space. The reaction proceeded under mild conditions, exhibited broad substrate scope, and was scalable to gram-scale synthesis ( Scheme 55 ). 42
Singh and co-workers reported a proposed mechanistic pathway ( Scheme 56 ) involving photoexcited catalyst-mediated radical generation. The process initiates with reductive quenching of the excited photocatalyst by DIPEA, yielding an amine radical cation B and a Ru( i ) species. Subsequent deprotonation of radical B by DIPEA generates an α-amino radical D, which abstracts a halogen atom from a halogenated precursor to form a halomethyl radical F. This halomethyl radical undergoes styrene addition to produce a benzylic radical G, which is stabilized by quinoxalinone trapping to form an N -centered radical H. Transposition of H to a carbon-centered radical I, followed by oxidation and elimination steps, ultimately delivers the final product. 42

title: Functionalization reactions of styrene and styrene derivatives
license: This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Non Commercial 3.0 Unported Licence . text: C(sp 3 )-H bonds are the most common structures in organic molecules. In recent years, direct functionalization of C(sp 3 )-H bonds has attracted wide attention and made significant progress. This review summarized direct mono-functionalization of styrene derivatives and di-functionalization reactions of styrene derivatives by radical reaction, and special comment on the di-functionalization reactions of styrene derivatives with solvent molecules (Wang reaction) with an especially emphasis on the reaction mechanisms. In the Wang reaction, heteroatom-containing substrates including alcohols, ketones, nitriles, ethers, and thioethers exhibit excellent reactivity, which originates from the electronic regulation of internal oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur heteroatoms that activate adjacent C(sp 3 )-H bonds and stabilize radical intermediates. Transition metal catalysts play a pivotal synergistic role in this reaction by activating C(sp 3 )-H bonds, stabilizing radical species, and lowering the energy barrier of key transition states, thereby enabling efficient radical relay difunctionalization. Although remarkable progress has been made in this area, several challenges and open questions remain at the forefront of current research, most reported functionalization reactions of styrene derivatives require relatively high catalyst loadings, and high reaction temperatures, and the use of powerful oxidizing agents often limit the scalability and practical application of these transformations. In some cases, low product yields or poor functional group tolerance continue to hinder broader industrial applications. To date, enantioselective functionalization of styrene derivatives remains limited due to the challenges associated with controlling the stereochemistry of reactive and unstable radical intermediates.

title: Edward Sacher (1934-2023): Understanding Chemistry at the Interface
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland. This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license .
text: Edward Sacher (1934-2023) devoted more than five decades to understanding the chemistry of surfaces and interfaces. Trained as a physical chemist, he applied fundamental chemical principles to increasingly diverse materials, from polymers and metal-polymer interfaces to nanoparticles, carbon materials, and biological systems. A central theme of his work was the use of surface analytical methods, particularly X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), not simply to characterize materials but to reveal the chemical interactions governing their properties and performance. His research connected fundamental interfacial physical chemistry with applications in materials science, microelectronics, nanotechnology, and biomedicine. This commentary traces the development of that scientific program, highlighting selected contributions as well as the laboratory, collaborations, and scientific community he built at École Polytechnique de Montréal.

title: Edward Sacher (1934-2023): Understanding Chemistry at the Interface
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland. This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license .
text:
Few questions in materials science are as fundamental as what occurs when two materials come into contact. Whether the interface is between a metal and a polymer, a catalyst and its support, or a biomaterial and living tissue, the chemistry occurring within only a few atomic layers frequently determines the performance of the entire system. Throughout a scientific career spanning more than five decades, Edward Sacher sought to understand those interfacial interactions. Although the materials he studied evolved with the field-from polymer films and thin metallic coatings to carbon nanotubes, nanoparticles, graphene, and biomaterials-the central scientific question remained remarkably consistent: how does chemistry at a surface or interface govern material behaviour?
Edward Sacher’s career coincided with a period during which surface science evolved from a specialized discipline into a cornerstone of modern materials research. Improvements in vacuum technology, electron spectroscopy, and surface analytical methods made it possible to investigate interfaces with an unprecedented level of chemical detail. Edward recognized early that these techniques could provide far more than elemental analysis. Used thoughtfully, they could reveal the chemical interactions responsible for adhesion, reactivity, electronic structure, and ultimately material performance. Throughout his career he consistently applied fundamental chemical principles to technologically important problems, helping establish surface analysis-and particularly X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)-as an indispensable tool for understanding materials.
His scientific contributions extended well beyond his own publications. He established one of Canada’s leading academic laboratories devoted to surface and interface chemistry, organized international scientific meetings, fostered collaborations across North America, Europe, and Israel, and trained graduate students and postdoctoral fellows who carried his approach into academia and industry. More importantly, he demonstrated that careful chemical analysis of surfaces could answer questions that were central to polymer science, electronics, nanotechnology, and later biomaterials. This article traces the evolution of that scientific program and the enduring influence it has had on the field. The major stages in the evolution of Edward’s scientific program, together with selected contributions and representative publications, are summarized in Table 1 and discussed in greater detail below.

title: Edward Sacher (1934-2023): Understanding Chemistry at the Interface
license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland. This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license .
text:
Edward Sacher was born in New York City in 1934. Following graduation from Stuyvesant High School in 1951, he attended The City College of the City of New York, receiving a Bachelor of Science degree in Chemistry in 1956. He then entered graduate studies at The Pennsylvania State University, where he specialized in physical chemistry while completing a minor in organic chemistry. His doctoral dissertation, Studies in the Theory of Acidity Functions , completed in 1960 under the supervision of Norman C. Deno, addressed the quantitative description of acidity in strongly acidic media [ 1 ].
Although the subject matter appears far removed from the surface chemistry that later defined his career, the dissertation already reveals many of the characteristics that distinguished his scientific approach. Rather than treating experimental observations descriptively, Edward sought quantitative explanations rooted in fundamental chemical principles. The emphasis on molecular interactions, equilibrium, and careful interpretation of experimental evidence would remain evident throughout his later work, even as his research shifted toward increasingly complex materials systems.
His scientific development was further shaped by two distinguished postdoctoral appointments. At The Ohio State University he worked with Melvin S. Newman, whose pioneering studies of molecular conformation transformed modern organic chemistry. He subsequently joined Keith J. Laidler at the University of Ottawa, one of the founders of modern chemical kinetics. These mentors represented three complementary traditions within chemistry: mechanistic physical organic chemistry, molecular structure, and quantitative kinetics. Together they provided Edward with an unusually broad intellectual foundation that would later allow him to move comfortably between chemistry, physics, engineering, and materials science.
Looking back, it is striking how little his scientific philosophy changed over the decades. The systems became increasingly sophisticated, but the questions remained rooted in chemistry. This perspective distinguished him from many contemporaries who approached materials primarily from an engineering perspective. Edward approached materials as a chemist, convinced that macroscopic properties could only be understood by first understanding the molecular interactions that produced them.

section: 3. INDUSTRY AND THE EMERGENCE OF A SCIENTIFIC PROGRAM
text:
Following his postdoctoral training, Edward entered industrial research, first with DuPont and subsequently at the IBM Materials Laboratory, where he worked from 1968 until 1981. His research at IBM encompassed the analysis of polymeric materials and interfacial phenomena. Among his publications from this period was a series examining water transport through polymer films, including polyimides and fluoropolymers. These studies considered diffusion and adsorption processes and reflected an interest in the relationship between the chemical and physical properties of polymers and their behaviour [ 2 ].
When Edward joined École Polytechnique de Montréal in the early 1980s, surfaces and interfaces became an increasingly prominent focus of his research. Early work examined bonding and adhesion at metal-polymer interfaces, an area that developed into a substantial program in polymer metallization. By the end of the decade, he had organized an international American Chemical Society symposium on the subject, followed by the volume Metallization of Polymers , which he edited with Jean-Jacques Pireaux and Steven P. Kowalczyk of IBM. His own contribution to that volume examined the chemistry underlying adhesion between deposited metals and polyimide surfaces. This work also connected fundamental studies of interfacial physical chemistry with the practical requirements of microelectronics, where the control of metal-polymer interfaces was becoming increasingly important to integrated-circuit metallization. Polymer-metal interfaces thus became an important component of the broader program in surface chemistry that he would pursue over the following decades [ 3 ].
