section: PHOTOCATALYTIC DEGRADATION MECHANISMS OF ORGANIC POLLUTANTS
text:
Advanced photocatalytic materials improve performance primarily through band-structure engineering, heterojunction construction, surface functionalization, and defect or dopant introduction [ 133 ]. For instance, heterostructure photocatalysts (e.g., Z-scheme or S-scheme systems) promote efficient separation of photogenerated electron-hole pairs, thereby increasing the lifetime and availability of reactive species such as ·OH, ·O₂⁻, and h⁺ for pollutant oxidation [ 134 ]. Bandgap tuning through metal or non-metal doping extends light absorption into the visible range, enhancing solar utilization and reaction kinetics [ 135 ]. Surface modification with cocatalysts or oxygen-containing functional groups improves pollutant adsorption near active sites, facilitating interfacial charge transfer and accelerating degradation pathways [ 136 ]. Importantly, photocatalytic degradation does not inherently guarantee detoxification or complete mineralization; partial oxidation can generate intermediate compounds that may exhibit equal or greater toxicity than the parent pollutants. Recent studies emphasize the need to track degradation pathways, intermediate formation, and total organic carbon (TOC) removal rather than relying solely on apparent pollutant disappearance. According to [ 137 , 138 ]these works demonstrate that rational photocatalyst design can steer reaction pathways toward deeper oxidation and mineralization while suppressing the accumulation of hazardous intermediates, underscoring the necessity of coupling material innovation with comprehensive toxicity and pathway analysis for realistic environmental applications.
Type-II heterojunctions are described as systems formed between two semiconductors possessing staggered band structures [ 139 ] where photogenerated electrons migrate from the conduction band (CB) of one semiconductor to the lower CB of the second semiconductor, while holes transfer in the opposite direction between valence bands (VBs) [ 140 ]. This spatial separation significantly suppresses electron-hole recombination and enhances charge carrier lifetime. However, the migration of electrons and holes to lower-energy bands often reduce the overall redox potential of the system, thereby limiting the generation of highly reactive oxidative and reductive species required for complete pollutant mineralization. To address this limitation, explains Z-scheme heterojunction systems, which mimic the natural photosynthetic Z-scheme electron transfer pathway. In these systems, electrons from the CB of one semiconductor recombine with holes from the VB of another semiconductor, preserving the highly oxidative holes and strongly reductive electrons on opposite semiconductors [ 141 ]. As a result, Z-scheme photocatalysts exhibit enhanced redox capability, improved generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and superior degradation efficiency toward recalcitrant organic pollutants [ 142 ]. The study also distinguishes between traditional mediator-based Z-schemes and direct Z-scheme systems, emphasizing that direct interfacial charge transfer improves stability and minimizes energy loss [ 143 ]. Furthermore, an explanation of S-scheme heterojunctions, which represent a recently developed charge transfer mechanism designed to combine efficient charge separation with strong redox ability [ 144 ]. In S-scheme systems, internal electric fields and band bending at the heterointerface selectively retain electrons with high reduction potential and holes with high oxidation potential while facilitating recombination of low-energy charge carriers [ 145 ]. Compared to conventional type-II heterojunctions, S-scheme architectures maintain stronger photocatalytic oxidation and reduction capacity while simultaneously suppressing recombination losses [ 146 ]. Their enhanced interfacial charge dynamics and efficient utilization of visible light make them highly promising for environmental remediation applications. Study also discusses Schottky junctions, which are formed at metal-semiconductor interfaces [ 147 ]. Due to differences in Fermi energy levels, electrons migrate from the semiconductor to the metal until equilibrium is reached, creating a Schottky barrier [ 148 ]. Noble metals such as Ag, Au, and Pt function as electron sinks, trapping photogenerated electrons and preventing electron-hole recombination [ 149 ]. This mechanism improves interfacial charge separation and prolongs carrier lifetime, thereby enhancing photocatalytic degradation reactions. Additionally, surface plasmon resonance effects in certain noble metals can broaden visible-light absorption and improve photocatalytic efficiency under solar irradiation [ 150 ]. Finally, the section now includes a discussion of p-n junction heterostructures formed between p-type and n-type semiconductors [ 151 ]. Upon contact, charge redistribution occurs across the interface, generating an internal electric field that drives directional migration of photogenerated electrons and holes [ 152 ]. This built-in electric field facilitates rapid charge separation and suppresses recombination, thereby improving photocatalytic activity and stability. p-n junction systems are particularly effective in enhancing visible-light-driven photocatalysis and have shown strong potential for degradation of dyes, pharmaceuticals, and emerging contaminants.

text: Electrocatalytic remediation relies on externally applied potential to drive oxidation or reduction reactions at electrode surfaces [ 19 ]. Organic pollutants are degraded either directly through electron transfer or indirectly via electrogenerated oxidants such as hydroxyl radicals, ozone, or active chlorine species [ 153 ]. Mechanistically, electrocatalytic degradation is governed by electrode material composition and surface structure, applied potential and current density, mass transfer and diffusion of pollutants to reactive sites. Advanced materials such as doped carbon electrodes, metal oxide coatings, and conductive polymer composites enhance electron transfer efficiency and catalytic stability [ 154 ]. Research trends emphasize selective electrocatalysis, aiming to control reaction pathways and minimize by-product formation.

text:
Solar-driven systems integrate photocatalysis with renewable energy utilization, enabling sustainable and decentralized wastewater treatment. These systems rely on visible-light-active materials capable of efficient photon absorption and charge utilization under natural sunlight [ 155 ]. Hybrid systems that combine adsorption and photocatalysis exhibit synergistic mechanisms. Pollutants are first concentrated at the material surface through adsorption, followed by localized photocatalytic degradation [ 156 ]. This approach improves reaction kinetics and reduces catalyst deactivation, representing a major research direction for scalable solar remediation technologies.
Transport phenomena, interfacial interactions, and material surface chemistry govern membrane separation. Advanced membranes enable precise control over mass transfer while addressing challenges such as fouling and energy consumption [ 157 ].
Nanofiltration and reverse osmosis membranes operate through a combination of size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion and solution-diffusion mechanisms [ 158 ]. Advanced materials enhance these mechanisms by tailoring pore size distribution, surface charge, and hydrophilicity [ 159 ]. Nanomaterial-incorporated membranes create preferential water transport pathways, increasing permeability without sacrificing selectivity [ 160 ]. Interfacial water-membrane interactions and nano-scale transport channels play a critical role in determining flux and rejection behavior [ 161 ].

text:
Membrane fouling arises from adsorption and deposition of organic matter, microorganisms, and inorganic salts [ 162 ]. Advanced antifouling membranes are designed to minimize foulant adhesion through surface hydration layers, electrostatic repulsion, and antimicrobial activity [ 163 ]. Self-cleaning membranes introduce active mechanisms such as photocatalytic degradation of foulants under light irradiation or stimulus-responsive surface restructuring [ 131 ]. These materials continuously regenerate active surfaces, reducing the need for chemical cleaning and extending membrane lifespan.
The remediation performance of advanced materials is strongly governed by pollutant-specific interaction mechanisms and environmental operating conditions. Electrostatic attraction predominantly influences the adsorption of charged contaminants such as dyes, pharmaceuticals, and heavy metal ions, where solution pH and ionic strength significantly alter surface charge and adsorption efficiency. π-π interactions are particularly important for the removal of aromatic organic pollutants, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and antibiotic residues, through interactions between conjugated carbon structures and aromatic contaminant molecules. Hydrogen bonding contributes to the adsorption of polar compounds containing hydroxyl, amino, or carboxyl functional groups, whereas pore diffusion controls the transport and accessibility of contaminants within porous adsorbent structures such as MOFs, COFs, and activated biochar. Surface complexation and chelation mechanisms play dominant roles in heavy metal sequestration through coordination interactions with oxygen-, nitrogen-, or sulfur-containing functional groups. In contrast, redox transformation mechanisms are crucial for degrading persistent organic pollutants and reducing toxic metal ions into less hazardous forms. However, under realistic environmental conditions, factors such as competing ions, natural organic matter, fluctuating pH, salinity, and complex wastewater matrices may significantly influence these interaction pathways, thereby affecting remediation efficiency, selectivity, and long-term material stability.

text:
The complexity and diversity of environmental contaminants demand remediation strategies that are both mechanism-driven and adaptable to varying chemical structures, concentrations, and environmental matrices. Advanced materials have emerged as powerful tools for environmental remediation by enabling selective adsorption, catalytic transformation, immobilization, and separation of contaminants [ 164 ]. In Table 2 the uses of advanced materials are listed for environmental remediation, these advanced materials are used for the removal of organic pollutants, heavy metals and metalloids and other emerging contaminants.
Organic pollutants constitute one of the most pervasive classes of environmental contaminants, originating from industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, domestic wastewater, and pharmaceutical residues [ 165 ]. Their persistence, toxicity, and resistance to conventional treatment methods necessitate the use of advanced material-based remediation strategies. Dyes, widely used in textile, paper, and leather industries, are characterized by complex aromatic structures and chromophore groups that impart chemical stability and recalcitrance [ 166 , 167 ]. Advanced materials such as carbon-based nanomaterials, functionalized polymers, and porous frameworks remove dyes primarily through adsorption mechanisms involving π-π stacking, electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and pore confinement [ 168 ]. In parallel, photocatalytic materials enable oxidative degradation of dye molecules into smaller, less toxic intermediates and, ultimately, mineralized products [ 169 ]. Hybrid adsorption-photocatalysis systems are particularly effective, as adsorption concentrates dyes on catalyst surfaces, enhancing degradation kinetics [ 170 ] . Pesticides including organochlorines, organophosphates, and carbamates, pose significant risks due to their persistence and bioaccumulation. Remediation materials target pesticides through hydrophobic interactions, surface complexation, and catalytic transformation [ 171 ]. Porous carbon materials and polymer-nanocomposites adsorb pesticides efficiently, while photocatalytic and electrocatalytic materials promote bond cleavage and detoxification [ 172 ]. Pesticide remediation increasingly focuses on selective degradation pathways that minimize the formation of toxic by-products [ 173 ]. Pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) represent a rapidly growing class of micropollutants. Their diverse molecular structures and biological activity at trace concentrations challenge conventional treatment processes [ 174 ]. Advanced materials such as MOFs, COFs, and tailored membranes remove pharmaceuticals through size-selective adsorption, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic interactions. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), supported by photocatalysts and electrocatalysts, enable complete mineralization or transformation into less active compounds [ 175 ]. Research increasingly emphasizes understanding transformation pathways and identifying potentially harmful intermediates using high-resolution analytical techniques.
Heavy metals and metalloids, including lead, cadmium, mercury, chromium, arsenic, and selenium, are non-biodegradable and persist indefinitely in the environment. Their remediation relies on removal, immobilization, or transformation rather than destruction [ 176 ]. Adsorption mechanisms dominate metal remediation strategies and are governed by surface complexation, ion exchange, chelation, and electrostatic attraction [ 177 ]. Functionalized materials containing oxygen-, nitrogen-, sulfur-, or phosphorus-based groups form strong coordination bonds with metal ions [ 178 ]. Biopolymers such as chitosan and alginate exhibit high affinity for metal ions through chelation. In contrast, metal oxides and hydroxides provide reactive surfaces for inner-sphere complex formation [ 179 ]. Immobilization strategies aim to reduce metal mobility and bioavailability rather than complete removal. Materials such as biochar, clay minerals, and phosphate-based composites stabilize metals through precipitation, encapsulation, or redox-induced transformation [ 180 ]. For instance, iron-based materials can reduce toxic Cr(VI) to the less mobile Cr(III), followed by adsorption or precipitation[ 181 ]. Immobilization is particularly relevant for soil and sediment remediation, where complete removal may be impractical. Advanced techniques, including magnetic separation, electrokinetic remediation, and membrane-based metal recovery, further expand the toolkit for metal remediation. Magnetic nanocomposites allow rapid separation and regeneration, while electrochemical systems enable selective metal recovery and resource reclamation, aligning remediation with circular economy principles [ 182 ].
Emerging contaminants encompass a broad range of substances that are not fully regulated but pose potential risks to ecosystems and human health [ 183 ]. Their structural diversity and persistence demand innovative, material-driven remediation approaches. Microplastics and nanoplastics are ubiquitous pollutants originating from plastic degradation and synthetic textiles [ 184 ]. Advanced materials address microplastic pollution through filtration, adsorption, and magnetic separation [ 185 ]. Functionalized membranes and fibrous filters physically retain microplastics in contrast, surface-engineered materials promote aggregation and capture. Research is increasingly exploring photocatalytic and enzymatic materials capable of degrading plastic polymers into benign by-products [ 186 ]. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are highly persistent due to strong carbon-fluorine bonds. Their remediation represents a major challenge, as conventional treatment methods are largely ineffective [ 187 ]. Advanced materials such as tailored adsorbents, ion-exchange resins, and high-surface-area carbons capture PFAS through hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions [ 188 ]. Emerging approaches integrate adsorption with electrochemical or plasma-based degradation to break C-F bonds, reflecting a shift toward destructive remediation strategies. Endocrine-disrupting compounds (EDCs), including hormones, plasticizers, and certain pharmaceuticals, interfere with biological signaling even at trace concentrations [ 189 ]. Advanced porous materials and membranes remove EDCs through selective adsorption and size exclusion, while photocatalytic materials enable oxidative degradation [ 190 ]. Conceptually, the remediation of EDCs emphasizes sensitivity and selectivity, given their activity at ultra-low concentrations. Additional emerging contaminants include antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), nanoparticles, disinfection by-products, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and cyanotoxins [ 191 ]. Advanced materials such as antimicrobial membranes, redox-active catalysts, and multifunctional adsorbents are being developed to address these challenges through combined physical, chemical, and biological mechanisms [ 192 ].
Beyond individual material classes, modern remediation increasingly relies on integrated techniques that combine multiple mechanisms within a single system. Examples include adsorption-photocatalysis hybrids, membrane-bioreactor systems, electrochemical-adsorptive processes, and nature-based material integrations. Conceptually, these approaches aim to maximize treatment efficiency, reduce secondary pollution, and enhance system resilience under variable environmental conditions [ 193 ].

section: INTEGRATION OF AI AND SMART TECHNOLOGIES
text:
The convergence of advanced materials with artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and smart sensing technologies is redefining environmental remediation strategies. These digital tools accelerate material discovery, optimize treatment processes, and enable real-time monitoring, thereby enhancing efficiency, adaptability, and sustainability [ 194 ].
AI-driven approaches enable rapid screening and rational design of advanced materials by predicting structure, property, performance relationships [ 195 ]. Machine learning algorithms analyze large datasets of material compositions, synthesis parameters, and remediation performance to identify optimal material architectures with minimal experimental effort [ 196 ]. In environmental remediation, AI has been increasingly applied to predict adsorption capacity and selectivity of porous materials such as MOFs, COFs, and biochar, optimize photocatalyst bandgaps and charge separation efficiency, guide surface functionalization strategies for enhanced contaminant affinity [ 197 ]. These approaches significantly reduce trial-and-error experimentation, lower development costs, and accelerate translation from laboratory-scale discovery to practical applications.
AI-based process modeling enables real-time optimization of water and wastewater treatment systems [ 198 ]. Data-driven models integrate operational parameters such as pH, temperature, pollutant concentration, hydraulic retention time, and material dosage to optimize treatment efficiency and energy consumption [ 199 ]. Digital twins and predictive models facilitate adaptive control of treatment processes under fluctuating wastewater composition, optimization of regeneration cycles and material lifespan, and reduction of chemical and energy inputs. Such intelligent process control is particularly valuable for decentralized treatment systems and industrial wastewater management [ 200 ].
Machine learning models have emerged as powerful tools for predicting contaminant removal performance across diverse materials and environmental conditions [ 201 ]. Supervised learning algorithms, including random forests, neural networks, and support vector machines, are used to forecast adsorption kinetics, degradation efficiency, and fouling behavior [ 202 ]. ML-based predictive tools enable rapid assessment of treatment feasibility for emerging contaminants, risk-based prioritization of remediation strategies, and design of multi-contaminant treatment systems. The integration of ML with experimental and field data enhances decision-making and supports scalable deployment of advanced remediation technologies [ 203 ].The use of machine learning algorithms such as artificial neural networks (ANN), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), gradient boosting, and deep learning models for predicting adsorption capacity, photocatalytic degradation efficiency, membrane fouling behavior, and contaminant removal performance[ 204 ]. Specific examples have been added showing how AI models have been used to optimize MOF and COF structures for selective adsorption, predict bandgap and charge-transfer properties of photocatalysts, and model structure-property-performance relationships in nanocomposite systems. In addition, the datasets and data-driven approaches are used for remediation process optimization, including adsorption isotherm databases, photocatalytic degradation datasets, sensor-generated water quality data, and real-time operational datasets from wastewater treatment systems. The study incorporated recent case studies demonstrating AI-assisted optimization of wastewater treatment parameters, predictive contaminant removal modeling, smart sensing integration, and digital twin approaches for adaptive remediation process control [ 205 , 206 ].
Smart sensing systems incorporating advanced materials enable real-time detection and monitoring of contaminants [ 207 ]. Nano sensors, electrochemical sensors, and optical sensors functionalized with selective materials provide high sensitivity and specificity toward pollutants such as heavy metals, pesticides, and endocrine disruptors [ 208 ]. When integrated with wireless communication and AI-based analytics, smart monitoring systems enable early detection of contamination events, automated feedback control for treatment systems, long-term environmental surveillance. These technologies are critical for ensuring regulatory compliance, protecting public health, and enabling adaptive water management [ 209 ].
The overall objective of integrating AI and ML into environmental remediation is to develop more efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable remediation technologies. However, despite significant progress, several limitations remain associated with AI-assisted remediation systems. Effective training of AI and ML models requires high-quality, comprehensive, and standardized datasets, as incomplete, inconsistent, or biased data can result in inaccurate predictions and unreliable model performance [ 205 ].

section: SUSTAINABILITY, TOXICITY, AND ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT
text:
Life cycle assessment provides a holistic evaluation of environmental impacts associated with material production, use, and disposal [ 210 ]. LCA frameworks assess energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, water use, and resource depletion across the material life cycle [ 211 ]. For remediation materials, LCA highlights trade-offs between high performance and environmental cost, guiding the development of materials with lower carbon footprint, energy-efficient synthesis, and extended service life [ 212 ].
Nanomaterials and chemically functionalized materials may pose ecotoxicological risks if released into the environment. Potential concerns include bioaccumulation, toxicity to aquatic organisms, and disruption of microbial communities. Systematic ecotoxicity assessments, including acute and chronic toxicity studies, are essential to ensure material safety. Surface modification, immobilization, and encapsulation strategies are increasingly employed to mitigate environmental risks [ 213 ].The potential environmental and biological risks associated with nanomaterials, including nanoparticle leaching, persistence in aquatic and soil environments, bioaccumulation, trophic transfer, oxidative stress generation, and possible toxicity toward microorganisms, aquatic organisms, plants, and human health [ 214 ]. Particular attention has been given to the post-treatment fate of nanomaterials after remediation processes, including aggregation, dissolution, surface transformation, sedimentation, and release of metal ions or reactive intermediates under environmental conditions [ 215 ]. Material recovery and containment remain major challenges for nanoscale remediation systems, especially under realistic wastewater conditions. Strategies such as immobilization of nanoparticles onto supports, magnetic recovery, encapsulation, surface coating, and development of biodegradable or bio-derived nanomaterials approaches to minimize environmental release and improve operational safety [ 216 ].
Material recyclability and regeneration are critical for sustainable remediation. Advanced materials are increasingly designed for multiple use cycles without significant loss of performance [ 217 ]. Magnetic separation, chemical regeneration, and thermal treatment enable efficient recovery and reuse of adsorbents and catalysts. Recyclable materials reduce operational costs, minimize secondary waste, and support circular economy principles [ 218 ].
Green synthesis strategies aim to minimize environmental impact during material fabrication by using renewable feedstocks, non-toxic solvents, low-temperature processes, and waste-derived precursors [ 219 ]. Biochar, biopolymer composites, and biologically synthesized nanoparticles exemplify sustainable material design [ 220 ]. The adoption of green chemistry principles ensures that remediation technologies contribute positively to environmental sustainability throughout their life cycle.
These materials in terms of synthesis cost, raw material availability, scalability of fabrication methods, regeneration efficiency, operational stability under realistic environmental conditions, energy demand, maintenance requirements, and compatibility with existing treatment infrastructurea[ 221 ]. In addition, the study now highlights key barriers limiting industrial and field-scale deployment, such as solvent-intensive synthesis, membrane fouling, nanoparticle recovery challenges, structural instability, and high production costs associated with certain advanced materials. Furthermore, the section emphasizes the importance of techno-economic analysis (TEA), life-cycle assessment (LCA), and pilot-scale validation for translating laboratory-scale technologies into practical environmental remediation systems [ 222 ]. The discussion also compares low-cost and sustainable alternatives such as biochar and biopolymer-based materials with high-performance but economically challenging systems such as MOFs and multifunctional nanocomposites [ 223 ]. This addition strengthens the practical relevance and critical depth of the review by bridging the gap between laboratory research and real-world environmental application.

section: ROLE OF ADVANCED MATERIALS IN ACHIEVING SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGS)
text:
Advanced materials play a transformative role in addressing global environmental challenges and are increasingly recognized as key enablers of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) [ 224 ]. By enabling efficient resource utilization, pollution mitigation, and the development of low-carbon technologies, next-generation materials bridge the gap between technological innovation and sustainable development. Their multifunctionality, scalability, and integration with smart systems make them essential tools for achieving environmentally resilient and inclusive growth [ 225 ]. In Table 3 listed the important advanced materials and their application in environmental remediation with sustainability and relevance with respective SDGs.
Ensuring universal access to safe and affordable drinking water and adequate sanitation remains a global priority. Advanced materials significantly enhance water and wastewater treatment efficiency by enabling the removal of complex, persistent, and emerging contaminants that are inadequately addressed by conventional technologies [ 226 , 227 ]. High-performance adsorbents, nanocomposites, MOFs, COFs, and functionalized membranes enable effective removal of dyes, heavy metals, pharmaceuticals, pathogens, and microplastics from water sources [ 228 ]. Photocatalytic and electrocatalytic materials further contribute by degrading organic pollutants into non-toxic products, reducing reliance on chemical disinfectants [ 229 ]. These materials support decentralized and point-of-use water treatment systems, which are particularly valuable in rural and resource-limited regions. Advanced membranes with antifouling and self-cleaning properties improve desalination and water reuse, reducing freshwater extraction and enhancing water security [ 230 ]. Several trade-offs associated with these materials, including high-cost and solvent-intensive synthesis routes, energy-intensive fabrication processes, dependence on rare or metal-based precursors, membrane fouling, nanoparticle or metal-ion leaching, limited recyclability, and uncertainties regarding long-term environmental fate and end-of-life recovery. These factors may offset some sustainability benefits if not properly addressed through green synthesis strategies, regeneration protocols, and life-cycle optimization. Additionally, the meaningful contribution toward SDG 6 must also consider parameters such as treated water quality relative to regulatory contaminant limits, water reuse and recovery potential, operational reliability under realistic wastewater conditions, energy consumption, affordability, scalability, rural and decentralized applicability, material regeneration efficiency, and long-term system stability. Similarly, the contributions toward SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) are now discussed in relation to circular economy compatibility, carbon footprint, renewable feedstocks, waste minimization, and life-cycle environmental impacts [ 231 ].
Advanced materials are central to promoting sustainable industrialization and resilient infrastructure. By enabling cleaner production processes, waste minimization, and efficient resource recovery, material innovation drives industrial transformation toward sustainability [ 232 ]. In industrial wastewater treatment, next-generation materials facilitate high-efficiency pollutant removal and water recycling, reducing environmental discharge and operational costs [ 233 ]. Advanced catalysts and membranes improve process efficiency. In contrast, AI-assisted material design accelerates innovation and technology transfer. Furthermore, modular and scalable material-based treatment systems support resilient infrastructure capable of adapting to changing industrial and environmental demands. The integration of advanced materials into smart manufacturing, pollution control systems, and green infrastructure fosters innovation-driven industrial growth while minimizing environmental impact, directly supporting the objectives of SDG 9 [ 234 ].
Rapid urbanization has intensified challenges related to water scarcity, air pollution, waste management, and environmental health in cities [ 235 ]. Advanced materials contribute to sustainable urban development by enabling efficient environmental remediation, smart monitoring, and resilient urban infrastructure [ 236 ]. Material-enabled water purification systems improve urban water supply and wastewater treatment, while advanced air-purifying materials reduce particulate matter and toxic gas emissions. Smart materials integrated with sensors enable real-time monitoring of pollution levels, supporting proactive environmental management and informed urban planning [ 237 ]. In addition, materials that promote waste valorization, such as biochar and catalytic materials for waste-to-energy conversion, contribute to circular urban systems. These innovations enhance urban livability, public health, and environmental resilience, aligning closely with SDG 11 goals [ 238 ].
Advanced materials play a crucial role in promoting sustainable consumption and production patterns by enabling resource efficiency, waste reduction, and circular economy practices [ 239 ]. Materials designed for recyclability, reusability, and long service life reduce dependence on virgin resources and minimize waste generation [ 240 ]. Green synthesis approaches, including the use of renewable feedstocks, waste-derived precursors, and low-energy fabrication methods, reduce the environmental footprint of material production [ 241 ]. In remediation applications, reusable adsorbents and regenerable catalysts enable closed-loop treatment systems, minimizing secondary pollution. Furthermore, advanced materials facilitate resource recovery from wastewater, such as nutrient and metal recovery, transforming waste streams into valuable resources [ 242 ]. These practices directly support SDG 12 by decoupling economic growth from environmental degradation.
Climate change mitigation and adaptation require technologies that reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance energy efficiency, and promote low-carbon solutions. Advanced materials contribute to climate action by enabling energy-efficient environmental remediation, carbon capture, and renewable energy integration [ 243 , 244 ]. Low-energy water treatment technologies, solar-driven photocatalytic systems, and advanced membranes reduce the carbon footprint of environmental infrastructure [ 245 ]. Materials such as biochar and MOFs contribute to carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas capture, while catalytic materials support cleaner energy production and storage [ 246 ]. Additionally, advanced materials enhance climate resilience by improving water security, reducing pollution-related climate stressors, and enabling adaptive infrastructure. Through these multifaceted contributions, next-generation materials play a vital role in advancing SDG 13 and supporting global climate goals [ 247 ]. Table 3 .
Sustainability and SDG relevance of advanced materials
The role of advanced materials extends beyond individual SDGs, creating synergistic benefits across multiple sustainability objectives [ 224 ]. Innovations in material science not only address environmental remediation but also foster social equity, economic development, and climate resilience. By integrating performance, sustainability, and scalability, advanced materials represent a powerful pathway toward achieving the SDGs and building a more sustainable and resilient future [ 258 ]. In Fig. 4 , we have illustrated the integration of advanced materials with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for environmental protection and climate resilience. The major quantitative indicators used to evaluate the sustainability, efficiency, techno-economic feasibility, and SDG relevance of advanced materials for environmental remediation [ 259 ]. The performance of remediation materials should not be assessed solely based on pollutant removal efficiency, but also through broader sustainability and operational metrics [ 260 ]. Parameters such as adsorption capacity, degradation efficiency, membrane flux, mineralization rate, and contaminant selectivity provide direct measures of treatment performance and remediation effectiveness. At the same time, indicators including regeneration efficiency, number of reuse cycles, carbon footprint, energy consumption, secondary waste generation, and renewable feedstock utilization are essential for assessing long-term environmental sustainability and circular economy compatibility. Techno-economic indicators such as synthesis cost, operational treatment cost, and scalability further determine the feasibility of translating laboratory-scale materials into practical industrial and decentralized treatment systems [ 261 ]. Metrics related to resource recovery, material recyclability, and AI/ML model accuracy demonstrate the growing importance of intelligent and sustainable remediation strategies [ 262 ]. These quantitative indicators provide a comprehensive framework for critically comparing advanced remediation materials and evaluating their realistic contribution toward Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDGs 6, 9, 11, 12, and 13 [ 263 ]. section: CHALLENGES, KNOWLEDGE GAPS, AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
text:
Despite substantial progress in the development of next-generation materials for environmental remediation and sustainable development, several scientific, technological, and socio-economic challenges continue to hinder their large-scale deployment. Addressing these challenges requires a holistic understanding of material behavior under real-world conditions, integration of sustainability principles, and coordinated efforts among researchers, industry stakeholders, and policymakers [ 264 ]. In contrast, knowledge gaps discussion specifically highlights unresolved scientific questions and limitations in current understanding. These include insufficient mechanistic understanding of contaminant-material interactions at molecular and interfacial levels, limited knowledge of long-term environmental fate, transformation pathways, and ecotoxicological impacts of advanced materials, lack of standardized methodologies for evaluating photocatalytic mineralization and toxicity of degradation intermediates, inadequate understanding of material behavior under realistic multi-contaminant and variable environmental conditions, and limited predictive models correlating material structure, surface chemistry, and remediation performance.
One of the most significant barriers to the practical implementation of advanced remediation materials is scalability [ 265 ]. Many high-performance materials such as MOFs, COFs, engineered nanomaterials, and multifunctional composites are typically synthesized using complex, multi-step laboratory procedures that rely on high-purity reagents, organic solvents, and energy-intensive conditions. These factors significantly increase production costs and limit feasibility for large-scale or decentralized applications [ 266 ]. In addition, material performance demonstrated under controlled laboratory conditions often declines when applied to real wastewater matrices containing competing ions, organic matter, and fluctuating physicochemical parameters [ 267 ]. This discrepancy highlights the need for scalable synthesis methods that ensure consistent material quality and performance at industrial scale [ 268 ]. Future efforts must focus on developing low-cost, high-throughput synthesis routes using abundant or waste-derived raw materials, simplifying material architectures without compromising functionality, conducting pilot-scale and field-scale demonstrations to validate economic and operational feasibility.
The long-term stability of advanced materials under operational and environmental conditions remains poorly understood. Many materials exhibit excellent short-term performance but suffer from degradation, fouling, leaching of active components, or loss of structural integrity over extended use [ 269 ]. Environmental factors such as pH fluctuations, temperature variation, salinity, and exposure to natural organic matter can significantly affect material durability [ 270 ]. Equally important is the environmental fate of materials after use. Nanomaterials and chemically functionalized materials may persist in the environment if not properly recovered, raising concerns about accumulation, toxicity, and unintended ecological impacts [ 271 ]. Knowledge gaps remain regarding long-term transformation and degradation pathways of materials in aquatic and soil environments, bioavailability and trophic transfer of released material components, interactions with microbial communities and ecosystem processes, addressing these gaps require systematic long-term studies, standardized aging protocols, and integration of environmental fate modeling with experimental validation.
The absence of clear regulatory frameworks and standardized testing protocols poses a major challenge to commercialization. Many advanced materials fall outside existing regulatory categories, leading to uncertainty in approval processes for environmental deployment. Regulatory agencies often require extensive data on material safety, performance, and environmental impact, which may not be readily available for novel materials [ 272 ]. Furthermore, the transition from laboratory research to market-ready technologies is hindered by limited industry-academia collaboration, high initial investment costs and perceived technological risk, lack of incentives for adopting innovative remediation technologies. Bridging of this gap requires early engagement with regulatory bodies, development of standardized performance metrics, and demonstration of long-term safety and cost-effectiveness. Public-private partnerships and policy-driven innovation incentives can play a crucial role in accelerating commercialization [ 273 ].
Future research aimed at overcoming the current limitations of next-generation materials for environmental remediation must adopt a multidisciplinary, application-driven, and systems-oriented approach to enable large-scale deployment and real-world impact. A central priority is the design of materials with scalability and sustainability in mind, emphasizing green and low-energy synthesis routes, modular and cost-effective fabrication strategies, and life-cycle optimization to minimize environmental footprints while maintaining performance. The development of multifunctional and hybrid materials that seamlessly integrate adsorption, catalytic degradation, sensing, and in situ regeneration within a single platform represents another critical direction, as such systems can significantly enhance treatment efficiency and operational flexibility. In parallel, AI- and data-driven innovation is expected to play a transformative role by accelerating material discovery, enabling structure-property-performance prediction, supporting digital twin development, and optimizing treatment processes under dynamic conditions. To bridge the gap between laboratory success and practical implementation, future studies must prioritize real-world validation through pilot-scale demonstrations, long-term field trials, and performance monitoring in complex environmental matrices. Equally important is the adoption of safety-by-design strategies, wherein ecotoxicity, human health risks, and environmental fate are assessed at early stages of material development to ensure regulatory compliance and public acceptance. Finally, system-level integration of advanced materials with biological processes, electrochemical technologies, and nature-based solutions will be essential for developing holistic, resilient, and sustainable remediation frameworks capable of addressing the multifaceted challenges of environmental pollution.

text:
Advanced materials have emerged as promising solutions for sustainable environmental remediation because of their tunable surface chemistry, multifunctionality, high adsorption capacity, and catalytic efficiency. This review highlighted the applications of nanomaterials, polymeric composites, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), advanced membranes, photocatalysts, electrocatalysts, and smart hybrid materials for the removal of dyes, heavy metals, pharmaceuticals, PFAS, microplastics, and other emerging contaminants. Mechanistic interactions including electrostatic attraction, π-π interactions, hydrogen bonding, surface complexation, redox transformation, photocatalytic charge transfer, and membrane separation were critically discussed to establish structure-property-function relationships governing remediation performance. The integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, smart sensing technologies, green synthesis approaches, and life-cycle assessment further demonstrates the transition toward intelligent and sustainable remediation systems.
Several key conclusions emerge from this review. First, no single material can universally address all remediation challenges, highlighting the importance of multifunctional and hybrid systems integrating adsorption, catalysis, sensing, and regeneration. Second, sustainability considerations such as recyclability, low energy demand, renewable feedstocks, and reduced secondary pollution are becoming equally important as treatment efficiency. Third, AI-assisted material design and predictive modeling offer significant potential for accelerating material discovery and process optimization. Despite remarkable progress, important research gaps remain regarding long-term stability, fouling behavior, ecotoxicity, regeneration efficiency, and environmental fate of advanced materials under realistic conditions. Furthermore, scalability, synthesis cost, nanoparticle recovery, and limited pilot-scale validation continue to restrict practical implementation. Future research should therefore prioritize green and scalable synthesis, recyclable and biodegradable materials, techno-economic assessment, life-cycle analysis, and integration with AI-driven and renewable-energy-assisted treatment systems to develop sustainable, cost-effective, and resilient environmental remediation technologies aligned with global Sustainable Development Goals.

text:
Benzimidazole compounds have laid a strong foundation both in the domains of synthetic organic chemistry and in biological advances. The green synthesis of these materials, which favour sustainability with respect to nature is highly important. Photocatalysis, microwave-assisted and ultrasound-assisted synthesis of benzimidazoles have numerous advantages over conventional methods of synthesis. Various modes of synthesis and catalysis have been developed to take benzimidazole chemistry to different levels, producing attractive compounds in high yields and lowering the formation of impurities. Apart from their synthetic protocols, benzimidazoles have shown great performance in their biological actions in antimicrobial, anticancer, anti-inflammatory and antimycobacterial evaluations. Therefore, we here discuss recent progress in the green synthetic methods of benzimidazoles with their advances in producing biologically active compounds - possibly future potential drug candidates!

text:
Azoles have attracted great biological interest from chemists and biologists worldwide. 1-4 Their synthesis is a prime aspect of importance, focusing on their sustainability, eco-friendly protocols, and green principles for their production. 5,6 Likewise, benzimidazole has left an indelible mark both in the fields of synthetic and medicinal chemistry. 7,8 Benzimidazole is an aromatic system comprising of fused six- and five-membered rings having two nitrogen atoms as in imidazole. 9,10 Basically, benzimidazole is amphoteric having the properties of both acidic and basic nature. The 2-position of benzimidazole is highly susceptible for substitution and modification and this has been a site of medicinal interest for many years now. 11,12 The impact of benzimidazole drugs in market has been instrumental in boosting and accelerating research on benzimidazole core molecules. 13,14 As years progress, the cost-effectiveness of drugs have been increasing and have kept helping mankind to deliver good treatment for various types of ailments. Specifically, benzimidazole drugs are sold worldwide as antimicrobials, 15,16 anthelmintics, 17,18 anticancer, 19,20 anti-inflammatory, 21,22 antitubercular 23,24 agents etc. Benzimidazoles are interesting heterocyclic molecules that have significantly contributed to the field of biology. There are several drugs available on the market, that aid in treating various diseases and health-related ailments. Few of them, including liarozole, 25 pracinostat, 26-28 telmisartan, 29-31 ridinilazole, 32,33 omeprazole, 34,35 tiabendazole, 36 flubendazole, 37,38 mebendazole, 39,40 and albendazole 41,42 etc. have greatly influenced the synthesis of similar benzimidazole-containing heterocyclic analogues ( Fig. 1 ).
Conventional techniques for performing organic synthetic reactions encounter limitations, including extended reaction durations, unsatisfactory yields, excessive use of solvents, expensive reagents, hazardous chemicals, and elevated reaction temperatures, ultimately resulting in products that are not economically viable. Heterogeneous systems can lead to challenges with mass transfer resistance, which varies according to the number and different type of phases involved. Additionally, these systems may cause agglomeration of particles, a reduction in the surface area, and consequently a decrease in the reaction rate. To address these problems and challenges, employing ultrasound emerges as an economical approach to enhance a variety of reactions, including both aqueous and non-aqueous homogeneous reactions, heterogeneous reactions, phase-transfer reactions, metal-organic frameworks, and bio-enzymatic processes, among others. 43-46 Numerous name reactions, multicomponent synthesis, cycloadditions etc. , have been reported using photocatalysis, microwave and ultrasound techniques to produce compounds in high yields in the shortest time possible. 47-50 Likewise, they have great scope for the synthesis of azoles such as benzimidazoles, the target compound of this review.
This review highlights the importance of sustainable approaches for the synthesis of benzimidazoles and recent advancements in biological insights. Green techniques have taken a major role in synthesizing benzimidazole and their fused derivatives. The scope of the review lies on providing sustainable and greener impact of synthetic methods having a coverage of past five years. Nevertheless, his would greatly help in understanding the chemistry behind biologically active benzimidazoles. Their structure-activity relationship (SAR) is discussed to understand the influence of various substituents at different positions of benzimidazoles. With this intent, advances in green synthetic approaches and biological evaluations, including antimicrobial, anticancer, anti-inflammatory and antimycobacterial evaluations, are discussed in detail, which could pave the way for the growing phase of drug discovery and benzimidazole-based chemistry.

section: SUSTAINABLE SYNTHETIC STRATEGIES OF BENZIMIDAZOLES AND THEIR FUSED HETEROCYCLES
text:
Photocatalysis has been a widespread method for the development of various heterocyclic scaffolds of medicinal interest. Over the years, several modifications have been made, resulting in the efficient synthesis of organic compounds. 51,52 It is a wonderful phenomenon for the generation of biologically active heterocycles. 53,54 As a green method of synthesis, there are various attempts being made worldwide for the successful production of interesting fused heterocycles such as benzimidazole. 55,56 Various catalysts have enhanced the performance of the reaction by significantly accelerating the rate of reactions and triggering the formation of products from condensations, cyclizations etc . 57,58 Likewise, their optimizations have paved a new way for scale-up processes in industries and pharmaceutical companies.
Abdelhamid and coworkers prepared benzimidazole derivatives via photocatalysis promoted by metal-organic framework-derived ZrOSO 4 @C. Zirconium oxosulfate was embedded in carbon for this organic synthesis of benzimidazole motifs. UiO-66, a metal organic framework was used as the precursor for the synthesis involving carbonization in the presence of conc. sulfuric acid. o -Phenylenediamine 1 was reacted with different aldehyde derivatives 2 in the presence of DMF with minimal incorporation of the Zr catalyst in the reaction medium. This was subjected to light radiation for approximately one hour or without light for 6-8 h at room temperature to yield benzimidazole products 3 in excellent yields ranging from 77-96%. Here, condensation and cyclization took place in a single vessel with the triggering action of the Zr catalyst ( Scheme 1 ) ( Fig. 2 ). 59
Tayebee et al. demonstrated a method of using a TiO 2 /AgSbO 3 nanophotocatalyst for the efficient synthesis of benzimidazoles 5. Various benzyl alcohol substituents 4 were mixed with o -phenylenediamine 1 in the presence of ethanol with the desired amount of photocatalyst. The reaction vessel was illuminated with a green laser with an absorption maximum of 535 nm and the products were purified via column chromatography to achieve yields ranging from 89-96% ( Scheme 2 ). 60
However, TiO 2 remains the most widely studied photocatalyst for organic reactions because of its remarkable properties, such as excellent stability, good catalytic activity, nontoxicity and low-cost. In contrast, its lower quantum efficiency and wide band-gap remain crucial factors for its use to be limited in terms of experimental aspects. However, many reactions are reported to be driven by visible light, among which NiO-doped graphitic carbon nitride photocatalyst successfully resulted in the production of benzimidazoles. o -phenylenediamine 1 when treated with various aromatic aldehydes 6 in the presence of methanol, irradiated with 12 W white LED light for 3-4 h furnished benzimidazole hybrids 7 in high yields. The NiO@g-C 3 N 4 photocatalyst showed excellent sustainability, reusability and efficiency, highlighting its superior performance in synthetic procedures ( Scheme 3 ). 61
Wang et al. reported a new radical route for the synthesis of benzimidazoles 10 via a radical-induced cross-coupling reaction between various o -phenylenediamine derivatives 8 and different classes of alcohols 9. Here, the initiation of the reaction was facilitated by the highly reactive C-centered radicals produced from alcohols, preventing the formation of aldehyde intermediates and evolving H 2 gas as a solar fuel, contributing to high-atom economy. The simultaneous production of H 2 is the key aspect of this work along with the synthesis of different benzimidazole derivatives in good yields under mild conditions enabling the use of Xe lamps. Pd-modified ZnO nanosheets were used here upon which hydrogen evolution took place efficiently. The evolution of H 2 corresponds to high-atom economy, as it is used as a fuel avoiding the wastage of side-products. The mechanistic approach shows the formation of a radical driven by the introduction of Pd-modified ZnO nanosheets, which results in charge separation and supplies active sites for the breaking of the αC-H bonds of alcohols ( Scheme 4 ) ( Fig. 3 ). 62
The concurrent evolution of H 2 became the most interesting aspect of the study. Therefore, several experiments were carried out to synthesize benzimidazoles with the simultaneous evolution of H 2 . Chen and coworkers used bifunctional Au 4 Pd 5 nanoparticles embedded with a nitrogen-doped TiO 2- x support for the synthesis of benzimidazole 12. The synergistic activation of o -phenylenediamine 1 and ethanol 11 took place because the reinforced Pd-active centres served as Lewis acidic sites and reinforced O-Lewis basic sites, respectively. The intermediate path proceeds from the generation of ethoxy radical from ethanol and the subsequent formation of acetaldehyde, leading to the selective synthesis of 2-methyl benzimidazole 12 in yields 60-94%. Electronic modulation and oxygen vacancy engineering protocols were used for the formation of Lewis acid-base pairs. This reaction has high scalability under natural conditions, i.e. , when sunlight is used. This scalability could be achieved naturally rather than making use of toxic chemicals to fasten the reaction. The starting materials were first purged with argon for efficient initiation of the synthetic route via the removal of dissolved oxygen ( Scheme 5 ). 63
The conversion of alcohols into value-added chemicals is important in the field of chemical production. Likewise, Kundu and coworkers used hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) reagents such as HCl, HBr, and H 2 SO 4 , along with 9-mesityl-10-methylacridinium perchlorate as efficient photocatalysts for the synthesis of chlormidazole 14, a well-known antifungal drug. HAT reagent was used to activate aliphatic alcohols which further enables effective oxidative cyclization for the formation of benzimidazole core molecule. The utility of HAT reagent and their role in the synthesis is better understood in the mechanistic pathway ( Fig. 4 ). This reaction proceeded in the presence of blue LED light at room temperature in the presence of oxygen for 12 h to yield chlormidazole in 77% yield ( Scheme 6 ). 64
Gupta et al. used a porphyrin analogue for the photocatalytic reaction of o -phenylenediamine 1 and various aldehydes 15 producing benzimidazole scaffolds 16. This reaction was accelerated under air with the irradiation of blue light in the presence of ethanol and chloroform. In contrast, there are issues with the solubility of synthesized porphyrin catalysts with ethanol. Hence, it was combined with various solvents, such as DMF, MeCN, THF, CH 2 Cl 2 , chloroform and toluene and the catalytic activity was optimized. As a result, ethanol with chloroform yielded the best results compared with the other combinations. Importantly, oxygen plays a significant role in this process, resulting in no reaction in the absence of oxygen. Here, ethanol is used as a green solvent for the reaction, whose production is done from fermenting plant-based sugars ( Scheme 7 ). 65
Zhang et al. illustrated a method of synthesizing mono-substituted benzimidazole via a metal-free bipyridinium photocatalyst with a Lewis acid site and redox centre. In a pure oxygen environment, the yield of the products was significantly high. Here, an equimolar ternary mixture of solvent (CH 3 CN-CH 3 CH 2 OH-H 2 O) was employed to synthesize a monosubstituted product. The single solvent system furnished mixtures of mono- and di-substituted compounds in trace/low yields whereas the binary-solvent system produced di-substituted compounds 20 in high yields. By increasing the time, major mono-substituted product 19 was obtained. Light irradiation was also an imperative factor for the reaction, where 365 nm range light furnished products 19 in good yields and increasing the light to longer wavelengths decreased the overall yield ( Scheme 8 ). 66
Zhao et al. demonstrated the use of a CuO-AgVO 3 photocatalyst for the efficient one-pot synthesis of 2-substituted benzimidazoles 22, similar to previous reports discussed above. The reusability of the photocatalyst was the key factor in this reaction. The catalytic efficacy was significant under mild conditions and its reusability accounts for its low-cost without the use of toxic chemicals making it an eco-friendly method of synthesis. The stability of the synthesized products was tested via the hot filtration method, which enables its power to withstand hot conditions. The CuO-AgVO 3 photocatalyst was also incorporated with electron scavengers such as EDTA, IPA and BQ. o -Phenylenediamine was reacted with various aldehydes in a sun simulator for an average of 20 min to yield products which were further isolated via column chromatographic techniques affording yields ranging from 55-96% ( Scheme 9 ). 67
Metal-organic frameworks have also been employed for the efficient synthesis of new benzimidazole derivatives. The inclusion of these compounds in organic synthesis has opened new doors for the facile production of heterocycles. Similarly, multifunctional 2D Pt/Ni-Fe-MOF nanosheets were used to generate benzimidazoles 25 from various o -phenylenediamines 23 and alcohols 24 initiated via light-induced synthesis. Here, the evolution of H 2 occurs along with the formation of the product. In addition to furnishing the desired product, the production of hydrogen gas also makes it more sensible and reliable as the world is more focused on the production of green fuel. The incorporation of a minimal amount of Pt nanoparticles strengthened the catalytic performance of the MOF nanosheets. Additionally, upon several optimizations, the benzyl alcohol/toluene (2 : 1) solvent system was found to be an excellent medium for successful reactions, with yields exceeding 75% with a maintained N 2 atmosphere. This is a metal/ligand/guest-based catalytic system merged with MOF-based catalysis, which is one of the rare methods reported in the field of synthetic organic chemistry ( Scheme 10 ). 68 The overall comparison between different benzimidazole compounds discussed under photocatalysis has been provided in Table 1 .
Microwave-mediated organic synthesis has been widely studied for the generation of various medicinal as well as constructively attractive heterocyclic moieties. Thus, its utility has been a great mode of synthetic protocols. Microwave-assisted organic synthesis has become one of the most important methods for simplifying organic reactions. 69,70 The microwave technique offers numerous benefits compared to conventional approaches used for many years. 71,72
Porcheddu et al. used microwave-promoted synthetic technique for the copper catalyzed aerobic oxidation of o -phenylenediamines 26 to produce benzimidazole derivatives 28. Here, oxone is used as an oxidant for the reaction and toluene as the desired solvent. The scope of substrates was studied and optimized for better yield, which in turn produced compounds with both low and high yields. The use of readily available starting materials accelerated this synthesis. However, the reaction time was still a challenging factor, requiring almost 10 h to achieve completion of the reaction. This factor may be due to the additive oxone as oxidant taking prolonged time even under microwave irradiation ( Scheme 11 ). 73
Sundharaj and Sarveswari demonstrated a microwave-assisted organic synthetic method for the production of benzimidazole-bearing C-C compound 37 via Suzuki coupling. However, acid-amine coupling was facilitated by the coupling reagent HATU and the reaction was carried out at room temperature for 6 h. Microwave-reaction was confined to the Suzuki coupling, producing compounds with high yield with the reaction time of just 5 min. The mechanism for the Suzuki coupling is depicted below to show the incorporation of the Pd-complex in the reaction and its recovery at the final termination step ( Scheme 12 ) ( Fig. 5 ). 74
Katariya and coworkers constructed 1,4-dihydropyrimido[1,2- a ]benzimidazole derivatives 41 via microwave-irradiation involving a reaction between thiophene-2-carbaldehyde 39, 4-methyl-3-oxo- N -phenylpentanamide analogues 38 and 1 H -benzo[ d ]-imidazole-2-amine 40 to yield the desired products 41 in the presence of acetonitrile as ideal solvent for the reaction. The key factor of this reaction is the maintenance of pH using triethylamine, otherwise the reaction may arrest due to the non-desired reaction conditions. Apart from acetonitrile, other solvents such as ethanol, methanol, DMF, THF, toluene were used which resulted products in lower yields when compared to that of acetonitrile ( Scheme 13 ). 75
Kaplan et al. synthesized 2,2′-bisbenzimidazol-5,6′- dicarboxylic acid 45 in an interesting way by combining 3,4-diaminobenzoic acid 43 with oxalic acid 44, with nucleophilic and electrophilic addition using microwave irradiation without any use of solvents, making it a greener approach avoiding the utility of hazardous solvents ( Scheme 14 ). 76
Verma et al. demonstrated the utility of potassium periodate as the desired catalyst for the production of various class of benzimidazoles 47 from o -phenylenediamines 45 and different class of aromatic aldehydes 46 using both microwave as well as traditional mode of synthesis. Potassium periodate serves as a catalyst with favourable compatibility across different substrates, straightforward removal, operational simplicity, easy handling, and the ability to perform under ambient or mild conditions. This condensation-cyclisation reaction performs very well in the presence of potassium periodate, resulting products in excellent yields. Using microwave chemistry, it was easy to perform, took lesser time than the traditional approach, produced products 47 in good yields; few of them even directly recrystallized without any further purifications such as column chromatographic techniques making use of silica gel toxic to human health ( Scheme 15 ). 77
Hashem et al. synthesized new benzimidazole residues 50 and 51 via microwave chemistry by reacting 2-phenylacetyl isothiocyanate 48 with different classes of amines in dry acetonitrile at room temperature for 3 h to yield four different intermediates which upon condensation with benzoyl chloride under microwave irradiation led to the formation of benzimidazole core moieties in two different forms 50 and 51, which were further recrystallized from ethanol to give products in high yields ( Scheme 16 ). 78
Zhang and coworkers used solid and liquid phase microwave techniques for the synthesis of triphenylamine derived benzimidazole derivatives 54. p -Toluenesulfonic acid (PTSA) acted as a catalyst whereas sodium metasulfite (Na 2 S 2 O 5 ) served as both a catalyst and an oxidant for the reaction. Here, the use of PTSA evidently increased the yield of the products to 22%. On the other hand, this reaction was also catalyzed using silica gel using sodium metasulfite and the yield was not as high as that of PTSA. A plausible mechanism revealing various steps in the synthesis of benzimidazole is depicted below. The precursor aldehyde 53 was synthesized via a well-known Vislmeir-Haack formylation reaction using DMF and POCl 3 . This reaction produced mono- and di-substituted aldehydes over triphenylamine. The obtained final products were screened for their luminescent properties and the increase in the fluorescence quantum yield was inferred to be due to the increase in the number of substituents on the triphenylamine. The luminescent properties suggested that the different substituents at the 5th position of the benzimidazole had greater effects on the luminescence. However, this microwave-promoted reaction could furnish products in lesser time than taking long hours using conventional heating procedures. The comparative yields could be observed between solid-phase and liquid-phase synthesis enabling to choose appropriate method of synthesizing such benzimidazole derivatives in upcoming years ( Scheme 17 ) ( Fig. 6 ). 79
Dao et al. used microwave technique for the construction of trinuclear benzimidazole-fused analogues 57 via transition-metal free tandem catalysis. 2-(2-bromovinyl)- and 2-(2-bromoaryl)-benzimidazoles 55 were coupled along with their cyclization with 2-methoxybenzimdiazoles 56 to generate trinuclear N -fused benzimidazole scaffolds 57 in the presence of CsF. The proposed mechanism involves the initial attachment of the nucleophile to generate a resonance stabilized carbanion known as the Meisenheimer complex, which is a key step in the entire reaction. This is followed by a nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction to generate further intermediates and final elimination of alcohol to give the desired trinuclear N-fused benzimidazole core molecule ( Scheme 18 ) ( Fig. 7 ). 80
Another efficient synthesis using microwave assisted method was used via catalysis by sodium hypophosphite as the catalyst for the generation of benzimidazoles 59 in high yields. Sodium hypophosphite being inexpensive, water soluble and easy to handle, and serves as a good catalyst for the reaction. Microwave technique afforded desired products within shortest time span of 4-6 min without the use of complicated purification procedures ( Scheme 19 ). 81 The comparison between different benzimidazole compounds discussed under microwave-assisted synthesis is provided in Table 2 .
Ultrasound has been utilized as a tool for process intensification in the frequency range of 20 kHz to 5 MHz, aiding in the removal of biologically active substances in nanoscale operations and the development of pharmaceuticals. 71,82,83 The activity of the chemicals is enhanced by ultrasound due to the creation and collapse of cavitation bubbles within a liquid medium. Ultrasound waves travel through a liquid by alternating between compression and rarefaction, leading to the formation of cavities. When the attractive forces of the liquid are exceeded during the rarefaction phase, these cavities expand to their maximum size and subsequently implode, resulting in the release of energy. 84-86
Pavan et al. designed benzimidazole tethered quinoline hybrids using Montmorillonite K-10 (MK10) powder as an efficient catalyst for the synthesis via ultrasonication. This facile synthesis produced products in moderate to high yields at room temperature with shorter reaction times. The MK10 catalyst was reused for up to 4 cycles, thus highlighting the reusability and recycling performance of the catalyst. 2-Chloroquinoline-3-carbaldehydes 61 were reacted with different o -phenylenediamines 60 in methanol and irradiated with ultrasonic waves of 20 kHz and 120 W power for 30 min to obtain desired products 62. The induction of MK-10 into the aldehyde plays a key role in the mechanism followed by the addition of the amine ( Scheme 20 ) ( Fig. 8 ). 87
Liu et al. synthesized 1,2-disubstituted benzimidazoles 65 via ultrasonication facilitated by vitamin B1-catalyzed one pot synthesis. This reaction is metal-free, easy to handle, inexpensive and eco-friendly, making the synthesis simple and easy. 20% of Vitamin B1 in the presence of equal amounts of ethanol and water solvent system aided the production of benzimidazoles ( Scheme 21 ). On the other hand, PTSA was also used here for the incorporation of sulfonyl groups in the moieties. 88
Dandia et al. used CuO-decorated reduced graphene oxide (rGO) nanocomposite for the ultrasonic synthesis of 2-substituted benzimidazoles 69. 2-haloanilines 66 when treated with aldehydes 67 and sodium azide 68 in aqueous medium, furnished benzimidazoles 69 in good yields. In comparison with the traditional methods, the use of CuO-rGO nanocomposite increased the yield of the products up to 20 folds. This is due to the synergistic effects between water, catalyst functionalities and ultrasonication played a vital role in the synthesis as well as the major factor responsible for the increased yield. The catalyst could be easily recovered by centrifugation and reused for other slots of reactions ( Scheme 22 ). 89
Lin et al. reported a new method that produces considerable quantities of CF 3 -substituted benzo[4,5]imdazo[1,2- a ]pyrimidine analogues 72 from readily available starting materials 70 and 71 in an eco-friendly and efficient manner. This technique was particularly beneficial for synthesizing physiologically active compounds that feature the benzimidazopyrimidine unit, a versatile building block for creating N -fused heterocycles. This synthetic method operates without metals, solvents, additives, or catalysts. Moreover, by using ultrasound in an open-air setting, a variety of polyfluoro-ynones 70 with 2-aminobenzimidazole 71 produced polyfluoroimidazo[1,2-a]pyrimidine hybrids 72 in significant yields ( Scheme 23 ). 90
Shah et al. synthesized benzimidazoles 74 via a catalyst-free green approach in an ultrasonicator reacting o -phenylenediamine 1 and various aromatic aldehydes 73 in ethanol at 50 °C to give products in high yields ranging from 82-95% ( Scheme 24 ). 91 Likewise, ZnFe 2 O 4 when used as a catalyst furnished products 77 in excellent yields in the presence of ethanol at 70 °C under ultrasonic conditions ( Scheme 25 ). 92
Bougrin et al. doped Fe 3 O 4 @keratin nanocomposite in Cu( ii ) as a reusable heterogeneous catalyst for the synthesis of benzimidazoles fused with triazoles and pyrimidines 81. Ultrasound cavitation significantly enhanced the reaction rate. Keratin was extracted from chicken feathers using ultrasound-mediated alkaline-oxidative hydrolysis. Benzimidazopyrimidines 78 were propargylated using propargyl bromide 79 to respective alkynes 80 and then carried out with click reaction using Cu-catalyzed alkyne azide cycloaddition (CuAAC) with azides to give 1,2,3-triazole derivatives linked with benzimidazo-pyrimidines 81 in greater yields ( Scheme 26 ). 93 The comparison between benzimidazole compounds discussed under ultrasound-assisted synthesis is given in Table 3 .
