organic chemistry. -
The previous review papers focused on recent advances in dual
catalysis
in organic synthesis, particularly visible-light-mediated N -heterocyclic carbene catalysis combined with photocatalysis
involving either metal-based or organocatalysts and also NHC-catalyzed
radical coupling reactions. These strategies have enabled the generation
of diverse organic intermediates via NHC-catalyzed radical reactions. - The review articles by Ohmiya, Studer, and Hopkinson mostly discussed
carbene-catalyzed radical-radical C-C/C-HA cross-coupling
reactions proceeding via single-electron transfer (SET) processes
in the presence of NHC catalysts, with or without a photocatalyst. -
,
This review mainly focuses
on the most recent synthetic applications
in dual photocatalysis reported between 2020 and 2025 for the sustainable
preparation of various carbonyl compounds and their derivatives by
combining NHC organocatalysts with metal-based photoredox catalysts
such as Ir or Ru complexes. The presented NHC-catalyzed dual photocatalytic
approach provides efficient and practical routes for the useful synthesis
of diverse carbonyl compounds and the late-stage functionalization
of bioactive molecules, drugs, and natural products. Moreover, the
use of visible-light harvesting and earth-abundant catalysts is expected
to further expand the impact of this approach in diverse research
areas such as synthetic and medicinal chemistry, pharmaceuticals,
fine chemicals, polymers, and advanced materials. The described NHC-mediated
catalytic methods and reaction scopes are expected to facilitate the
future novel design and development of triple, quadruple, or multicatalytic
systems. -

title:
Cooperative NHC
and Photoredox Dual Catalysis for
the Construction of Carbonyl Compounds
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0
text:
Hopkinson and co-workers
efficiently developed a dual NHC and photoredox-catalyzed radical
cross-coupling of aroyl fluorides with benzyl silanes as alkyl radical
sources. The reaction of acyl fluorides 1 with organosilanes 2 in the presence of NHC (20 mol %), Ir-PC (2 mol %), with
Cs 2 CO 3 (1 equiv) in CH 3 CN at room
temperature for 24 h afforded the desired functionalized aryl ketones 3 . Under photoredox conditions, benzyl silanes 2 underwent single-electron oxidation followed by desilylation to
form radical species E . The radical-radical cross-coupling
reaction of intermediates C and E, followed
by the elimination of NHC, finally furnished the corresponding aryl
ketone products 3 . Electron-rich silane substrates reacted
most efficiently under the optimized conditions; however, the authors
also demonstrated that less-activated silyl derivatives, including
primary benzylic substrates, could be successfully coupled. Moreover,
the coupling reaction scope was expanded to include acyl fluorides 1 bearing various functional groups. Notably, organosilane
scaffolds 2 , tolerating N-, O-, and S-heteroatoms, also
underwent the most efficient carbon-carbon cross-coupling reactions.
This dual catalysis study established the broad utility of diverse
organosilane derivatives as suitable substrates for acyl-alkyl
coupling reactions and produced moderate to good yields of highly
substituted ketone moieties 3 ( Scheme ).
In 2024, Han, Li, and their
groups developed the first NHC/Ir-catalyzed
1,2-boron migrative acylation, accelerated by dual photocatalysis
using blue LED. The success of this transformation lies in the novel
design of a unique TCNHPI boronic ester coupling substrate, which
can generate β-boron radical species D through
a single-electron reduction process. This photocatalytic strategy
enables the rapid synthesis of a wide range of β-boryl ketones 6 from aldehyde 4 and TCNHPI boronic ester 5 using NHC (20 mol %), Ir-PC (2 mol %) in a DCM/THF 4:1 ratio
of solvents under mild conditions. The broad applicability of this
strategy was demonstrated via late-stage modifications of bioactive
drugs and natural product scaffolds such as diflunisal, tolmetin,
naproxen, citronellol, ciprofibrate, pterostilbene, and zingerone,
as shown in Scheme . Detailed mechanistic studies, including control experiments, photophysical
analysis, and DFT calculations, were conducted to provide insight
into NHC-catalyzed acylation and the associated 1,2-boron migration
process. The authors proposed a plausible radical pathway in which
the Ir­(III) photocatalyst is excited under visible light irradiation.
The excited-state photocatalyst, Ir­(III)*, then undergoes a single-electron
transfer (SET) with the TCNHPI boronic ester 5 , generating
an alkyl radical species C along with the oxidized photocatalyst
Ir­(IV). The alkyl radical C subsequently undergoes a
facile 1,2-boron migration to form a more stable radical species D . In parallel, aromatic aldehyde 4 condenses
with carbene catalyst A to generate the deprotonated
Breslow intermediate B under basic conditions. This electron-rich
Breslow intermediate then undergoes a SET with the oxidized photocatalyst
Ir­(IV), regenerating the ground-state Ir­(III) species and producing
ketyl radical species E . Alternatively, under thermal
conditions, a direct SET between Breslow intermediate B and TCNHPI ester 5 may occur, forming alkyl radical C , which can similarly convert into the more stable radical D , along with ketyl radical E . A subsequent
radical-radical cross-coupling between species D and E followed by elimination of the carbene catalyst,
furnished the desired carbonyl products 6 ( Scheme ).
In 2023, a robust radical coupling method for
1,2-sulfonylacylation
of allenes, employing inexpensive and readily accessible aroyl fluoride
through visible light-promoted dual photocatalysis by a combination
of NHC and iridium photocatalysts, was reported by Wang et al. This
versatile photocatalytic strategy provides an elegant synthetic approach
for obtaining medicinally useful sulfonyl group-containing allyl ketones
under mild conditions, in a short time (15 min), with excellent regioselectivity.
The respective C-C and C-S coupling reactions between
aroyl fluoride 1 , allene 7 , and sodium sulfonate 8 were achieved using catalytic amounts of NHC and an Ir-photocatalyst
under blue LED irradiation. This method produced the corresponding
vinyl sulfonyl ketones 9 in good yields with tolerance
of a wide range of functional groups and accessible starting materials.
Mechanistic investigations indicated that the 1,2-sulfonylacylation
step proceeded through an unprecedented cross-coupling of a triazolium-carbene-stabilized
ketyl radical C and an allyl radical B ,
which opened a new avenue for the radical difunctionalization of allene
derivatives via dual photocatalysis ( Scheme ).
Wu et al. developed a new dual
catalytic method that combines NHC
catalysis with Ir-photocatalysis under mild conditions for the useful
carbonylation of alkenes 12 , allowing the efficient synthesis
of valuable 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds 13 in good yields.
In this transformation, three new C-C bonds and two carbonyl
(CO) groups were constructed in a one-pot process with a broad substrate
scope and tolerance of various functional groups. Furthermore, the
synthetic practicality of the approach was demonstrated through the
effective construction of important heterocyclic compounds such as
furan, pyrrole, and pyridazine, as well as 1,4-diol derivatives. This
method offers new insights into NHC-photoredox-catalysis-driven
multicatalytic systems design for CO utilization under economical
and sustainable conditions ( Scheme ).
Wang et al. reported an effective
photocatalytic strategy involving
NHC and photoredox iridium cocatalysis for the three-component symmetrical
and unsymmetrical 1,2-dicarbonylation of olefins, aroyl fluorides,
and α-keto acids under extremely mild conditions using readily
available starting materials. The visible light-mediated multicomponent
reaction of functionalized alkenes 12 , acyl fluorides 1 , and α-keto acids 14 were carried out
in the presence of carbene catalyst (15 mol %), Ir-photocatalyst (1.5
mol %), and Cs 2 CO 3 as a base in a MeOH/H 2 O solvent system at 30 °C for 12 h under green
system, affording the desired 1,2-dicarbonylated products 15 in up to 88%. Mechanistic experiments indicated that the transformation
proceeds via a radical cross-coupling pathway. The
distinct reactivity of the acyl radical and the NHC-stabilized ketyl
radical enabled excellent selectivity. The authors successfully developed
a regioselective method for the 1,2-dicarbonylation of alkenes with
two different aroyl and alkanoyl groups. This novel catalytic procedure
represents a significant advancement in the selective multicomponent
coupling of 1,2-dicarbonylation of alkenes, enabling the installation
of both aroyl and alkanoyl functionalities. The radical transformation
proceeds under mild conditions with broad substrate scope and tolerating
various functional groups, offering a general and practical strategy
for the synthesis of both symmetrical and unsymmetrical 1,2-dicarbonyl
compounds 15 ( Scheme ).
In 2022, a new photocatalytic method was developed
for
the direct
1,2-dicarbonylation of alkenes via cooperative NHC
and iridium photocatalysis to access 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds 17 reported by Fan, Feng, and co-workers. The radical reaction
was carried out between olefins 16 and aroyl fluorides 1 in the presence of NHC (10 mol %), Ir-based photocatalyst
(1.5 mol %), and Ph 3 P (1.5 equiv) in Cs 2 CO 3 (2 equiv) in DCM for 24 h. Visible-light-induced NHC involved
catalytic process enabled the facile synthesis of a series of symmetric
1,4-diketones 17 in 41-79% yield, with a broad
substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Furthermore,
unsymmetric diketones were formed readily by varying the acyl and
alkene precursors through three-component coupling of amide, benzoic
acid, and alkene combination. This method exhibits remarkable generality
and offers potential for late-stage modification of therapeutically
relevant arenes and heteroarenes ( Scheme ).
Wang and colleagues developed a cost-effective,
convenient method
for the efficient synthesis of difluoromethylated ketones 19 via a three-component coupling reaction of olefins 12 , aldehydes 4 , and 2-((difluoromethyl)­sulfonyl)­benzo­[d]­thiazole 18 under NHC-Ir photoredox catalysis. The reaction was achieved
with Na 2 CO 3 (1.5 equiv) in the presence of an
Ir-based photocatalyst (1 mol %), carbene catalyst (20 mol %), and
450 nm blue LED irradiation. This dual photocatalysis strategy enabled
the simultaneous incorporation of a difluoromethyl moiety known for
its enhanced biological activity and a carbonyl group into substituted
olefins 12 . The method showed a broad substrate scope
and was compatible with various aromatic aldehydes and alkenes under
sustainable conditions. Moreover, its utility was demonstrated by
the successful late-stage functionalization of therapeutic agents
and drug-like molecules, which produce numerous physiological effects,
including antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, etc. Further
investigations into the NHC-mediated radical coupling process are
expected to expand its synthetic applicability across diverse areas
of chemistry ( Scheme ).
Chi and co-workers recently developed a convenient
and straightforward
method for the synthesis of aryl alkyl ketones 22 through
radical-radical cross-coupling of carboxylic acids 20 and acids/acyl imidazoles 21 by merging NHC and metal
photocatalysis. The acyl imidazoles can be readily generated in situ
via the reaction of a carboxylic acid with CDI (carbonyldiimidazole),
providing an effective method for the streamlined photochemical synthesis
of a series of ketone moieties 22 from two distinct carboxylic
acids (aryl or alkyl groups). The mild reaction conditions, operational
simplicity, and readily available carboxylic acids as both acyl sources
and radical precursors make this synthetic approach more versatile
and convenient. Moreover, this methodology could be suitable for modifying
various natural products, pharmacological agents, and their fragments,
including nalidixic acid, fluorbiprofen, indoprofen, ketoprofen, naproxen,
etc. Remarkably, this method was further extended for the NHC-catalyzed
cross-coupling three-component reaction by the addition of an alkene
moiety as a third coupling partner under mild conditions, enabling
the rapid assembly of structurally complex carbonyl products from
simple, commercially available acids and alkenes ( Scheme ).
Studer and his groups reported a visible light-mediated
fluoro-aroylation
of benzofuran, indole scaffolds 23 via cooperative NHC and iridium photoredox catalysis, achieved using
catalytic amounts of NHC (20 mol %) and iridium catalysts (2 mol %)
with the addition of K 2 HPO 4 (2 equiv) and 5
W blue LED irradiation. Acyl fluorides 1 acted as bifunctional
reagents, enabling the incorporation of the aroyl group and a fluoride
moiety into benzofuran derivatives 24 . Based on these
experimental results and previous literature reports, Studer et al.
proposed a plausible mechanistic pathway for the formation of the
O-heterocyclic product 24 via radical cross-coupling
between an NHC-bound radical intermediate B and a benzofuran
radical species C . Upon blue LED irradiation, benzofuran 23 ( E 1/2 = 1.28 V vs SCE) is oxidized
to its radical cation C by photoexcited Ir­(III)*. On
the other hand, the reaction of acyl fluorides 1 with
the NHC furnishes the acyl azolium ion A ( E 1/2 = -1.29 V vs SCE), which is reduced by Ir­(II)

title:
Cooperative NHC
and Photoredox Dual Catalysis for
the Construction of Carbonyl Compounds
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0
text:
= -1.37 V vs SCE) to regenerate Ir­(III) with the formation
of the persistent NHC-connected ketyl radical B . This
photocatalytic strategy displayed a broad substrate scope and a good
functional group tolerance. Moreover, N -acyl indoles
were found to be suitable substrates for the dearomative 2,3-difunctionalization
of the indole moiety. The synthetic scope of this method was further
demonstrated by showing that anhydrides can also serve as alternative
bifunctional reagents in the difunctionalization of benzofuran scaffolds.
In addition, mechanistic investigations indicated that these transformations
proceed via a rare radical-radical cation
cross-coupling reaction, which serves as a key step in this method
( Scheme ).
Wang et al. described the most efficient 1,4-sulfonylacylation
of 1,3-enynes 25 and acyl fluoride 1 by
merging N -heterocyclic carbene (NHC) with photocatalysis
under blue LED irradiation. This photocatalytic transformation offers
a facile and direct approach to tetrasubstituted allenyl ketone derivatives 26 under sustainable conditions, exhibiting excellent chemo-
and regioselectivity. This method is compatible with a wide range
of functional groups and is suitable for late-stage functionalization
of drug molecules including cholesterol derivatives, mefenamic acid,
telmisartan, etc. Mechanistic investigations revealed that the key
step involves radical-radical cross-coupling between allenyl
and ketyl radicals, providing a novel pathway in NHC-catalyzed reactions.
The stable ketyl radical was generated from acyl fluorides via oxidative
quenching of the excited photocatalyst. This method holds potential
for the late-stage modification of various pharmaceuticals and bioactive
compounds ( Scheme ).
The acylative Suzuki-type
cross-coupling of aroyl fluorides and
alkyl trifluoroborates system was reported by Li and co-workers by
merging NHC catalysis and photoredox catalysis. Using this novel dual
catalytic strategy, a broad spectrum of aryl methyl ketones was efficiently
prepared from readily available starting materials under mild conditions.
The radical reaction was performed between aroyl fluorides 1 and alkyl trifluoroborates 27 in the presence of catalytic
amounts of a carbene catalyst (15 mol %) and an Ir-based photocatalyst
(2 mol %) under blue LED irradiation to afford corresponding ketone
products 28 in high yields, including a variety of electron-rich
and electron-poor functional groups, such as F, Cl, Br, Me, and OMe.
To further demonstrate the generality of the method, catalytic acylation
of silyl group attached carbazoles 29 with acyl fluoride 1 was also successfully carried out. In addition, possible
mechanistic investigations were conducted to elucidate the unique
sequential energy transfer and single-electron transfer activation
pathway, including cyclic voltammetry analyses, photophysical experiments,
and computational simulations ( Scheme ).
Wang et al. discovered that dual NHC/photoredox
synergistically
catalyzed the aminoalkylacylation of alkenes 12 with
α-silyl amines 31 and benzyl fluorides 1 in the presence of NHC (20 mol %) and Ir catalyst (1 mol %) and
furnished the γ-aminoketones in moderate yields. This approach
displayed excellent functional group tolerance and easily accessible
starting materials and provided straightforward access to a diverse
range of γ-aminoketones 32 under mild reaction
conditions. The utility of this method was further demonstrated through
the late-stage functionalization of biologically active compounds
and pharmaceutical drugs ( Scheme ).
A visible light-promoted radical
cross-coupling method was developed
for the preparation of the corresponding α-amino aryl ketones 34 from carboxylic acids or amides 33 via dual catalysis reported by Wang and co-workers. The
combination of NHC and Ir-photoredox catalysis permits the single-electron
reduction of acyl azolium intermediates, followed by radical-radical
coupling to efficiently construct a C-C bond, yielding the
desired bioactive α-amino ketones 34 in good yields.
This catalytic method employs simple operation or readily available
aromatic acid 10 and functionalized amine derivatives 33 and exhibits broad substrate scope and good functional
group tolerance under eco-friendly conditions. The corresponding α-amino
ketones were further transformed into a terminal olefin through a
Wittig reaction, an α-amino alcohol through NaBH 4 reduction, and α-amino oximes using hydroxylamine under standard
conditions ( Scheme ).
Scheidt and co-workers outlined
this approach via hypothesis-driven
experimentation guided by computational investigation. In addressing
a standard limitation of single-electron carbene processes, the authors
provided mechanistic insights that could advance this catalytic platform,
expand the substrate scope, and accelerate the utility of NHCs in
molecular design and synthesis. The modularity of these single-electron
operators involved in a dual catalysis by combined NHC-catalysis and
metal-based photoredox catalytic method for preparing aliphatic ketones 37 from carboxylic acids 35 or amide 10 in the presence of silicon reagents 36 . By modulating
the steric and electronic parameters of the NHC, they achieved increased
yields of up to 65% compared to their previously reported results.
Moreover, they significantly expanded the reaction scope by directly
functionalizing readily available amino acids to obtain the corresponding
α-amino ketone scaffolds 37 through a one-pot procedure.
The utility of this method was further demonstrated through the late-stage
functionalization of biologically active agents and pharmaceutical
drugs ( Scheme ).
In 2020, the groups of Scheidt, Chen, and co-workers
demonstrated
a photocatalytic method for effectively preparing ketones 37a from amide 10 and amino ester 38 via dual
photocatalysis merging NHC and iridium catalysts, leading to the formation
of highly functionalized carbonyl compounds with a wide range of synthetic
utility and pharmaceutical applications. This method summarizes the
potential of incorporating radical processes into NHC catalysis. Bioactive
carbonyl molecules and drug-like compounds were synthesized from derivatives
of dehydrocholic acid, micardis, and prandin using an NHC catalyst
(15 mol %) and a photocatalyst (1 mol %) under visible-light irradiation.
NHC-derived acyl azolium and alkyl radical intermediates were expected
to find significant synthetic applications in NHC-catalyzed asymmetric
reactions and related biological studies. This method operates under
mild conditions and tolerates sensitive functional groups well. Remarkably,
the NHC involved photocatalytic strategy applies to the late-stage
derivatization of various bioactive organic intermediates, producing
a valuable tool for conveniently synthesizing biobased products ( Scheme ).
A three-component
coupling strategy was developed by Studer et
al. for the convenient synthesis of β-trifluoromethylated aryl
ketones via NHC-catalyzed coupling reactions involving radical intermediates.
The respective radical reaction involved cross-coupling of aroyl fluorides 1 , olefins 12 , and the Langlois reagent (CF 3 SO 2 Na) 39 under the described method,
which furnished the corresponding various β-trifluoromethylated
ketones 40 in good yields up to 88% with excellent functional
group tolerance achieved through cooperative photoredox/NHC catalysis.
The coupling reaction was conducted using a catalytic amount of NHC
(20 mol %) and an Ir-based photocatalyst (2 mol %) in DCM under photochemical
conditions. Studer and co-workers proposed a visible-light-mediated
dual photocatalytic approach for alkene acyltrifluoromethylation,
which proceeds via a domino-type carbon radical coupling between the
NHC-bound ketyl radical B and the benzylic radical D . Upon blue LED irradiation, the excited state of [Ir­(ppy) 2 (dtbbpy)]­PF 6 undergoes a well-known reductive quenching
by the trifluoromethanesulfinate anion 39 , producing
the corresponding Ir­(II) complex [ E 1/2 (Ir 3+ /Ir 2+ ) = -1.51 V vs SCE] and the
trifluoromethylsulfonyl radical C , which subsequently
fragments to release SO 2 and generate the trifluoromethyl
radical D . The resulting Ir­(II) complex then reduces
the acylazolium intermediate A ( E 1/2 = -1.29 V vs SCE) via a single-electron transfer
(SET) process. The acylazolium intermediate, generated in
situ from aroyl fluorides 1 and the NHC, affords
the persistent ketyl radical B along with regeneration
of the Ir­(III) complex, thereby closing the photoredox cycle ( Scheme ).
In 2025, Dong and Wang et al. developed an NHC-catalyzed
cross-coupling
reaction involving arylated alkenes 12 , amides 10 , and 1,3-benzodioxole 41 as coupling reagents,
and also serving as the solvent. Visible-light-mediated dual catalysis
enabled the practical and novel synthesis of highly substituted ketone
scaffolds 42 in the presence of NHC (10 mol %) and an
Ir-photocatalyst (2 mol %) under sustainable conditions. This practical
method was successfully applied to the late-stage functionalization
of bioactive molecules and drugs. The approach features mild reaction
conditions, excellent selectivity, operational simplicity, broad functional
group compatibility, and scalability ( Scheme ).
In 2025, Chi et al. developed a novel NHC-mediated
photocatalytic
method for benzyl alcohol para -selective C-H
acylation. The C-C cross-coupling reaction proceeds through
cooperative NHC and Ir-photoredox catalysis. Benzyl and arylethyl
alcohols 43 were selectively acylated at the para -position of the phenyl ring, affording the corresponding
variety of diaryl ketones 45 bearing a carbamate moiety.
Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies support
the proposed reaction pathway and reveal exclusive para -selective C­(sp 2 )-H acylation. The NHC-catalyzed
direct aryl C-H functionalization strategy is expected to find
broad applications in synthetic and medicinal organic chemistry ( Scheme ).
Chi et al. developed a cooperative NHC and Ir-photocatalyzed
approach
for the convenient synthesis of 3-acylated N -methylindoles,
from indole 46 , amide 10 and provided an
efficient method for structurally diverse 3-acylindoles via NHC catalysis.
The presented dual catalytic approach enables the synthesis of various
substituted 3-benzoylindoles 47 and several analogs of
aldose reductase inhibitors, demonstrating the potential utility of
this acylation strategy. Some of the obtained 3-acylindole derivatives
exhibited notable antibacterial activities. A series of 3-acylindoles
was achieved via aryl radical cations reacting with NHC-bound ketyl
radicals. This work will find various applications and further challenge
synthetic chemists ( Scheme ).
Han et al. developed NHC-catalyzed regioselective
bis-acylation
of alkenes by merging NHC organocatalysis and Ir-photoredox catalysis.
The reaction of alkenes 12 , ketoacids 48 , and amides 10 in the presence of catalytic amounts
of an NHC catalyst and an iridium photocatalyst in 1,2-DEC at 60 °C
for 12 h afforded a broad range of 1,4-diketones 49 in
good yields using readily available starting materials, a wide range
of functional group tolerance, and under mild conditions. Interestingly,
the 1,4-dicarbonyl products could be readily converted into various
heterocyclic compounds such as substituted furans, pyrroles, and pyridazines.
Moreover, mechanistic experiments supported understanding this NHC
and photoredox dual catalytic radical cascade coupling process ( Scheme ).
Zhao et al. discovered a dual-catalyzed radical
alkene aminoacylation
reaction of compound 50 and amide 10 via
cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis under blue LED irradiation
conditions. Hydrazones single-electron transfer (SET) oxidation produces
an N-centered hydrazonyl radical intermediate, which undergoes regioselective
6-endo-trig cyclization as a key step. This method efficiently produced
diverse 1,4,5,6-tetrahydropyridazines 51 in moderate
to good yields, exhibiting excellent functional group tolerance under
mild reaction conditions ( Scheme ).
Feng et al. described a novel strategy for the
trifunctionalization
of unactivated alkenes via a combined NHC/Ir-dual photocatalytic radical
relay alkylacylation in the presence of acid 20 , alkene 52 and sodium trifluoromethanesulfinate 8 under
mild conditions. The NHC-catalyzed cross-coupling reaction was carried
out using catalytic amounts of NHC (15 mol %) and an Ir-based photocatalyst
(5 mol %) in 1,2-DCE at rt for 24 h under photochemical conditions.
This approach provides an efficient strategy for molecular framework
construction, involving multistep C-C bond formation and cleavage
through remote 1,4-cyano migration and alkylacylation. Additionally,
theoretical calculations and mechanistic studies supported the proposed
mechanism and explained the regioselectivity of the 1,4-CN migration
( Scheme ).
Sun and Zheng et al. reported an efficient dual
catalytic radical
1,4-mono/difluoromethylative acylation of 1,3-enynes by combining
NHC organocatalysis and Ir-photocatalysis. This transformation proceeds
under mild conditions using bench-stable and commercially available
Hu’s reagents, CFH 2 SO 2 Na or CF 2 HSO 2 Na, as fluoromethyl radical sources. The reaction
of Hu’s reagents 55 and 1,3-enynes 54 with readily available benzoyl fluorides 1 as acylation
partners, providing direct access to value-added -CFH 2 - and -HCF 2 -containing allene ketone scaffolds 56 . The key step of the transformation involves a cross-coupling between
allenyl and ketyl radicals enabled by dual photocatalysis ( Scheme ).
Ren et al. developed
a step- and atom-economical synthetic protocol
for the facile synthesis of valuable α-indole methyl ketones 58 from 3-methylindole 57 . The NHC-catalyzed
coupling reaction proceeds via the direct acylation of indole methyl
C­(sp 3 )-H bonds under dual NHC and photoredox catalysis
under mild conditions. This approach enables the efficient synthesis
of both α-2-indolyl methyl ketones and α-3-indolyl methyl
ketones by simply switching between 2- and 3-alkyl indole substrates.
The successful synthesis of α-indole methyl ketones highlights
their potential applications in the synthesis of biologically active
indole-based natural products and heterocyclic compounds ( Scheme ).
Recently, Wang et
al. reported a visible-light-mediated alkylacylation
of vinylarenes 12 with tertiary arylamines 59 and acyl fluorides 1 for the efficient synthesis of
γ-aminoketones 60 under sustainable conditions
in good yields. The presented dual catalytic method employs an NHC
catalyst (20 mol %) and a photoredox catalyst (2 mol %) under mild
conditions. This reaction demonstrates good functional group tolerance
and utilizes readily available starting materials. Furthermore, a
wide range of γ-aminoketones bearing a quaternary center were
obtained via radical coupling using dual catalysis ( Scheme ).
In 2025, Jin et al.
developed a green and mild dual catalytic system
by merging photoredox/NHC catalysis to enable the efficient synthesis
of structurally diverse α-N-aryl amino ketone scaffolds 62 in good yields via radical-radical coupling between N -methyl radicals and persistent radical species derived
from NHC intermediates. This method exhibits excellent compatibility
with both secondary and tertiary arylamine substrates. Moreover, NHC-mediated
radical transformations offer a green and sustainable approach to
access α-N-aryl amino ketone derivatives ( Scheme ).
In 2023, an innovative
photocatalytic method was developed for the elegant synthesis of 3-benzoylbicyclo[1.1.1]­pentane-1-acetates 65 through a three-component coupling reaction of aldehydes 4 , [1.1.1]­propellane 63 , and diazoalkanes 64 , enabled by cooperative NHC and iridium cocatalysis described
by Jiang and his team. The visible-light-promoted radical C-C
cross-coupling reaction for the synthesis of functionalized bicyclo[1.1.1]­pentanes
(BCPs) 65 in good yields was carried out using an NHC
catalyst (15 mol %), an iridium photocatalyst (2.5 mol %), and DMAP
(50 mol %) under 456 nm blue LED irradiation for 12 h. This study
highlights the method's operational simplicity, high atom economy,
and broad substrate scope, providing a powerful photochemical method
for constructing 1,3-disubstituted BCP ketones from readily available
starting materials using nontoxic reagents/catalysts. These compounds
will find broad synthetic applicability of BCP-type bioisosteres in
medicinal chemistry ( Scheme ).
Wang and co-workers demonstrated carbene and
iridium photoredox
cocatalyzed alkylacylation of alkenes 12 in the presence
of DMAP (50 mol %), using aryl aldehyde 4 and alkyl diazo
ester 64 . This strategy offers a novel approach for transient
radical generation, producing nitrogen gas (N 2 ) as the
only byproduct, a green and environmentally benign process. The developed
radical cross-coupling reaction afforded acyl ester scaffolds 66 in excellent yields under extremely mild conditions, employing
NHC (15 mol %) and photoredox catalyst (1 mol %), with a broad substrate
scope and good functional group tolerance. Notably, this radical reaction
involved a multicomponent reaction that utilized traditional carbene
precursors, diazo esters, as radical sources, preparing the first
report of such a radical process in NHC organocatalysis. Compared
with previously reported mechanistic pathways that generate radicals
and large waste fragments, this dual catalytic protocol exhibits excellent
atom economy. It represents a more sustainable synthetic application
in pharmaceutical chemistry ( Scheme ).
Jiang et al. outlined
an NHC/photosensitization relay catalytic
methodology that enables photoinduced energy transfer of an NHC-bound
intermediate D to furnish the desired ( Z )-allylic fluorides 68 with excellent stereochemical
control and high yields using NHC (10 mol %), Ir-PC (1 mol %), in
the presence of Selectfluor (fluoride source). The synthesis of α-fluoro
alkenyl ester moiety 68 from conjugated aldehyde 67 was systematically investigated, highlighting the influence
of NHC catalysts and Ir-based photosensitizers. Resulting in a highly
enantioselective α-fluorination step, the key ( E )-acyl azolium species E underwent in situ photoisomerization
before NHC turnover. It is proposed that π-π interactions
between the NHC and alkene moiety may enhance asymmetric induction,
and the choice of iridium photocatalyst plays a critical role in regulating
the rate and stage of isomerization. This unprecedented synergy between
photosensitization and NHC-based organocatalysis offers unique advantages
for accessing thermodynamically disfavored alkene isomers, particularly
in systems bearing various sensitive functional groups ( Scheme ).
Studer and co-workers
reported a convenient and novel catalytic
method for the 1,3-difunctionalization of arylated cyclopropanes using
NHC/Ir-based cooperative photoredox catalysis. This method enables
sequential C-O and C-C bond formation, affording a variety
of γ-aroyloxy ketone analogs 71 in good yields
with broad functional group tolerance and substrate scope. The dual
catalytic approach employed between cyclopropanes 69 with
anhydrides 70 using triazolium-based carbene catalyst
(10 mol %) and an Ir-photocatalyst (2.5 mol %) in the presence of
Cs 2 CO 3 and 1,2-dichloroethane as the best choice
of solvent. Mechanistic investigations disclosed that the cascade
proceeds through nucleophilic ring-opening of an aryl cyclopropyl
radical cation C , followed by radical-radical
cross-coupling B and D as key intermediates
for producing keto esters 71 . Notably, the authors found
that 1,2,3,5-tetrakis­(carbazol-9-yl)-4,6-dicyanobenzene (4CzIPN) organocatalyst
was found to be the best choice for employing the catalytic reaction
of acyl fluorides 1 and substituted cyclopropane 69 . This approach holds high potential for applications in
medicinal activity and active pharmaceutical ingredients ( Scheme ).
Huo et al. reported
a mild and straightforward system for the NHC/photoredox
dual-catalytic method for the α-carboxylation of N -aryl tetrahydroisoquinolines 72 and tertiary amine
C­(sp 3 )-H bonds using diethyl pyrocarbonate (DEPC) 73 . This approach provides a novel route for the synthesis
of α-amino acid derivatives 74 . The method exhibits
a broad substrate scope and simple starting materials, accommodating
both N-aryl tetrahydroisoquinolines (THIQs) and N -methylanilines. It also works well in large-scale reactions. Additionally,
this method is applied to the late-stage modification of various drugs
and pharmaceutical compounds ( Scheme ).
Yang et al. presented an NHC/photoredox-catalyzed
radical cross-coupling reaction for constructing α-keto amide
derivatives, offering a complementary approach to classical two-electron
processes. The decarboxylative acylation of oxamic acids 75 with acyl fluorides 1 enables the synthesis of a wide
range of useful α-keto amides 76 using NHC (20
mol %), Ir-PC (2 mol %) and Cs 2 CO 3 (2 equiv)
in DCM for 24 h under eco-friendly conditions, displaying good functional
groups tolerance including Me, OMe, Br, I, CF 3 , CO 2 Me. Mechanistic investigations revealed that the C­(sp 2 )-C­(sp 2 ) bond formation occurs via a radical-radical
cross-coupling between a carbamoyl radical and an NHC-derived ketyl
radical. This method represents the first example of a carbene-catalyzed
two-component radical cross-coupling involving C­(sp 2 )-centered
radical intermediates. Compared to previously reported methods based
on electron-pair mechanisms, this strategy offers a distinct advantage
in accessing sterically hindered α-keto amide scaffolds 76 in moderate to good yields ( Scheme ).
Shu and co-workers presented
a visible-light-promoted NHC/Ru-catalyzed three-component coupling
reaction of alkenes, disulfides, and alkenes, which afforded the corresponding
β-thiolated-α-arylated ketones 78 at room
temperature. The radical-radical cross-coupling proceeded using
a thiazolium-based NHC (10 mol %) and a Ru catalyst (2 mol %) in the
presence of KOAc, with DMSO as polar solvent under 30 W blue LED irradiation.
This NHC-catalyzed method allows the sequential addition of sulfides 77 to alkenes 12 and aldehydes 4 through rapid C-S and C-C bond formation. This catalytic
approach demonstrates excellent functional group tolerance, enables
the functionalization of drug-like molecules under mild conditions,
and affords direct access to β-thiolated-α-arylated ketones 78 from readily available starting materials. This photocatalysis
also applies to the late-stage functional groups derivatization of
therapeutic agents and bioactive organic compounds ( Scheme ).
In 2021, Shu and co-workers
reported, for the first time, a visible-light-mediated
NHC-catalyzed vinylation of aromatic aldehydes at ambient temperature.
This method relies on a site-selective and regioselective 2-fold sequential
C-H cross-functionalization. The reaction carried out between
an alkene 79 and an aromatic aldehyde 4 ,
in the presence of NHC (10 mol %), photocatalyst (2 mol %), Cs 2 CO 3 as base, and TTBDPB (1.9 equiv) under the presented
conditions, efficiently afforded vinyl ketones 80 in
high yield. The described photochemical reaction displays a broad
range of functional group tolerance, accepting various electron-withdrawing
and -donating aldehydes and functionalized alkenes. Mechanistic studies
indicated that the transformation proceeds through radical-radical
cross-coupling reactions. This NHC catalysis relay method represents
a promising platform for developing visible-light-promoted NHC and
Ru-catalyzed carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bond-forming
reactions under sustainable conditions ( Scheme ).
Wang and co-workers developed a convenient method
for the preparation
of α-aryl-β-monofluoromethyl ketones 82 via a three-component difunctionalization of alkenes through
dual catalysis by combining NHC/photoredox catalysts. A wide range
of alkenes 12 and aroyl fluorides 1 were
successfully studied, demonstrating good functional group tolerance
and the use of readily available starting materials. The activation
of a bench-stable and readily accessible fluorinating reagent (NaSO 2 CH 2 F) was achieved using a Ru-photocatalyst to
generate the CH 2 F radical via single-electron oxidation,
without the need for external oxidants. The late-stage functionalization
of diverse bioactive drug molecules and natural products further demonstrated
the synthetic utility of this strategy ( Scheme ).
NHC-catalyzed C-C bond
cleavage of γ-cyclopropane enals 83 followed by
γ-alkylation via a radical process under photoredox
dual catalysis was reported by Ye and co-workers. A variety of halogenated
alkylating reagents 84 were successfully employed. The
dual photocatalysis involved an NHC catalyst (10 mol %) and a Ru-based
photocatalyst (2.5 mol %), performed in the presence of various alcohols
in DCE at rt for 12 h. α-Bromomalonates bearing various substituents
such as cyano, ester, allyl, and nitro groups were tolerated well,
giving the corresponding γ-alkylated α,β-unsaturated
esters 85 in up to 95%. The reaction proceeds by adding
an alkyl radical to NHC-bound conjugated alkene intermediates, subsequent
single-electron transfer oxidation of homoenolate radical, and finally
reaction with alcohols to afford the corresponding ester products.
The reaction features exclusive γ-regioselectivity, a broad
range of functional group tolerance, reaction simplicity, and mild
reaction conditions ( Scheme ).
Xu et al. presented the remote
benzylation of γ-alkenyl-γ-oxidized
enals via cooperative photoredox and NHC catalysis, affording an array
of ε-benzylation products 88 in up to a 69% yield.
The reaction was carried out using an NHC catalyst (20 mol %) and
a Ru-based photocatalyst (5 mol %) under visible-light irradiation
in the presence of conjugated aldehyde 86 , alkyl bromide 87 , and various alcohols, under mild conditions. In this C-C
cross-coupling reaction, the benzylic radical was generated through
photoinduced single-electron reduction of benzyl bromide 87 . At the same time, trienolate intermediate B , derived
from the corresponding γ-alkenyl-γ-oxidized enal under
NHC catalysis, played a key role. The benzylic radical D selectively added to the ε-position of the trienolate intermediate B to form species C followed by the elimination
of the NHC catalyst to produce the conjugated ester 88 via SET. This catalytic system exhibited various functional group
tolerance, accepting electron-donating, electron-withdrawing, and
steric substituents on the aryl ring and also verified various alcoholic
substrates ( Scheme ).
In 2020, Dai et al. described an unprecedented
γ-difluoroalkylation
of γ-preoxidized enals via cooperative photoredox and NHC catalysis.
The photocatalytic reaction of α,β-unsaturated aldehyde 89 with difluorinated alkyl halides 90 , in the
presence of an NHC catalyst (10 mol %) and a Ru-photocatalyst (2 mol
%) using CsOAc as a base, using a variety of alcohols, afforded the
desired ester products 91 in good yields. Bromo- and
iodosubstituted difluoroacetates and difluoroamides worked well in
this transformation. The key step of this C-C cross-coupling
reaction involves the conjugated addition of a difluoroalkyl radical B , generated under photoredox conditions, to the dienolate
intermediate A formed via NHC catalysis. Subsequently,
radical-radical cross-coupling and subsequent addition to various
alcohols offer γ-difluoroalkylated α,β-unsaturated
esters 91 . This strategy allows efficient construction
of C­(sp 3 )-CF 2 R bonds at the γ-position
of carbonyl compounds, offering a novel approach for the cost-effective
preparation of γ-difluoroalkylated α,β-unsaturated
esters 91 and amides bearing all-carbon quaternary centers
( Scheme ).

title:
Cooperative NHC
and Photoredox Dual Catalysis for
the Construction of Carbonyl Compounds
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0
text:
This
review focused mainly on visible-light-mediated dual photocatalysis
merging NHC organocatalysts and Ir/Ru photoredox catalysts as a groundbreaking
recent radical method allowing the highly efficient and regioselective
construction of a broad range of highly functionalized carbonyl compounds,
including ketones, esters, and amides. These catalytic strategies
also facilitate the late-stage functionalization of drug-like molecules,
natural products, and bioactive compounds under mild conditions, products
exhibiting excellent functional group tolerance, available starting
materials, high yields of products, an atom-economical process, and
operational simplicity. Highly substituted ketones, esters, and amide
scaffolds derived via these photochemical transformations from easily
accessible starting materials have shown significant potential in
pharmaceutical, agrochemical, and materials science applications.
This review highlights recent developments in NHC-catalyzed radical
cross-coupling processes over the past six years (2020-2025),
discussing dual catalytic method design and their novel synthetic
applications, electronic and steric influences of the catalysts, mechanistic
insights, and current limitations related to functional group compatibility.
Additionally, the described methods are compatible with sensitive
functional groups on drugs, natural products, and bioactive compounds.
The presented NHC and Ir/or Ru-mediated catalytic methods and reaction
scopes are expected to facilitate the future design and development
of novel triple, quadruple, or multicatalytic systems as well as support
the green modification and construction of medicinally and pharmaceutically
active molecules.

title:
Domino Strategies
in Heterocycle Synthesis: Advancing
from Organocatalysis to Photo-/Organo-Autocatalysis
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0
text:
Abstract The increasing structural
complexity of heterocycles in pharmaceuticals,
agrochemicals, and functional materials continues to challenge synthetic
design, particularly when step economy, scalability, and sustainability
are considered simultaneously. Domino reactions, in which multiple
bond-forming events proceed sequentially in a single operation, offer
an inherently concise strategy to transform simple building blocks
into densely functionalized architectures while minimizing purification
steps and waste. In this Outlook , we examine the
evolution of domino heterocycle synthesis from classical organocatalysis
to photo- and organo-autocatalytic systems, highlighting how metal-free
activation, visible-light processes, and in situ -generated
catalytic species expand reactivity while improving catalyst, energy,
and atom economy. We discuss key advances in domino reactions toward
chiral heterocycles, heteroaromatic construction, total synthesis,
and self-catalyzed photochemical processes, emphasizing challenges
such as catalyst loading, robustness, photon efficiency, and reaction
scalability. The future development of domino synthesis will rely
on combining new mechanistic ideas with sustainability and rational
reaction design. By focusing on the deliberate development of efficient,
low-input organo - and photo/organo-autocatalyzed
domino reactions, we aim to spur progress toward streamlined and industrially
practical methods for heterocycle synthesis.

title:
Domino Strategies
in Heterocycle Synthesis: Advancing
from Organocatalysis to Photo-/Organo-Autocatalysis
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0
text:
Simplicity in organic
synthesis is achieved when molecular complexity
can be constructed efficiently, selectively, and with minimal resource
expenditure in a single operation. In recent decades, the synthesis
of complex heterocyclic frameworkscentral motifs in pharmaceuticals,
natural products, agrochemicals, ligands, and functional materialshas
matured into a highly sophisticated field of research. - Nevertheless, many established routes still rely on extended protecting-group
manipulations, discrete isolation of intermediates, and resource-intensive
purification steps that arise from traditional stepwise or “Stop-and-Go”
strategies ( Figure A). Such approaches, although reliable, remain distant from the ideals
of modern synthesis, which emphasize atom economy, step and pot efficiency,
reduced solvent use, and, ideally, protecting-group-free transformations. -
Strategies
for heterocycle synthesis: A) Classical Stop-and-Go
approach; B) One-pot approach; C) Domino reaction principle; D) Organocatalyzed
domino reaction; E) Photocatalyzed domino; F) Photoautocatalyzed domino;
G) Organo-autocatalyzed domino.
As organic chemistry increasingly aligns with the
principles of
sustainable development, efficiency and waste reduction have become
not merely a practical consideration but a defining design criterion. , Transformations are now commonly evaluated using quantitative metrics
such as atom economy and process mass intensity, while lifecycle thinking
continues to shape both academic research and industrial practice. In this context, a reaction design that minimizes
operational steps and maximizes bond-forming efficiency offers intrinsic
advantages.
One-pot processes - and domino reactions - have therefore emerged as powerful strategic concepts for constructing
molecular complexity from simple starting materials in a streamlined
and resource-conscious manner. Although often discussed together, , one-pot and domino reactions embody distinct operational philosophies.
In one-pot processes, individual transformations are performed sequentially
within a single reaction vessel; upon completion of each step, additional
reagents or catalysts are introduced to trigger the subsequent event,
culminating in product formation after a single final isolation ( Figure B). Domino reactions,
in contrast, are initiated in the presence of all necessary componentsreagents,
catalysts, and solventsuch that once the first bond-forming
event occurs, subsequent transformations proceed autonomously without
further external intervention ( Figure C). Each elementary step directly triggers the next,
enabling the uninterrupted assembly of structurally intricate architectures
through a self-propagating domino process. By reducing workup operations
and avoiding intermediate purifications, these methodologies significantly
reduce solvent consumption, material loss, and energy demand, underscoring
their growing importance as a superior tool for organic synthesis. -
While domino reactions had been known in racemic contexts
for decades,
the first example of an asymmetric domino reaction was reported in
1998 by Terashima and co-workers. The
synthesis of the naturally occurring acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
(-)-Huperzine A was accomplished through a Cinchona alkaloid-promoted
asymmetric two-step Michael addition/aldol reaction domino transformation
between a β-keto ester and methacrolein ( Scheme ). This domino process afforded the key intermediate
in 45% yield, which was subsequently elaborated to complete the total
synthesis of (-)-Huperzine A with 64% ee. This work pioneered
the idea that a single chiral organic compound could promote multiple
bond-forming events in a single operation with enantioselective control,
foreshadowing the later explosion of asymmetric organocatalytic cascade
methodologies. Subsequent developments in the early 2000s, especially
in asymmetric organocatalysis, built directly on this conceptual advance
to enable highly enantioselective reactions with broad synthetic utility.
Asymmetric organocatalysis, recognized with the 2021 Nobel
Prize awarded to Benjamin List and David MacMillan for its
development, , utilizes small organic molecules
as chiral catalysts, such as alkaloid derivatives, - amino acids, short peptides, (thio)­ureas, - and chiral Brønsted acids. -
Since its renaissance in the early 2000s by
MacMillan, List, and
Barbas, ,- organocatalysis has demonstrated
remarkable versatility, significantly advancing the field of asymmetric
organic synthesis. -
Over recent decades, a substantial body of research has demonstrated
the synthetic power of organocatalyzed domino reactions in the construction
of heterocyclic scaffolds. - This Outlook examines the conceptual principles and emerging directions of domino
strategies in heterocycle synthesis, with a focus on organo- , photo- , and autocatalytic systems
( Figures D-G). By
integrating metal-free activation modes, visible-light-driven processes,
and self-propagating catalytic networks, these approaches enable the
construction of diverse and densely functionalized heterocyclic frameworks
with high atom and step economy. Beyond showcasing the synthetic elegance
of domino reactions, this Outlook critically evaluates
how domino strategies can address contemporary challenges of catalyst
economy, robustness, reaction scalability, and potential industrial
applications. Special emphasis is placed on the transition from conventional
organocatalysis ( Figure D) and photo-catalysis ( Figure E) to photo-autocatalytic ( Figure F) and organo-autocatalytic ( Figure G) reactions, where substrates, in situ -generated intermediates, or products actively participate
in sustaining the catalytic cycle, thereby reducing external inputs
and improving sustainability metrics. Rather than cataloging reactions
exhaustively, this Outlook highlights representative examples and
advances that illustrate how domino reactions can reconcile molecular
complexity with operational simplicity. Key case studies from organocatalyzed
non-enantioselective and enantioselective heterocycle synthesis, heteroaromatic
construction, total synthesis of bioactive compounds, and photo-auto-
and organo-autocatalyzed reactions are discussed to demonstrate the
new directions of the field. By framing heterocycle construction through
the lens of single-operation synthesis, we aim to highlight the unifying
principles that connect organo-catalysis, photocatalysis, and photo-/organo-autocatalysis
and to inspire further developments toward increasingly streamlined,
waste-reducing, energy-conscious, and sustainable synthetic strategies
capable of meeting future environmental and industrial demands.
Beyond
showcasing the synthetic elegance of domino reactions, this Outlook
critically evaluates how domino strategies can address contemporary
challenges of catalyst economy, robustness, reaction scalability,
and potential industrial applications.

title:
Domino Strategies
in Heterocycle Synthesis: Advancing
from Organocatalysis to Photo-/Organo-Autocatalysis
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0
text:
The construction of chiral heterocycles
without the use of enantiopure
catalysts represents a conceptually distinct yet strategically useful
approach to complexity generation.
In such processes, multiple
stereogenic centers are established
in a single operation, often with high levels of diastereocontrol,
while the absolute configuration remains uncontrolled. From the perspective
of synthetic efficiency, these transformations are highly attractive:
they avoid the preparation of chiral catalysts or auxiliaries, simplify
reaction design, and frequently deliver functionalized scaffolds suitable
for downstream diversification and chiral resolution. The following
sections highlight representative advances in the non-enantioselective
domino synthesis of mono-, multi-, and bridged heterocyclic frameworks.
These structures
are key motifs in medicinal and synthetic organic chemistry, valued
for their three-dimensionality, drug-like properties, and prevalence
in bioactive molecules. Recent reviews have summarized advances in
their preparation, including direct alkene difunctionalization strategies
and modular approaches to saturated N-heterocycles from common building
blocks. Among notable organocatalytic
contributions, Lupton and co-workers reported an N-heterocyclic carbene
(NHC)-catalyzed domino strategy for the synthesis of dihydropyranones
( Scheme A). In this transformation, α,β-unsaturated
enol esters or acid fluorides react with TMS enol ethers via Lewis base-promoted fragmentation to generate reactive acyl
azolium intermediates. A three-step domino sequenceMichael
addition/proton transfer/cyclizing acylationfurnishes pyranones
in yields of up to 76%, with efficient catalyst regeneration. This
work demonstrates how transient acyl azolium species can be harnessed
to construct oxygen heterocycles through domino reactivity. Manolikakes
and co-workers developed a highly stereoselective domino protocol
for the synthesis of fully substituted tetrahydropyrans ( Scheme B). The process involves a 2-fold addition of enamides to aldehydes,
followed by cyclization, proceeding through a 1-carbonyl-ene-type/aza-ene-type/cyclization
sequence. Three new σ-bonds and five contiguous stereogenic
centers are formed in a single operation, often delivering a single
diastereomer out of 16 possible isomers. Notably, selective use of E - or Z -configured enamides enables controlled
access to distinct stereoisomeric products, underlining the power
of substrate-controlled stereodifferentiation in achiral catalytic
systems.
These compounds,
including fused and annulated systems, are prominent structural motifs
in natural products and bioactive molecules. Their rigid architectures
often enhance biological activity and metabolic stability. While transition-metal
catalysis has long dominated their synthesis, organocatalytic domino strategies have emerged as complementary,
more cost-efficient, and operationally simple alternatives.
In this context, Huang, Chen, and co-workers
reported a phosphine-catalyzed domino reaction enabling access to
highly substituted trans -2,3-dihydrobenzofurans with
excellent diastereoselectivity ( Scheme A). Salicyl N -thiophosphinyl imines and allylic carbonates, acting as 1,1-dipolar
synthons, undergo a four-step domino reaction comprising addition-elimination/nucleophilic
addition/isomerization/intramolecular annulation. The method affords
dihydrobenzofurans in yields of up to 99%, illustrating the efficiency
of phosphine catalysis in controlling multistep sequences. Takizawa,
Sasai, and co-workers developed a Lewis base-catalyzed domino
reaction between cyclohexadienones and alkynyl esters to synthesize
hydroindole-2-carboxylates and hydrobenzofuran-2-carboxylates ( Scheme B). The four-step sequenceMichael addition/umpolung
Michael addition/Michael addition/proton transferprovides
up to 20 derivatives in yields of up to 89%. This example highlights
the strategic use of polarity inversion (umpolung) within a domino
framework to access complex bicyclic systems ( Figure ). Along this line, Tong and co-workers disclosed
a phosphine-catalyzed synthesis of cyclopenta­[a]­pyrrolizine derivatives
from 2-acyl-3-(2-pyrrole)-acrylonitriles and β′-acetoxy
allenoates ( Scheme C). The three-step domino processaddition-elimination/aza-Michael
addition/intramolecular [3 + 2] cycloadditionfurnishes products
in yields of up to 95%. Complementarily, Piersanti and co-workers
described a phosphoric acid-catalyzed approach to 3-NHAc-naphtho-
and benzofuranones from 2-acetamidoacrylates and naphthols or phenols
( Scheme D). Proceeding via dual activation
through protonation and hydrogen bonding, the two-step domino sequenceaza-Friedel-Crafts
reaction/intramolecular cyclizationdelivers products in up
to 67% yield.
Plausible
mechanism for the domino transformation presented in Scheme B
These structures
represent complex architectures frequently encountered in natural
products and bioactive compounds. Their synthesis poses significant
challenges due to ring strain and the requirement for precise stereochemical
control.
Domino strategies have proven particularly well-suited
to their rapid assembly. Along these lines, Tong and co-workers developed
a phosphine-catalyzed domino reaction between β′-acetoxy
allenoates and 2-acyl-3-methyl-acrylonitriles to access 2-oxabicyclo[3.3.1]­nonane
derivatives ( Scheme A). In this five-step domino processaddition-elimination
step/nucleophilic addition/intramolecular Michael addition/H-shift/S N 2-type reactionthe β′-carbon of the allenoate
serves as an electrophilic center, while the β′- and
γ-carbons function as a 1,4-dipole ( Figure ). Up to 15 derivatives were synthesized
in yields of up to 87%, underscoring the efficiency of sequential
bond construction within a single operational setting.
Proposed
mechanisms for the domino reaction depicted in Scheme A.
The Tsogoeva group reported an imidazole-catalyzed
domino reaction
between malononitrile and substituted aldehydes, enabling access to
complex aza- and carbo-bicycles ( Scheme B). The six-step
sequenceKnoevenagel condensation/dimerization/intermolecular
addition/intramolecular aza-Michael reaction/intramolecular addition/tautomerizationprovides
11 derivatives in up to 59% yield. This transformation exemplifies
how simple organocatalysts can control intricate reaction networks
to generate bridged frameworks from readily available starting materials.
The examples discussed in this chapter illustrate that achiral
catalytic systems can deliver highly complex, stereochemically rich
heterocycles through carefully designed domino sequences. While non-enantioselective
approaches offer advantages such as operational simplicity, easy access
to catalysts, and rapid scaffold construction, enantioselective catalysis
remains essential for directly obtaining single enantiomers.

title:
Domino Strategies
in Heterocycle Synthesis: Advancing
from Organocatalysis to Photo-/Organo-Autocatalysis
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0
text:
The enantioselective construction of chiral
heterocycles represents
a central objective in modern synthetic chemistry, particularly in
view of the profound influence of absolute configuration on biological
activity and pharmacological properties. - Domino strategies,
when combined with asymmetric organocatalysts, enable the simultaneous
formation of multiple stereogenic centers with high levels of enantiocontrol
in a single operational step. Asymmetric organocatalyzed domino reactions
combine step economy with control over stereochemistry, making them
a powerful tool for building complex chiral molecules. Despite recent impressive advances, major challenges
remain, including substrate generality, chiral organocatalyst cost,
and the compatibility of highly reactive intermediates within complex
domino manifolds. Furthermore, the translation of optimized academic
examples to industrially viable processes continues to represent a
significant hurdle. The following subsections highlight representative
examples in which carefully designed chiral organocatalysts facilitate
domino processes to access enantioenriched heterocyclic compounds
with excellent levels of diastereo- and enantioselectivity. The question
is not only how high the enantiomeric excess can be driven, but how
broadly applicable, and sustainable such asymmetric domino strategies
can ultimately become.
Among the
notable contributions exemplifying recent advances is the work by
Ye and co-workers who demonstrated the enantioselective synthesis
of challenging β-lactams. The reported method employs chiral
NHC precatalysts to activate ketenes, followed by reaction with a
variety of N-tert -butoxycarbonyl arylamines ( Scheme A). The reaction proceeds via a two-step nucleophilic
addition/intramolecular cyclization domino process ( Figure ) affording cis-β -lactams in good yields and in up to 99% ee. While the method delivers
excellent enantioselectivity, the reliance on preformed ketenes and
tailored NHC precatalysts may limit large-scale adoption, highlighting
the ongoing need for more readily accessible catalytic systems and
milder activation modes.
Plausible reaction mechanism
for the domino transformations presented
in Scheme A.
Highly functionalized tetrahydrothiophenes with
three contiguous
stereocenters were synthesized by the group of Lattanzi using trans-α -cyano-α,β-unsaturated ketones, trans-tert -butyl 4-mercapto-2-butenoate, and a bifunctional
chiral amine-thiourea organocatalyst ( Scheme B). The transformation
proceeds via a two-step sulfa-Michael/Michael domino
process, delivering 15 examples with high diastereoselectivity and
enantioselectivity (up to 99% ee) and excellent yields of up to 98%.
The formation of multiple contiguous stereocenters in a single operation
illustrates the power of bifunctional catalysis. Using a chiral phosphoric
acid Zhu and the team established an enantioselective synthesis to
access morpholinone substrates from aryl/alkylglyoxals and 2-(arylamino)­ethan-1-ols
( Scheme C). ,
A total of 23 derivatives were synthesized in excellent yields
and up to 95% ee through a three-step domino reaction comprised of
imination/cyclizing azetalization/1,2-aryl-alkyl shift.
Such
domino transformations highlight the synthetic creativity
enabled by asymmetric organocatalysis, yet mechanistic complexity
and potential competing pathways underscore the delicate balance required
for reliable domino reaction design.
A highly diastereoselective
and enantioselective synthetic route toward 1,3-disubstituted isoindolines
was reported by the Sasai group utilizing a chiral bifunctional (acid-base)
organocatalyst for the reaction of electron-deficient alkenes with N -tosylimines ( Scheme A). 8
The transformation describes a five-step Michael
addition/Mannich
reaction/intramolecular aza-Michael/proton transfer/retro-Michael
domino reaction yielding the final products in good yields and in
up to 93% ee. The control of five consecutive elementary steps within
a single catalytic cycle demonstrates the sophistication of modern
domino design; nevertheless, increasing reaction robustness and reducing
sensitivity to electronic effects remain ongoing challenges.
An interesting approach for the in situ generation
of activated trienamines was developed by the group of Jørgensen
( Scheme B). The organocatalyzed activation of 2,4-dienals
forms the reactive trienamine species which undergo a two-step aza-Diels-Alder/cyclizing
hemiaminal formation domino process to yield the desired azaheterocycles
in moderate to good yields (up to 71%) in up to >20:1 d.r. and
92%
ee.
The application of the method was further demonstrated by
transforming
the obtained azaheterocycles into tetrahydropyridine motif found in
palustrine derivatives such as (-)-methyl palustramate or (+)-cannabisativine.The
synthetic utility toward complex alkaloid frameworks is notable; and
further improvements in yields and reducing catalyst loading would
enhance the practicality of such activation modes.
For the asymmetric
synthesis of thiochromenes, Wang and co-workers
reported an organocatalyzed two-step sulfa-Michael aldol condensation
domino reaction ( Scheme C). The activation of α,β-unsaturated
aldehydes with chiral organocatalyst followed by a reaction with 2-mercaptobenzaldehyde
provided the final products in high yields and up to 95% ee. Subsequently,
an asymmetric synthesis of functionalized 4 H -chromenes
was developed by the same group. The novelty of this work was the
unprecedented iminium-allenamine cascade activation resulting
from the utilization of alkynals as starting materials ( Scheme D). This undergoes a two-step oxa-Michael/Michael domino reaction with
2-( E )-(2-nitrovinyl)-phenols affording the products
in high yields and up to 99% ee.
Innovative activation concepts
such as iminium-allenamine
cascades ( Figure )
expand the conceptual toolbox of asymmetric catalysis, yet they also
raise questions concerning generality and long-term operational simplicity.
The synthesis of barbiturate-tetrahydropyran fused heterocycles utilizing
a bifunctional (amine-thiourea) organocatalyst was presented by Li,
Chen and co-workers ( Scheme E). A two-step Michael addition/intramolecular
6- endo-trig annulation domino reaction between N , N ′-dimethylbarbituric acid and
Morita-Baylis-Hillman (MBH) acetates of nitroalkenes afforded the
fused structures in good yields and up to >19:1 d.r. and 97% ee.
Future
progress will likely depend on integrating such highly selective systems
with scalable reaction engineering and reduced catalyst loadings.
Proposed
mechanisms for the domino reaction depicted in Scheme D.
Ohsawa and
his team reported the first catalytic asymmetric reaction of 3,4-dihydro-β-carboline
and 3-buten-2-one in combination with chiral catalyst ( S )-Proline to yield 3,4,6,7,12,12b-hexahydro-1 H -indolo­[2,3- a ]­quinolizin-2-one ( Scheme A). The target compound
was obtained via a two-step Mannich reaction/aza-Michael
addition domino sequence, providing the product in good yield and
92% ee. The obtained scaffold represents a valuable structure for
the total synthesis of indole alkaloids. Such examples illustrate
how asymmetric domino catalysis can rapidly access alkaloid-like frameworks.
However, expanding these strategies to more densely functionalized
substrates remains an important frontier.
The enantioselective synthesis of pyranocoumarins
using a bifunctional
amine-thiourea organocatalyst was achieved by Li, Chen, and co-workers
( Scheme B). Hydroxycoumarins and Morita-Baylis-Hillman
acetate of nitroalkene react in a two-step domino reaction consisting
of Michael addition and intramolecular 6- endo-trig annulation to produce biologically active pyranocoumarins in excellent
yields and up to 93% ee.
Subsequently, Chen, Enders, and co-workers
developed an N -heterocyclic carbene-catalyzed domino
reaction toward
tricyclic coumarin derivatives via α,β-unsaturated
acyl azolium intermediates ( Scheme C). The six-step domino
reaction comprising oxidation/Michael addition/intramolecular aldol
reaction proton shift/δ-lactonization/dehydration yields the
coumarin derivatives in good-to-excellent yields and up to 99% ee.
The increasing length and sophistication of domino sequences highlight
both the opportunity and the intrinsic challenge of cascade chemistry:
as complexity rises, so too does the possibility of competing pathways
and diminished reproducibility.
An enantioselective
synthesis of spirocyclic, polyfunctionalized cyclohexenes was reported
by the Enders group ( Scheme A). The organocatalyzed transformation
features the possibility of oxidizing the resulting nucleophilic enamine
with o -iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX) into the electrophilic
iminium intermediate, enabling a four-step Michael addition/oxidation/Michael
addition/aldol condensation domino reaction. The final products were
obtained in good yields and up to >20:1 d.r. and 99% ee. The integration
of oxidation steps using IBX within domino process expands synthetic
flexibility, yet it also introduces considerations regarding reagent
economy, sustainability, and waste generation.
The application of bifunctional organocatalyst
in the enantioselective
synthesis of spirocyclic derivatives was demonstrated by Du and co-workers
( Scheme B). The two-step Michael/Mannich domino reaction
between rhodanine derivatives and N -(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl)­isatin
ketimines involves hydrogen-bonding and protonation interactions with
the chiral bifunctional catalyst enabling the asymmetric synthesis
of bispiro­[oxindole-pyrrolidine-rhodanine]­s in good to excellent yields
and up to 99% ee. Spirocyclic frameworks remain highly attractive
in drug discovery; continued efforts toward broadening functional-group
tolerance will further enhance their practical value.
An enantioselective
reaction between α,β -unsaturated cyclic
ketones, formaldehyde and aryl amines catalyzed by ( S )-proline, was established by Sundén and the team to afford
azabicyclic ketones. ( Scheme A). The products were obtained
in up to 90% yield and with up to 99% ee through a two-step domino
reaction including a Mannich reaction and an intramolecular aza-Michael
addition.
Yamamoto and his working group reported a highly
enantioselective
synthesis toward a nitroso Diels-Alder adduct by applying a
chiral pyrrolidine-tetrazole catalyst ( Scheme B). In this
process, nitrosobenzene and cyclic enone react via a two-step domino reaction comprised of O -nitroso
aldol reaction and intramolecular aza-Michael addition, to produce
eight derivatives with yields up to 64% and up to 99% ee. Although
high enantioselectivity is achieved, improving yields and expanding
substrate scope are necessary to enhance the broader applicability
of such nitroso-based cascades. A novel asymmetric organocatalytic
synthesis toward bridged benzoxazocines using α,β -unsaturated aldehydes, anilines, and electron-deficient salicylaldehydes
was presented by Jørgensen, Albrecht and co-workers ( Scheme C).
The chiral pyrrolidine-catalyzed reaction proceeds via a three-step domino reaction consisting of condensation/Mannich-initiated
cyclization/intramolecular oxy -Michael addition ( Figure ), furnishing the
desired products in very good yields and high enantioselectivity of
up to 91% ee.
Proposed mechanism for the domino reaction presented in Scheme C.
Bridged systems represent some of the most demanding
targets
for
asymmetric domino catalysis; future advances will likely require deeper
mechanistic understanding, improved catalyst design, and enhanced
predictability of cascade behavior.
All presented examples demonstrate
the remarkable progress achieved
in enantioselective organocatalyzed domino synthesis. In the broader
quest for synthetic simplicity, such enantioselective methodologies
demonstrate how molecular complexity can be constructed in a single
operation, minimizing step count while maximizing structural elaboration.
Yet the field now faces a new phase: moving from proof-of-concept
demonstrations toward general, and scalable asymmetric domino processes.
Achieving lower catalyst loadings, broader substrate generality, and
industrial relevance will define the next generation of enantioselective
domino strategies in the quest for synthetic simplicity.

title:
Domino Strategies
in Heterocycle Synthesis: Advancing
from Organocatalysis to Photo-/Organo-Autocatalysis
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0
text:
The domino
synthesis of heteroaromatic
compounds represents a particularly
powerful strategy for the rapid assembly of conjugated and structurally
rigid frameworks that are ubiquitous in bioactive compounds, natural
products, and functional materials. ,,, In contrast to saturated
heterocycles, the construction of aromatic systems often requires
oxidative steps or elimination events, introducing additional redox
processes that may complicate catalyst turnover and sustainability
profiles. Thus, a central challenge in this area lies in balancing
cascade efficiency with redox economy, operational simplicity, and
avoidance of stoichiometric oxidants.
The organocatalyzed synthesis
of bicyclic heteroaromatic compounds
was demonstrated, for example, by the groups of Song and Chi reporting
an NHC catalyzed reaction between diones and α,β-γ,δ-diunsaturated
enals ( Scheme A). Upon carbene addition, a key step for this transformation
is a subsequent oxidation using 3,3′,5,5′-tetra- tert -butyldiphenoquinone (DPQ) for the generation of acyl
azolium intermediate which enables the following 1,6-addition. The
reaction encompasses an eight-step domino oxidation/1,6-addition/cyclizing
intramolecular acylation/isomerization/aldol reaction/decarboxylation/oxidative
aromatization process furnishing the 3-ylidenephthalides in good yields.
The remarkable coordination of eight consecutive elementary steps
within a single reaction flask highlights the conceptual elegance
of domino design. However, the requirement for stoichiometric amounts
of external oxidant DPQ (2.0 equiv) illustrates a limitation: redox-intensive
cascades may compromise atom economy and generate additional waste.
Future developments toward redox-neutral or catalytic oxidation protocols
would significantly enhance the sustainability of such heteroaromatization
strategies.
A secondary amine catalyzed synthetic route
toward substituted
quinolines was reported by the group of Hayashi ( Scheme B). Herby, di­(2-ethyl)­hexylamine was employed as an organocatalyst for
the four-step 1,6-addition/nucleophilic cyclizing addition/nucleophilic
cyclizing addition/elimination domino reaction of dicyanoalkenes with
enynals to afford the final products in good to excellent yields.
This transformation demonstrates how simple amine catalysis can trigger
complex annulation sequences leading to valuable quinoline scaffolds.
Nevertheless, expanding the substrate scope beyond electronically
activated partners and improving functional-group tolerance remain
important objectives for broader synthetic applicability. Overall,
the domino synthesis of heteroaromatic compounds vividly illustrates
the dual nature of domino chemistry: unparalleled step economy on
the one hand, but increasing mechanistic and redox complexity on the
other.
As the field advances, key challenges will include minimizing
stoichiometric
oxidants, improving catalyst turnover, enhancing scalability, and
ensuring predictable domino reaction behavior. Ultimately, the development
of redox-economical and operationally robust domino aromatization
processes will be essential for translating these elegant laboratory
demonstrations into broadly applicable industrial synthetic tools.

title:
Domino Strategies
in Heterocycle Synthesis: Advancing
from Organocatalysis to Photo-/Organo-Autocatalysis
license: This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0
section: TOTAL SYNTHESIS OF BIOACTIVE HETEROCYCLES VIA DOMINO REACTIONS
text:
In the context of total synthesis,
domino
reactions play a particularly
strategic role, as a single domino transformation can determine the
overall efficiency and practical feasibility of an entire synthetic
route. Several contributions by Tsogoeva
group have already demonstrated the integration of organocatalyzed
domino processes with one-pot strategies for the synthesis of bioactive
heteroaromatic scaffolds, including quinazolines ,- and phthalazines with antiviral and anticancer properties. Furthermore, the combination
of asymmetric organocatalyzed domino reactions with one-pot protocols
has been effectively exploited for the enantioselective multistep
synthesis of diverse heterocycles by several research groups, including
those of Jørgensen, - Hayashi, , List, and Lattanzi. Such approaches enable the rapid construction of complex
molecular frameworks while minimizing purification steps and improving
step economy. Organocatalyzed domino reactions have therefore become
valuable tools for the synthesis of key heterocyclic motifs within
complex natural products. Their utility has been demonstrated in several
total syntheses, including those of the potent cytotoxic alkaloid
camptothecin ( Scheme A) and natural product 4-dehydroxydiversonol ( Scheme B).
An important dihydroquinoline
precursor for the synthesis of the
anticancer agent camptothecin was reported by the group of Yao starting
from simple substrates via an organocatalyzed domino
reaction ( Scheme A). The pyrrolidine-catalyzed two-step
Michael addition/aldol condensation domino reaction allowed for the
formation of the dihydroquinoline derivative in 75% yield. This intermediate
can be further modified toward naturally occurring camptothecin in
13 steps. While the domino step efficiently establishes the core dihydroquinoline
scaffold, the overall sequence still requires multiple transformations,
illustrating that even highly effective domino reactions must be integrated
thoughtfully into longer synthetic plans to maximize overall step
economy.
Bräse and co-workers established an asymmetric
organocatalyzed
reaction to a precursor for the total synthesis of the natural product
4-dehydroxydiversonol ( Scheme B).
The transformation
of salicylaldehydes and senecialdehydes using
Jørgensen catalyst proceeds through a four-step Michael addition/aldol
reaction/vinylogous aldol reaction/vinylogous Michael domino process
to yield the precursor in 74%. After 5 additional steps, 4-dehydroxydiversonol
can be obtained. This example highlights the ability of asymmetric
organocatalysis to construct functionalized frameworks rapidly. Nevertheless,
further reducing catalyst loading and improving turnover numbers will
be crucial for industrial implementation.
Starting from tryptamines
and α,β -unsaturated
aldehydes, the group of MacMillan developed an enantioselective organocatalytic
method for the synthesis of pyrroloindolines using a chiral imidazolidinone
catalyst. These scaffolds represent valuable structural motifs for
the total synthesis of the natural product (-)-flustramine
B ( Scheme C). Seven derivatives were generated with excellent
yields and enantioselectivities of up to 99% ee via a two-step Michael addition/intramolecular cyclization domino reaction.
Later on, MacMillan and co-workers also developed an enantioselective
approach to an important precursor of (-)-minovicine ( Scheme D). With the use of a chiral amine catalyst, 3-butyn-2-one
and a vinyl indole derivative form the product via a three-step [4 + 2] cycloaddition/beta-elimination/heteroconjugate
addition domino reaction with a yield of 72% yield and 91% ee. The
success of these strategies shows how asymmetric organocatalyzed domino
processes enable rapid access to complex bioactive frameworks; however,
extending such methodologies to more structurally diverse natural
product families remains an open frontier.
Recently, a TsCl-mediated
reaction toward a synthetically valuable
4-quinolone derivative was reported by the group of Xu ( Scheme E). Chromone-3-carboxaldehydes and amines undergo
a five-step condensation/Michael addition/ring-opening sulfonation/tautomerization/intramolecular
nucleophilic substitution domino reaction to afford precursors for
quinolone-based antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, perfloxacin and
norfloxacin, as well as for the cystic fibrosis drug ivacaftor, in
very good yields of up to 90%.
Although domino reactions efficiently
deliver pharmaceutically
relevant intermediates, the use of activating reagents such as TsCl
raises considerations regarding reagent economy and waste generation.
Future developments aimed at milder, catalytic activation modes would
